hibition in that city, assisted by his trainers, young
Donnelly and Jack Madden, as well as local box-
ers. He will be back this morning, when the
following communication from Christol, received

at this office yesterday, will doubtless receive his
| attention:
To the Editor of the Globe-Democrat:

CnicaGo, March 10, 1875.—Dear Sir: I have
seen in your honorable journal the conversation
with Mr. Tom Allen, in which he desires to back
Bauer to wrestle against me. If M. Bauer is will-
ing to come to Chicago, lam ready to meet him.
I will be in Chicago for six weeks, and itis beter
for me to wrentie bere than to go to St. Louis.

Yours respectfully. ANDRE CHRISTOL,

Champion of France.

In view of the fact that Allen brought Baner out

here from Boston, on the assertion of a Well-

_ known Chicago friend that Christol would wrestle

| him here, the above epistle looks very much as
though Andre wanted to back out. He doubtless
appreciates the fact that Bauer is neither a Car-
teron nora Rigal, but the most scientific wrestler
in the world, as his record proves. Bauer has
never suffered defeat in this country, but has in
turn defeated Miller, Vanderdecken, Christol,
Regnierand Heyster. InChristol’s late match
with Rigal at Chicago, the latter claims that he
was very unfairly treated, and that he lost the
match through the ignorance of the referee, who
did not understand the rules of Greco-Roman
wrestling. Can this be the reason why Christol is
so anxious to wrestle there? :

After the receipt of Christol’s letter a reporter
hunted up Bauer and notified him of its contents.
Bauer appeared surprised, but stated that he
would take no action in the matter until Allen ar-
rives to-day. Whatthat action will be remains to
be seen.

In connection with Greco-Roman wrestling in
this country a great deal has been said in regard
to hippodroming, and much of it is doubless just.
Bauer has, however, a clear record, and his
friends are legion from the Atlantic to the Pacific,
for the reason that he prefers reputation to
money. This is demonstrated by the fact that he
has never lost a match, and as he has never
met his equal, and thousands of dollars have been
put up on the result of these contests in San Fran-
cisco, Boston and New York, had he been willing
to sell out to the clique of gamblers that controls
each of those cities, he could now be possessed of
a large fortune.

Since the above was written atelegram has been
received at <Allen’s, stating that Chicago men
have been found who will back Christol to wrestle
here, and that one of them will arrive in a day or
twe to bind the match, if Bauer and Allen are
willing to have it goon. To this a reply was sent |
that Allen would send a definite answer to-mor- |
row, which will doubtless be in the affirmative. |

title: Tom Allen Boxing Exhibition Announced
text:
AGAIN VICTORIOUS.
———__
Prof. Bauer Beats the German Champion
! .
| at His Own Game.

A Splendid Exhibition of Strength and
Skill at the Temple Last Evening.
——

The second wrestling match between Prof.
Bauer and Herr Heygster for $250 aside came
off last night at the Temple before a crowded
house. There was considerable excitement
Manitest on accountot the terms of the match,
which were thatthe first fallssould be wres-
tled for according to German andthe second
according to Greco-Roman rules. It was be-
lieved that this would give Heyysterthe ad-
‘Vantage, because the German style is mainly
anu exhibition of strength, und there is no
coubt regarding his superiority in this respect
to Bauer, who relics in a great measure upon
| his skill ane activity. 4
| Tom Allen,the champion pugilist, introduced
the men to the audience at twenty-three min-
utes past § o’clock. Leon Schuler appearing as
umpire’ for Bauer and Carl Boehm tor Heyg-
ster.
| Atthe start the contestants forget that the
first bout was uccording to German rules, and
| had to make afreshstart. They began by a
series of wrist grips, which were continued tun-
til Heygster got a left arm body hold on Baner,
when he tried hard to get both arms around
his body and secure a lock, but Bauer turned
the tables on him, and gained the very lock
Heygster was striving for. He lost it, how-
ever, and some very clever marncuvring wus
done, Heygster at length setting
2 very good body hoid, which
Bauer broke by main strength = aiter
a hard struggle. Quick changes and inter-
aster of holds followed, Bauer being com-
pelled to wipe his hands frequently on his
trunks, owing to the perspiration which flowed
so treely from the ponderous Gerinan. The
bout throughout was fought desperately.
Heygster at one time had a body grip, side
hold, but lost it. He then forced Bauer to his
knees, but it was only fora part of a second,
‘the latter gaining his feet with the agility of a
eat. Heygster on several occasions also secured
good — shoulder locks, but Bauer
invariabiy fought until he treed
himself. At length the bout was_ ended
by Bauer getting a fair body-grip and forcing
Heygster to the carpet on his side, when he
rolled him over, threw his weight across his
chest and the shoulders of the German gave
way and touched the carpet. Bauer was loud-
ly cheered. This bout lasted 18 minutes.

An interinission ot twenty minutes was then
taken. During the recess Tom Allen an-
nounced that at the close of the performance a
silver belt, which Bauer's friends had gotten
uptor bim as the champion Greco-Roman
ga of America, would be presented to

iim.

When time was caHed for_the second bout,
which wus wrestled according to Grwco-RKo-
man rules, Bauer bounded upon the stage
looking as rosy as a girl. Heyyster followed,
but with anything but an elastic step. This
bout was fierce trom the start, and jno time
was lost by either man. Ali the tricks known
were practised by each wrestler. Bauer got
his favorite neck-lock, baving his left arm
around Heygster’s ueck and beth hands
clasped under his chin. It can easily be seen
that this is a terrible grip and # mun
can easily be choked while in such
a position, yet Bauer held his burly antag-
onist thus securely locked for seveyal minutes
and finally forced him to his kneés, wheu he
took a good back hold and raised the 300
pounds of fiesh off the stage in
his arms, but lost his grip,
when MHeygster gained his feet. In en-
dedvoring ‘ulterwards to get another good
hold, Bauer received an ugly knock in the
head, just between the eyes from Heygster’s
left shoulder, but instead of unnerving him it
seemed to madden himand he swiftly gained
a side hold, made Heygster tall to his
knees, and then secured a body
grip and ended the bout by rolling
Heygster over on the stage until both shoul-
ders touched the carpet. This decided the
contest in Bauer’s favor, andthe audience at
once set up a tremendous roar.

Bauer was called out, when the silver belt
alluded to above was presented to him. '

It is not likely that Heygster will again essay
to tackle such a man as Bauer, who is vastly
his superior. as a wrestler. Bauer leaves
soon for California, unlessa match is arranged
between him and Maj. McLaughlin of Detroit.

title: Tom Allen and Joe Goss Championship Fight Set for September
text:
THE THUMPERS.
Joe Goss and Tom Allen at Thoir Train-
ing Quarters.
‘
Current Gossip Concerning the Fight for
the Championship.

The fight which isto take place in September
for a big bundle anu the championship of Amer-
ica, between those noted exponents of the fistic
art, Tom Allen and Joe Goss, continues to create
much comment in sporting circles, and opinion is
pretty evenly dividea as to whether the ‘‘mill’’ is
to be decided on its merits, or whether it-is a
neatly put-up job to lure the unwary into paying
steep prices for excarsion tickets to witness a
sham battle in which one or the other of the prin-
cipals will at the proper moment acknowledge
himself vanquished.

The match was broughtabout in a rather peculiar
way. It appears that wigile Mace was sojourning
in England, prior to.his last visit to America, the
report gained credence that Allen was so very fat
that it would be an utter impossibility for him to
again get in condition to fight. Mace, who is as
shrewd as he is clever with his fists, thought that
it would be a good idea to match Goss against
Allen, and as Joe had never been to this country,
should the match be made he would ‘prove a pay-
ing card in the way of sparring exhibitions.

NEGOTATIONS
were entered into, and as Allen was anxious to
have ashy at his old antagonist, with whom he
had fought a draw in three rings, there was very
little difficalty in coming to terms, and when the
men met at Cincinnati, for the purpose of draw- |
ing up articles, the documents were signed in
short order. At that meeting Goss was very |
much surprised to find that Allen was the picture |
of health,.and not at all corpulent. Shortly after
the making of the match, Goss and Mace dis-
solved partnership. The men were filling a spar- |

cause of the quarrel was a ‘‘kick’’ made by Joo
because he did not receive as much money for his
services asthe ‘‘gvpsy.’’ Mace tlien declined

Goss was thrown on his own resources. He was
astranger in a country where Allen is looked
upon as almost invincible, had ten weeks training
before him, which necessarily would entail a
heavy cxpense, and half of his share of the stakes
stullto produce. Where this money is to come
from is what gives the match
A FISHY LOOK. -

Bir Joseph, immediately after severing his con-
nection with Mace, went into training at Forest
Home, a delightful retreat a few miles outside of
Cincinnati, which is presided over by Eph Hol-
land, the Mike McDonald of Cincinnati. A great
deal of work had to be accomplished in the way
of ridding himself of superfluous flesh, as nine
year’s idleness had caused the pugilist to assume
aldermanic proportions. When the match was
made Joe weightd 210 pounds. To-day, under
the mentorship of Jimmy Cusick, who prepared
Heenan for his fight with Sayers, Goss pulls the
beam at 175, having reduced himself two anda
half stone by the hardest kind of work. This re-
sult has been brought about by judicious dieting,
long walks, dumb-bell exercise and cold baths.
He bas experienced no annoyance whatever from
the change of climate or strange water, and since
his arrival in America has enjoyed the best of

rae Why didn’t Goss beat him then? Is he

ct closer to bim, he might have a better chance.

ie did do better, but Mace was too much for him

Crxcrxwati, September 6.—There is

Will write you full particulars to-
night. Publish this in evening papers.

t Tom KELLY.

Crncrynati, Sept. 7.—The point

At seven o'clock. The fight begins at

First Round—Both men spar cauti-
ously, Goss falling into Allen’s corner.
The sparring is rather tiresome for the
crowd.

First Blood for Allen,
And a clinch and a fall, Goss on top.
Time, seven minutes.

Second Round—Allen strikes Goss on

for Alien.

At this point

Capt. Frank Wood, with the Coving-

been carried past the fighting grounds
by the conductor. Capt. Wood stopped
the train three miles past the point, and
the militia marched back, arriving at 8
o'clock.

Fourth Round—Exchanges fast and
heavy. Allen, by a terrible blow on
Goss’ neck, knocked him down. Time,
three minutes.

Fifth Rounc—After considerable spar-

ring, Allen struck out and fell short on
Goss’ face. In return he received a blow
in the stomach. This did net
appear to worry Allen, and he returned
heavily on Goss’ body, and a fearful one
on the damaged eye. Goss retaliated,
and, after sharp half-arm fighting, Goss
went down to avoid punishment.

Sixth Round—Both men promptly to
the scratch, Allen leading off, getting in
on Goss’ face. He repeated this, get-
ting in another blow on Goss’ damaged

»right eye. Allen finally fizhts Goss
down.

Seventh Round—When time was
called the Covington Light Guards ap-
peared ard the fight ceased.

W.G. Lobban, aidto the Governor,

And advised that the fight immediately
cease. Hoiland stated he wasa law

seven rounds had been fought.

Holland declares he will make the
men fight out the tight before they reach
Cincinnati to-night. Neither of the
men is mucb punished.

After being dispersed by the militia a
second ring was formed a short distance
below Walton, in Boone County. The
Sheriff was present, but had not sufi-_
cient posse to interfere.

Kighth Round—Goss threw Allen,
though the former was severely pua-
ished.

Ninth Round—Goss forced fighting.
Allen finished round for himself with
heavy blows on Goss’ face.

Tenth Round—Heavy blows exchanged.
Goss forced on the ropes, The fighters
were parted by seconds.

Eleventh Round—Goss leads the fight-
ing—the hardest fighting in this round.

Twelfth Round—Both of Goss’ eyes
badly swolien. Allen knocks Goss
down,

Thirteenth Round—Terrific blow on
Goss’ mouth. Goss on his knees.

Fourteenth Round—Goss threw Allen
by clinching. Foul claimed, but not
allowed.

Fifteenth Round—Heavy, close
figiting; both badly punished.

Sixteenth Round—In chasing Allen
about the ring Goss slips ard falls.

Seventeenth lNound—Goss knocked
over the repes.

Kighteenth Round—Goss plants a
stinger on Allen’s body. Close fizht-

-ing. Foul claimed by Guss, but not al-
lowed,

Nineteenth Round—Goss slips and
falis. Close fighting.

Twenticth Round—Both fall.

Twenty-first Round—In close fighting
Goss falls and is struck by Allen while
cn his knees. A foul claimed and al-
lowed. Fight decided in favor of Goss
at11:50a. m. Alien shows little orno
injury about the face; Goss terribly
beaten, almost blind. Time of fizht—
Cne hour and fifty-two minutes.

Allen Arrested,

CINCINNATI, O., Sept. 7.—Two trains
from the tight to-dey arrived at Newport

ities, and Tom Allen arrested.

‘Tom for $1,500 eaide, but at the last moment his |
heart failed him and he did not put in an appear-
ance. After considerable wrangling, it was at

Joe Goss
was born in Northampton, England, November
6, 1836. Heis consequently in his Sash arr
noosh but fora slight Delaness, he would not
look his age by five years. His father kept alarge
slhoe-making establishment, and at the proper
age he Icarned cordwaining. It was. this expe-
nece, perhaps, that bas enubled him te las? so
well in bis fights, and to welt the larger portion of
his opponents, causing them to peg out well
tasted. In his Youth he proved a tough bit of
stuff, ‘as many of his townsmen have cause to
know, and, carly developing a decided predilec-
tion for the ring, he found friends without trouble
to back him for £5 against George Ayers, of Long
Berkley. He was then but nineteen years of age,
but he beat Ayers to a stand-still in one hour and
thirty minutes.

He next met Jem Rickerson for £10 a side. Just

“when Meow f was within his grasp the police in-
terfered and stopped the mill: Goss received £17
of the stake money the next day to consent to
make the match a draw.

Joe waé next matched against Jack Rooke, and
fought him in the same ring where Tom Sayers
oe the ‘‘comether’’ on poor Bob Brettle. This

attle was for £25 a side, and was won cleverly

Patchet, of Wolverhampton, thought he  geark

Is didn't take Joe long to convince

a quick me fighter, and his

Posh Price, one of the best men who everpulled

They fought for £25 aside, and, though —-

£400 and the championship. Joe had at last gone

Goss nowcame to the conclusion that if he

Hantered to meet Mace ina sixteen-foot ring, he

His next match was for £100 a side, and his op-

As soon as the ring was ready, the men were
notified, and at precisely 6:45 o’clock Goss, at-
tended by Johnny Dwyer and his trainer, Jim
Cusick, made his appearance at the ring-side, and
modestly shied his castorinto the ring. He was
received with afew cheers, and, walking around
the ring, he selected a shady corner for his tem-
‘porary quarters. A chair was placed in the cor-
ner, upon which he sat while bis fighting shoes
were put on. At 7:03 Allen, accompanied by
Tom Kelly and char bal of st. Louis, put in
his appearance. To rew his slouch hat over
the ropes, but the wind caught it and it fell ont-
side the ring. This. considered a bad omen by
old-school fighters, who will now be more. posi-
tive in their delusion than ever before. A chair
was handed to Allen, upon which he seated him-
self while the prelifhinaries were being arranged.
Eph. Holland, who was Master of Ceremohies,now
called ‘‘Blacky’’ Edwards into the ring to notify
the men that they had just thirty minutes in
which to choose a referee, and that in tne event
of their failing to agree upan A suitable person
for the position, the duty of naming him devolved
onbim. The frst man named for the eer was
Johnny neaee the light-weight fighter, but
Johnny declined to serve, though mutually ac-
ceptable to the men and londly|called for by the
crowd. Dad Ryan was next nimed, but be said
he would not serve for twice the amount of the
battle-money. Jack Conway was next voted for
by the cried, which seemed to have an idea that
it bad an authoritative voice in the matter. Just
here Theowaud Bauer, who was one of Goss" es-
pecial adherents, and slightly under the influence
of liquor, got into a fight with Pat Mulloy about a
place at the ring-side. From words they came to
a clinch, which caused quite acommotion. Mal-
loy and a man named Jones downed Bauer
and while on his back one of them kicked
him in the face. Red Leary rushed to
Bauer’s assistance, and ina moment he had his
assailants CR yay beer down the hilllike scared
sheep. While the stampede was in progress some
one trea a pistol, the bal] fram which struck Mal-
loy in the posterior, inflicting a slight flesh
wound. This row was the only one that occurred
at the river side during the fight, and was soon
guelled. Atthe expiration of balf an hour the
men had not agreed upon a referee, and Blacky
Edwards semen kph Holland aschicf function-
ary. Eph positively declined the proffered honor,
stating that he was the triend of both parties,
and had been selected by them to nanage the af-
fair. ‘‘Somuchthe more reason for your serv-
ing,’’ said Dad Ryan. fhe crowd roared and
howled for Holland to serve, and Dad Ryan gave
him another talking to, at the end of which he
suddenly said: ‘*Very weil, I will serve, then,
and I notify you men before you put up your
hands that! will give the fight to the best man.’’

Allen and Goss now advanced to the center of
the ring. where Joe tossed up a copper to decide
who should have choice of corners. Allen won
the flip and took the southwest corner, that being
the highest ground. They now commenced to
sirip, being assisted by their seconds. They
bad donned their fighting togs in the cars and had
their ordinary street clothes over them. When
partially undressed, Goas stepped over into
Allen's corner with arollof greeubacks, of the
value of $1,000, and offered to Let it on the reault,
Allen, nothing loth, produced an equal amount,
and the bet was made. Jack Brown was Goss’
umpire, and Dad Ryan officiated in the same
capacity for Allen. John Leary now offered
to wager §1,000 that Goss would win the
fight, and said something about the match
being between Cincinnati and St. Lauis.
‘‘Hits the Heaet hagin the West,’’ yelled
abold Britieher. ‘‘It's not a match between
Cincinnati aud st. Louis, or of the Kast against
the Weet, butone between Tom Allen and Joe
Goss,'* said Tom Kelly. This remark evoked a
round of applause. cf this time the men were
poms and presented a beautiful appearance.

SJoth wore white flannel! knee-breeches and white
stockings. Goss’ colors were while, “ey a broad
blue border, striped and cross-barred with white,
Allen wore a small American flag for his colors,
and the wrists of both wen were encircled with
strengthening plasters. As soon as the last rab-
bing down was concluded, Eph Holland said,
‘*Are you ready?"’ ‘'Yes,’’ was the ip eg of
both men. ‘‘Shake hands then,’’ said Eph, and
amoment later the ‘‘six hands across’’ of men
and seconds was given, and the seconds returned
to their corners, while the men stood up at 7:32 for

THE FIGHT.

Round 1—Allen was the tallest, leaviest and
longest man in the reach, and in additivn to these
advantages, was four years younger than his op-
ponent. Goss looked compact and rugged. The
skin of his face was as tight as a drum-bead, and
both looked in tip-top fettle. As they threw
themselves into position the disparity in their
seizes Was more apparent than real, Allen weigh-
ing 174 pounds, while Goss wus fully 165. It was
a comical sight, and about as appropriate a com-
mentary on the present status of the prize-ring in
this country as could be made, to sce two old
bald headed men, whose surviving locks were as
gray as a badger, sianding up in aring to contest
for the championship of America. Goss held his
left hand rather low,with his right well across his
mark, Allen kept his-left well extended, his right
covering his body and his head ‘thrown
back out of danger. It was at once seen
by Allen’s position that he meant to act
on the defensive and make a waiting fight of it.
Goss fiddled away for a iead for fully a moment,
but could find no opening. He then gradually
worked around to the other side of Allen, and
tried to get him to lead; Tom was toe wary, and
refased to be drawn out. Four times were these
tactics repeated, and four times did Allen’e can-
tion defeat them. After fully five minutes had
been put to waste in these maneuvers, Tom saw
his opening, and dashed out bis left, catching
Goss slightly on the mouth. A slight show of
biood followed, and Allen claimed drat blood.’’
Goss licked it awh with his tongue, and the
claim was not allowed. Allen's partisans cheered
him loudly. After some more cautious fiddilihg,
both countered on the nose, afler which they
broke away. Both cautious, though Goss was
making the pace. Joe seemed disinclined to run
against Allen’s left, and Tom seemed to have a
reverential respect for Goss’ right. At length
Tom ageis stabbed Joe in the mouth. Goss rushed
ip, and they engaged in ashort half-arm rally, in
which Jack was as good as bis master. It was
ended by_a clinch, in which Allien was thrown
heavily. Time, 13 minutes.

Round 2—Goss worked like a beaver in his at-
tempts to induce Allen to take the initiative, but
his efforts were futile, for Tom had made up his
mind to act on the defensive, and he was not to be
coaxed into leading. The men indulged in along
bout of SparTing. which was ended by Alillen
planting alittle oneon Goss’ ear; Goss, in the
attempt to counter, slipped down, but instantly
jumped up and resumed the round. Joe got a
chance and gave Allen atap on the nose, but the
blow lacked steam. Counter-bitting, Allen barely
on the breast, ity tel eens itinon Allen’s chin.
area TE abs a his distance cleverly, let fy with
his left on Goss’ mouth, and this time a tiny
stream of the ruby appeared. (First blood for
Allen.) He led again with the left, but was
short. Goss planted a good thump on Allen’s
breast and Tom countered on his mouth. A
rally, in which Allen goton to Goss’ nose, and
the latter retaliated on the mouth. Allen caught
Joe on the chin and “ear knocked him down,
Joe planted heavily on Allen's neck and napped
alittleone in return on the right cre: which
brought blood. A rally, in which Allen gave
Goss fits, and Joe slipped down to avoid punish-
ment. Time, 12 minutes.

Round 3—Goss' friends now began to chaff Tom,
saying, ‘‘1 thought you were a soing te lick him
in fifteen minutes.’’ Joe slapped Tom onthe
right ear, and Alien missed the return. Tom got
a pretty one on the breast, but paid it back, with
interest on the nose, Joe missed a well-intended
left-hander, but paneer and planted one on Al-
Jlen’schin. Arally, a clinch anda fall over the
ropes, Allen under.

Round: 4—Goss gave Tom a good one on
the car. Allen retaliated on the mouth.
A break-away, a pause and a walk-around. Al-
len planted a sockdologer on Goss’ mouth, knock-
ing him down. Aas Goss sat on the aronnes wait-
ing to be picked up by his seconds, he applauded
Allen’s hit. Herea “rg of ‘*The militia are com-
ing!’’ waa raised; and, sure enough, a company
of soldiers was seen marching along the railroad

Round 5—Allen missed a left-hander, and Goss
failed to counter. The soldiers by this time were

of the spectators, who fled precipitately from the
ine side, taking shelter bebind the hay-stacks

but in making a third hit for the body he nappeda
terrible Smash on the face. Goss missed a wicked
right-hander, which Tom éluded by jumping
away. Arally, which was ended by Goss knock-
ing Tom down. Mr. W.G. Lobben, Acting Ad-
jutant General of the State of Kentucky, now ad-
vanced to the ring and informed re Holland that
the fight must be stopped, but little attention was
paid to his behest. *

Round 6—Allien got in a terrible right-handed
smash on the face, Goss bleeding like a stuck pig.
A rally, a clinch, and Ajlen thrown.

Round 7—The men advanced to the seratch and
commenced sparring, when Mr. Lobben notified |
Mr, Holiand tbat unless the Agnes was stopped in |
two minutes, he would make ius men fire on the

ules.

It now looked as ifthe fight would have to be
made a draw; but Eph Hollend angrily denounced

8 bit, and announced that he would make them

The crowd was ordered on board the cars, and

tween John Leary und Barney Aaron on one side

the other. It resulted in Malloy’s having a terri*
ble head put on him, The train then moved down

ern Railroad. Atl0:45 a.m. Goss shied his castor
intothering. Allen followed a moment later.
Goss was Taaly marked on the forehead -and
cheek, and his right eye showed signs of closing.
Allen, with the exception ofa slight scratch on

Round 8—It was just Jl o’clock when the men

_ Allen stopped it; he was again short with the left,

Allen, and ordered the fight to goon. Allen

short with the left, a second endeavor was more

Counter bits, Goss on.the nose, Tom on the face;
Joe planted a good one on the body and dvdged :
the return. Goss hit Allenon the right cheek,

Goss rushed in and bit Allen ont’:e body, caught

Time, nine minutes,

-. Round $—Goss missed his left, and, as he fol-

R anted a terrible right-hander on Allea’s body. -

bis blow sounded all round the ring, and was
hailed with cheers by Goss’ adherents. Goss
worked away at Allen again, but just as he got

Joe reproachfully said, ‘*Do you want me now to
come all the ste 8 again?’’ Allen laughed and
said, ‘'That will be all Mgnt, Joe.’’ Allen let
him have alittle one on the nose. Goss, after
him, gave him a terrible right-hander on the ribs,
Alien returning a right-hander spank on the face.
Goss gotin a good left-hauder on the face, but,
endeavoring to repeat the dose, was countered

Tom again banged away at Goss’ badeye, Joe

fecily bewildered. Allen or fell fiom the

deavored to throw himseif on the ground he gave

the fall Goss was under-

Iound 10—Goss hit Tom on the eye; Allen coun-
tered cleverly on the face. Allen gave Goss a

ribly on the body inreturn. Allen led with the

As Allen returned to the center of the ring Mrs.

Round 11—Offers to bet $100 to $75 on Goss were
now made but found no takers. Joe missed

turned tailand ranaway. As he lurned Goas fol-
lowed him, and caught him a neat left-iander on
the mehteye. Joe again planted on the face,and
also got in a good oneonthe body. Allen ran
away. Joe followed him up, and Tom led we ?
another foot race. Goss ewe him a good one o
the enr—Allen for the first time bleeding. Joe
planted bis left on the right eye. Counter bits on
the jaw. Goss again piauied a good one on the
eye; Allen slow in return; a rally and clinch;

Round 12—Goss' lefteye was now swollen ter-
ribly. In working round the ring Allen got Goss
in a corner, and, : iy as he was about to go for
Goss, Barney Aaron, who saw that bis man was
im danger, claimed that Allen bad something in
his ty 4 hand. The referee ordered Allen to
open his hand, and the claim was found ground-
lese. Goss went for Allen's face ard body, but
missed both. A long ppell of sparring. Goss
planted his left on the ribs; Allen return-
edon the face. A reguiar slaughtering-match
now took place in the middle of the ring. Allen

ound 13—As the men came together Allen
anxiously looked into Goss’ eyes, a if to see how
much daylight remained in them. Joe stabbed
Allen witb the lefton Fi ht eal and was poul-
ticed in return on the batiright eye. Allen saw
his opening, and, gathering himself into shape,
gave Joe a terrible left-hander on the nose, and —
repeated the dose before he could get away. Goss
went for the body right and left, and Allen ran
away. As they came together, Goss planted his

little, edragte rh wes remarked, ‘‘That's
right, Joe; go for him; he doesn't like the gafl!’"’
Allen replied, ‘‘I'd like to know who does, if he
can avoid it.’’ Allen planted one in on the

Round 14—Goss missed a left-hander intended
for the face, bat succeeded in planting bis right
on the body. Joe next planted bis teft on Allen’s
nose. Tom rushed in, and a half-armed rall
ensned. Tom ducked to avoid sede ccretee anti
Goss caught him around the neck. In the strug- .
gie for the fall, which was wou by Goss, Allen

Round 15—The round opened with long spar-
Ting. Allen missed witb the left and Goss coun-
tered heavily on the body, and Allen again turned
tailand ran away. Joe succeeded in getting a
light tap on Allen’s face. Toin returned the ¢om-
ere by planting a fearful smasher on Joe’s—

vad eye. Tom planted right and left on the eyes,

and then a terrible slogging bout began. Allen ,

Round 16—Allen ted, but missed. Joe’s counter

Round 17—Allen napped it in the face. Both
rnshed in for slogging, and, after about two.

Round 18—Goss’ face presented a terrible ap-
fig ere His eet eye was almost closed, and |

is left was fast following suit. His forehead was
all bumps and lumps, and there wasa nie :
his left cheek-bone as big as a goose egg. om

-hit him im the face. Goss wave it to him mghtand |

Round 19—This was arattling slog from the

ing, and fought Goss to his knees, and while in

Aaron claimed foul, but the referee décided that

ney Aaron was unstintedin his denunciation of

public.’* He was ultimately pacified in a meis-@ |
urg. and time was calle for

ound 20—Goss was going blind very fast. A
little rally and a clinch, and Allen thrown,

Round 21, and Last—It was seen that, without
an accident, itwas impossible for Goss to win,
though the brave fellow, as game as ever, took

As soon as he faced his man he went for him right |
and left, but Allen outfought him at every point, |
and rushed him off his legs. Just as Goss fell on
his posterior Tom struck him green | on the
forehead. The blow evidently bad left Tom’s
shoulder before Goss etruck the ground, but when |
it alighted it was clearly a foul. Without waiting
for Goss’ umpire to claim the foul, Holland ex-—
claimed, ‘‘1 give this ight to Goss on the ground ©
that he has been struck afoul blow."’ Goss’
friends hailed the decision with joy, while Allen’s |
denounced it asafraud. Allen stood in the mid-
dle of the ring, protesting against the decision, :

cumstances of the Battle.

As soon as the ring was ready, the men were
notified, and at precisely 6:45° o’clock Goss, at-
tended by Johnny Dwyer and his trainer, Jim
Cusick, made his appearance at the ring-side, and
modestly shied his castorintothe ring. He was
received with afew cheers, and, walking around
the ring, he selected ashady corner for his tem-
‘porary quarters. A chair was placed in the cor-
ner, upon which he sat while bis fighting shoes
were put on. At 7:03 Allen, accompanied by
Tom Kelly and John Ryan, of st. Louis, put in
his appearance. Tom threw his slouch hat over
the ropes, but-the wind caught it and it fell ont-
side the ring. This is considered a bad omen by
old-school fighters, who will now be more. posi-
tive in their delusion than ever before. A chair
was handed to Allen, upon which he seated him-
self while the preliminarics were being arranged.
Eph. Holland, who was Master of Ceremohies,now
called ‘‘Blacky'’ Edwards into the ring to notify
the men that they had just thirty minutes in
which to choose a referee, and that in tne event
of their failing to agree upan a suitable person
for the position, the duty of naming him devolved
onhim. The frst man named for the retin was
Johuny Keating, the light-weight fighter, but
Johnny declined to serve, though mutually ac-
ceptable to the men and londly called for by the
crowd. Dad Ryan was next named, but be said
he wonld not serve for twice the amount of the
my tmineny Jack Conway was next voted for
by the crowd, which seemed to have an idea that
it bad an authoritative voice in the matter. Just
here Theovaud Bauer, who was one of Goss’ es-
pecin! adherents, and ore under the influence
of liquor, got into a fight witb Pat Malloy about a)
place at the ring-side. From words they came to
a clinch, which caused quite acommotion. Mal-
loy and a man named Jones downed Bauer
and while ‘on his back one of them kicked
him in the face. Red Leary rushed to
Bauer’s assistance, andina moment he had his
assailants scampering down the hilllike scared
bee! While the stampede was in progress some
one fired a pistol, the bal) fram which struck Mal-
loy in the posterior, inflicting a slight flesh
wound. This row was the only one that occurred
at the river side during the fight, and was soon .
quelled. Atthe expiration of balf an hour the

men had not agreed oy a referee, and Biacky
Edwards pamed Keb Holland .as chief function-
ary. Eph positively declined the proffered honor,
stating that he was the triend of both parties,
and bad been sclected by them to manage the af-
fair. ‘‘Somuchthe more reason for your serv-
ing,’’ said Dad Ryan. fhe crowd roared and
howled for Holland to serve, and Dad Ryan gave
him another eet | to, at the end of which he
suddenly said: ‘‘Very well, I will setve, then,
and I notify you men before you put vp your
hands that I will give the fight to the best man,’’

Allen and Goss now advanced to the center of
the ring. where Joe tossed up a copper to decide
who should have choice of corners. Allen won
the flip and took the southwest corner, that being
the highest ground. They now commenced to
strip, being assisted by their seconds. Fe |
had donned (rete fighting togs in the cars and ha
their ordinary street clothes over them. When
partially undressed, Goas stepped over into
Allen's corner with arollof greeiubacks, of the
value of $1,000, and offered to Let it on the result,
Allen, nothing loth, produced an equal amount,
and the bet was made. Jack Brown was Gosa’
umpire, and Dad Ryan officiated in the same
capacity for Allen. John Leary now offered
to wager $1,000 that Goss would win the
fight, and said something about the match
being between Cincinnati and St. Louis,
‘‘Hits the Heaet hagin the West,’’ yelled
abold Britieher. ‘‘It's not a match between
Cincinnati and st. Louis, or of the East against
the Weet, butone between Tom Allen and Joe
Goss,’’ said Tom Kelly. This remark evoked a
round of applause. <i this time the men were

eecled, and | ig pag a beautiful appearance.

stockings. Goss’ colors were white, dy broad

Allen wore a small American flag for his colors,
and the wrists of both men were encircled with

bing down was concluded, Eph Holland said
“*Are you ready?"’ ‘‘Yes,’’ was the respopes of

amoment later the ‘‘six hands across’* of men

to their corners, while the men stood up at 7:32 for

Round 1—Allen was the tallest, heaviest and
longest an in the reach, and in addition to these
advantages, was four years younger than his op-
ponent. Goss looked compact and rng Spe The
skin of his face was as tight as a drum-bead, and

themselves into position the coor peed n their |

ing 174 pounds, while Goss waa fully 165. 1t waa)
acomical sight, and about as appropriate a com-_
mentary on the present status of the prize-ring in

bald- headed men, whose surviving locks were as
gray a4 a badger, oe up in a ring to contest

mark, Alien kept his left well extended, his right
covering his yody and his head thrown
back out of danger. It was at once seen
by Allen's position that he meant to act
on the defensive and make a waiting fight of it.
Goss Giddled away for a iead for fully a moment,

worked around to the other aide of Allen, an
tried to get him to lead; Tom was toe wary, and

Round 2—Goss worked like a beaver in his at-

on the breast, i rry ee it inon Allen's chin.
yey! as tap «| his distance cleverly, let fly with

short. Goss planteda good thump on Allen’s

rally, in which Allen goton to Goss’ nose, and

Joe planted heavily on Alfen's neck and napped

Round 3—Goss' friends now began to chaff Tom,
esr ‘*I thought you were a going to lick him

ure, and time was called for

naeee 21, and Last—It was seén that, without

How He Looks and Talks--No More P. R.
for Him.

Tom Allen is back. The man who licked Joe
Goss, and who was cheated out of a fair fight by

the New York delegation that bet on Goss, ar-

rived in our city yesterday morning, and, from all
accounts, will make his home here henceforward.
During the day he visited his many friends, who
were anxiously awaiting. his return. Those who
baunt Tom Kelly's saw him first, and after that
he looked in at Jim Gayin’s, at Charley Henry’s,
and one or two other places, taking his dinner at
the Olive Street, where he isa registered, by the
way. In the evening he visited the Comique, and
was waited on by all the boys. It was a shake of
the hand with this one, a little chat with another,
8 drink with the third, a private confab with the
next, and a square talk with the GLoBE-DEMoO-
CRAT reporter.

. HOW DOES ALLEN LOOK?

He looked the very picture of physical health.
Hair just cropping out again, showing the gray,
however, a fact noticed by his friends. Nota
sign of punishment on his face, which is just be-
ginning to show the ‘‘moss’’ of a mustache, and
the first outgrowths of whiskers and beard. Lips
enregle. Hands O. K., the mght one holding a
gold-headed cane. Tom wore a dark hat, dark
frock-coat, light pants, cut close. You couldn’t
help noticing his small feet. Present weight, 180
ponnas.

There was little about him to betray the pugilist.
A certain sans souct alr indicated the man who
had, by dint of physical prowess, won a moral
regard from his fellows. He was evidentiy at
home, and made others feel so in his presence.
If he has ever been accused of rough talk, it didn’t
show last night. His accent told his nationality, |
but the choice of his words did him credit. He
had apparently forgotten that any newspaper had
ever spoken of him derogatively. No, not quite |
that, for the sting of the New York Clipper wasn’t |

quite gone yet; but, anyhow, the peer of Mace
and King was firmly convinced of the ability and |
disposition of the GLOBE-DEMOCRAT man to tell
the truth. !
THE TALK.

**Tfow about the stakes?’’ was the first question
asked.

‘‘Well, I attached the stakes the night of the
fight. They are all right.’’

‘*‘ButI saw in some paper or other that Goss
was showing the money he received from the
stakeholder and the money he giined as bets.
How's that?’’ r

‘*All he got was $500 and his expenses to Fn-
gland. He was to have left New York for England
on Saturday. Iguess he’s gone now. Stakes are
all right in Edwards’ hands.”

**Who’s your attornéy in the suit?’’

‘‘A man named Root and Gov. Carlisle, of Cov-
ington.’’

**Will you sue in Ohio or Kentucky?’’

‘*In Ohio, of course (with a sly twinkle). I
wouldn't stand much show in Kentucky.’’

**And the suit comes off when?’’

** About the 25th of this month. I'm going over
again to eee to it.”” .

**Now, that you are out of the ring—I suppose
hat’s'so, isn’t it? (Tom nodded assent)—what are
your intentions as to the future?’’

**I’m going to settle down—going to look out
some place—Il've been looking round all day to-
day—and stick to business.’’

‘*You can’t get @ square deal in the ring, can
you?’’

**Oh, no. It isn’t possible now.”

And then Tom looked across the parquette,and,
seeing a man sitting by a pillar who resembled
McCoole in facial outline, he said; ‘‘l guess
that’s Mike; no, it ain’thim either. Well, I'l
goand see anyhow.’’ But it wasn't Mike; he
wasn't in town, so Cool Herbert said, and the br-
standers echoed-that remark.

As to the actual

FIGHT WITH GOsA,

Allen volunteered no remark. It seemed as if the
matter had lost all interest for him, except as the
stakes are concerned. He casually remarked that
on Thursday night Miller, the champion wrestier
of the world, would engage 1n a fencing bout with
Mons. Schuler, while Regnier had volunteered to
perform his great cannon-ball feat. Bauer will
be there, but takes no active part in the even-
ing’s programme, the grand attraction of which
is, of course, the boxing between Allen and
Kelly.

* Tom expects a rousing house, in which, in all
probability, he will not be disippointed. When
his benefit is over, he will be a private citizen for
all future time.

AMUSEMENTS.
Olympic Tireatre-.

_ The presentation of ‘‘Pique’’ in this city is
one of the leading dramatic events of the sea-
son. We have heard of ‘‘Pigque’’ fora long
while. The name has been continually in the
newspapers fora year. It has been abundantly
advertised in the prints, and our citizens who
have seen it in all the glory of Daly's
Fifth avenue setting in New York
have sounded its praises in their
several circles. Our public was well pre-
pared forit, and the fashionable exhibition
in the auditorium of the Olympic last night
was an intelligent response to the fame of
both the attractions of the play, and its prin-
cipal figure, Miss Fanny Davenport. It was
soon after Miss Davenport’s visit here Inst
season, (which was her first acquuintance
with our prilic) that ‘*Pique’’ was pro-
duced in New York. Miss Davenport
had already made herself very sirong
in St. Louis. and her success in the new picce
Was a2 matter of keen interest to her St. Louis
friends. Now she comes with the piece itseli,
and the general interest in the actress and the
play, which showed itself when the box-oftice
was opened for the sale of seats a few days
ago, and again in the large attendance upon
the initial performance last night, was nata-
rally to be expected. ‘‘Pique’’ had been in
rehearsal ror a week at the Olympic.
Noxon and his forces lad been
busy a still longer time preparing
for it a new outfit of scenery. The company
had become ‘‘letter’’ perfect in their parts
and thoroughly drilled inthe business of the
play. Every possible preparation had been
made for the brilliant theatrical event, and it
might as well be stated now that the result last
evening fully answered the promisemade and
public expectation raised. The response in
numbers was full, the appreciation hearty,
and the enjoyment general.

Itis unnecessary ut present to tell the story
or dwell upon the plot of **Pique.’’ It is an
American society play, in which there is sutti-
cient friction between various classes to strike
fire and kindle interest. The clash comes be-
tween a New York society belle and an old
New England Puritan tamily, into which she
has married for pique. A child is born to her
and stolen, and the piot turns
upon the search for the child. The play is
full of incident, and compact with character,
and its dramatic effects are very ingeniously
contrived. They were all brought out, too, in
fine style, fora first presentation last night.
The lines were ali spoken, the dialogue was
rapid, and the perftormunce was over before
twelve o'clock. Hereafter the closing
time will be about half-past elev-
en. The sets are elaborate.
The first cannot be excelled for scenic beauty.
The curtain rises upon a conservatory of real
plants and garden trees; which mingling with
the artist’s colors makes a verfect Ulusion of
green and flowery iInxury. The second and
third (the same) presents a vivid picture of a
severe old Puritan home. The fourth is a
front street and snow scene, which opens into
the interior ofa hovel. The fiftn is a druwing-
room scene. The scenic efiects are brilliant
beyond anything heretofore done for a play in
this theatre.

Of the acting too much praise cannot be
pes Of course Miss Davenport’s Mabel

nfrew is superb in embodiment and cos-
tume and all the dramatic graces. The char-
acter is a frivolous woman redeemed by a
great sorrow, and elevated to the height of a
loving wife and mother. It comes a
glowing picture from Miss Davenport’s hands.

Matthew Standish (Frank Weston) is a splen-
aid character part, and Weston does it spien-
didly. His muke-upis severe, and the em-
bodiment is of tine breadth. We have seldom
seen a purer or more effective
bit of pathos, than his recon-
ciliation with his daughter-in-law. There are
few words, but his face is a volume of feeling.
Charles Rockwell, from Daly’s Fifth Avenue
theatre, does Capt. Arthur Standishin a very
sensible style. Without creat force he is care—
ful and correct. Dr. Gossitt, by_ Ferd.
Hight, is good. Raymond Lessinz
(L. R. Warwick) jacks vim. He
willimprove. Dymple and Gyll by the come-
dians, Chas. Plunkett and Harry Harwood,
respectively are excellent. Rag Money Jim,
by Hand, is welldone. The ladies of the com-
pany all do well, and are peculiarly notted for
the several roles that fall to their share.
The most conspicuous is Rachel—Miss Libbie
Noxon—who has a character part exactly fit-
ted to her, and she made a hit in it. Her
earlier scenes were probably a trifie over-
acted last evening, but she will doubtless
guard against this in future. The play inade a
hit, and it couldn’t Lbeipit. It will be repeated
until further notice.

De Bar’s Opera-House.

The oid style of Irish pieces has gone out of
vogue, and the stage Imshman, as a dramatic
attraction, isu figureof the past. He wasa
very funny fellow, but as a comic, did great
injustice to his class. He really did nothing
but burlesgue Irish character, and manners
and customs, and even therich brogue. He is
gone with the old styie ot delinea-
tors. Boucicauilt has done much
towards cultivating a better understanding cf
Irish character, by givingtruertyvpes. Others
have been at workin the same field with iike
objects. ‘‘Willy Reilly*’ isan example of the
tendency to truth in the later Irisn drama.
Dominick Murray is au actorin perfect bar-
mony with the object above set forth. An
Ttristuman born, an actor by nature and an art-
ist by culture, he is a worthy exponent of the
character, theught and feeling of Ireland.
Dowinick Murray is a genuine Irishman, and
no mere mouther of the brogue and burlesquer
of the character on the stage. When he pre-
sents an Irishman he appreciates the dra-
matic situation and feels the responsibility.
He is true to both his national and artistic in-
a und trusts to the integrity of his work
for effects. Thisis the groundwork of Mur-
ray’s treatment of Ivish subjects, and veing so
founded it cannot tail of its purpose. He
brings intimate kuowiedge, strong dramatic
forces and symputhizing nature to the task,
and these suarantee its masteriy performance.
 **Willy Reilly’’ was produced in excellent
style at De Bar’s, and was played weli. Itis
almost needless to say that Dominick Murray
made a superb character performance of Wii-
ly Rejlly. The churacter gave the actor scope
tor bis best Qualities, and he putthem to the
best use. Miss Florence Chase as
Helen Frolliardg, made a tine figure und truly
embodied this lovely character. Miss
Emnia Maddern as Yom thetIniuocent did
an excelent piece of churacter actiny. Mr.
oO. W. Blake as Andy wus true to the life,
and in fact the whole support wus good.
The play went of with sreat
spirit, and met with a generous
response from the audience, ‘*Willy Reilly’’
will be repeated every evening until Thursazy
inclusive, when Alr. Murray will introduce
**Innocent;or, The Gumbier’s Crime,’’ for
his benefit, and repeat it for Saturday matinee
and evening, which will close his engugement.

The German Drama.

Miss Marie Schaumberg, a noted German
soubrette, made her first appearance at De
Bar’s Opera-house on Sunduy evening and
was weil received. The play wus ‘‘Dear
Fatherland’’—paitriotic und popular and iuii
of merry music. lt wus thoroughly enjoyed by
a good audience. Mme. Metnoua scheller is a
permanent feature of Silberberg’s company
and avery strong one. In the pertoriajance
on Sunday a wur tableau was presented with
fine effect.

At the Olyimpic theatre on Sunday night Mr.
Wurster’s company did ‘*Honest Labor,’’ to
a full house ang made another success. Next
sonday evening this troupe will produce a
German version of ‘*Led Astray.’’

Theatre Comique.

The Theatre Comique opened the week on
Sunday dejar © with four new star teatures,
and several of the old favorites in new acts.
Among the attractions of the week are Rel
Muab the fire king and the French Twin Sis-
ters, sketches, songs und dances. The Pascal
sisters, Maude De Lisle and others remain.
The spectacular ballet of Estrella is stil! the
attraction in this line, with Mile. ida Idalie
as the premiere ieature. Tom Alien and Jem
Mace are announced fora boxing match this
and to-morrow evening.

Deagle’s Varieties Theatre.

The management of this popuiar house in-
troduced on Sunday evening the first of a series
of novelty combinations, which are promised
to follow each otherin uninterrupted succes-
sion throughoutthe season. The present com-
bination consists of the following features:
Harry Montague, «comic artist; Miss Carrie
Duncan, Will H, Stowe and his educated dogs;
Lew and Frank Collins, song and dance men;
Miss Leonie Forrest, vocalist; Gibson and Bin-
ney, clog, jig and reel dancers; Miss Muy
Antonio, serio-comic songstress; Mr. George
Forrest, Ethiopiun comedian and character
actor, and others. The new company was
well received.

Episcopal Orphans’? Home Benefit.

The notice of the public has been drawn to
the dramatic entertainment und hop to be
given for the benefit of the Episcopal Orphans’
Home at the Germuniaclub nall this evening,
and we again call attention to the subject.
This worthy Institution is in need of mouey to
meet the coming winter expenses, and all
charitably disposed people, regardless of re-
ligious feelings, shouid ieud « he:piug hand to
the lady managers inthis undertaking. Prep-
arations for this dramatic entertainment have
been going on tor some time past, and first-
Class talent will appeur in the comedy offered.
**Caste,’’ always ucceptabie to the public, will |
be presented with new scenery and elegant
costumes, and an amateur performance otf |
rare excellence may be looked for. The hop
after the performance will be pleasant, as no
better accommodations for dancing can be
found than those of the Germania club house.

Winter Garden.

Gregory’s Winter garden continues to be a
popular place of evening resort. Besides the
other comforts and pleusantries of the spa-
cious hall, there is an attractive variety en-
tertainment on the stage to interest and
amuse visitors.

title: Arthur Chambers interview on English prize ring conditions
text:
f The English Prize Ring.
[From the Philadetphia Sunday Item.1

As itis a matterof much interest to the sporting
fraternity of the United States to know what is )
goingon in prize ring matters in England (the
mother of the art of self-iefense), a reporter was
sent tothe Champion's Rest, 922 Ridge avenue,
to interview Arthur Chambers on his recent
es the ‘‘old country,’’ with the following
result:

Reporter. What is the condition of the prize
ring at the present time in England?

Chambers. No fighting at all, sir; @ man’s
lucky if he can be backed for £10 a side.

Rep. What is the reason for this radical
change?

Clambers, The license law; for the men who
— wantto make a match, micht took all day
and not get 4 publican either to back them or be
stakeholder, as it would result in the seizure of
his license atence. Thus the strictness of the
ae Operates against any ambition the men may

ve.

Pablic houses are closed on week nights at 11
o'clock, while on Sunday they are only permitted
woopen at 12:30 p. m., forced to close at 2:30,
permitted to open at 6, and forced to close again
at 10 o'clock, just as the business is becoming
or: If dominoes or cards are played even for
drinks, you musi do it with locked doors, fora
discovery by the police would result in a loss of
license. Even it I had a house presented to me
in London I Wouldn’t hare it there, to keep it in
— line, That is what has killed prize-fignt-

te. What has followed this result?

Chambers. Public and private exhibitions of
sparring; occasionally professionals, but fre-
quently among gentlemen amateurs; striculy am-
atcurs, as tlicy will not spar for money, but for
prizes, such as cups, belts, medals, etc.. Many
of these amateurs are equal to wie best profes-
sionals, and there is one gendeman amateur I
could name who could enter the ring with any
professional in England; indeed, he is able to
stand up with any boxer i know.

Rep. Is there any dJikelibood of the sport re-—
turning to its old popularitys

Chambers, No, sir, not while the present Li-
cense Law exists.

Rep. Whatisthe feeling amongthe peovle? _

Chambers, The feeling with the public, for a_
fair, square, up-and-up fight, is jost the same as
of old. The interest in the sport is unchanged. |

Rep. Many of the best men have left Soqeee? |

Chambers. Yes, sir. Tom Allen, Bill Ryall, |
Peter Morrissey, Abe Hicken (who is now in Aus-—
eee i Hicken, Jem Mace, Pooley, Ned |
O'Ba dwin, oe Goss, myself and nearly all the :
men of any importance have come to the United |
States, and I think itis due to these men to say
that their presence here has created and fostered
an interest in sporting matters of all kinds.

Rep. Who are the most prominent professional
men in London at the poser time?

Chambers, Charley vis, middle weight, and
Bat Mullins, light weight, both of London, are
the two best in England at the present time.

Rep. How were you received during your recent _
visit to England?

Chambers. With the greatest nape J and
kindness on ail sides, and ary camer mang at Oldbam
and Manchester. At the latter town, January 8,
at Owen Conroy's house, **The Three Legs of

Man,’’ on Portland street, I was tendered a com-

| ey dinner, at which I was presented with

a diamond badge, worth 50 sovereigns. Previous

to this 1 was tendered a testimonial benefit at

Free Trade Hall, which the people toid me was

the biggest event in the town for many years. I
wound — oung Nixey, of Liverpool:

Rep. ad yoR no fault to find with anything?

_ Chambers. » the Custom House officers,
contrary to law, charged me £5 10s duty on my
belt, which, although I did not wear it at a
times, was, nevertheless, person roperty.
They promised to restore the money, Bue have
not done it.

Rep. Who are the leading eparrers in Man-

chester?

Chambers. Jack Rooke (formerly middle-
weight champion, whose piace is at Locomotive
Inn, and who still a as well as ever), Tommy
Scattergood and Billy McCloud (who fought sev-
eral years ago), are among the leading sparrers.

Rep. You visited Oldham?

Chambers. Yes, and sony od at John Lees’

- Westburn Hotel, a svorting quarters, where
are to be seen the champion wresilers, pedestri-
ans and other prominent men. Itisa wonder-
fully busy litule town, and Jonn Lees is one of the
biggest-bearted men in England, and a great
friend of sport of all kinds.

Our representative, knowing Chambers’ inter-
est in such matters, then asked him if he brought
over any dogs or pigeons with him?

Chambers: Yes; I hada full-breed skye ter-
rier, named Venus, presented to me by John
Lees, a dog that took the nao hee at the exhibi-
tion of dogs by the Oldham Canine Society, on
New Year's day, 1877. 1 brought over two other
skyes, and ten oo said to be the best breed
in England, which I intend to ty this year.

Thanking the brilliant apende ‘or his politeness,
our representative left him; but he coytd rot
help hesitating for a moment to glance around at
the sporting relics with which the ‘‘Champion's
Rest’’ is crowded. iMere is Tom Hycr’s skeleton
hand, under a giaes; a cast of Jem Mace's
**lefs;"", portraits of Tom Sayers, Heenan, Mace,
Goss, and all the other worthies, past and pres-
ent; a stuffed champion bulldog, and endless
other features, the collections of many years and

much trouble and expense.

title: Lawsuit over failed Allen-Hogan boxing excursion in 1873
text:
| JACK LOONEY’S EXCURSION.
How the Allen-Hogan Prize Fight Fiz-
zled Out—A Law Suit About It.

Judge Boyle, who hasn’t been long enough on
the Bench to be au fait in matters of the ‘‘roped
arena,’’ or to become fully posted on the ‘‘new
rules of the London Prize Ring,’’ was engaged
yesterday inthe trial of a cause growing out of
the excursion to the mill (that didn’t come off)
between Tom Allen and Ben Hogan, in 1873. The
suit was brought by Capt. John McCloy, ownerof
the old steamer Continental, against John Looney,
of Looney’s Varietics, for $2,500 damages, suS-
tained by the boat in her interrupted trip to the
excursion. It seems that Loony chartered the
Continental for $500 for the purpose of conveying
passengers at $5 a head to the scene of the ap-
| omni conflict, twenty miles up the river, or

wenty miles down, as Providence might direct.
On the morning of the 20th of October, 1873, the
Continental swung loose from the St. Louis shore
with a large crowd ot roughs on board, and Bilty
Keefe at the wheel. As she aware out into the
current a storm arose that capsized her chimneys
and wafted her straightto the spot on the East
St. Louis side, where two Illinois sheriffs, each
with a large posse, were waiting to gobble 4 all
on board. As soon as her nozzle struck the shore
the officers leaped aboard, armed to the teeth,
and took the whole human cargo P gage mei
The Bogy bore alongside, an offered
to throw a tow-line to the fiag-ship
and pull her through, but a resolute
bull-dozer stood with a revolver at the head of the
engineer and threatened to send him to kingdom
come if he didn't hold her nose to the bank till
the last galoot jumped ashore. Jack Looney,
Arthur Chambers and a dozen other roughs were
led into captivity by the victorious Sheriffs and
taken to a Jvatice’s office in East St. Lonis.
Arthur Chamberg, being a feather verre: floated
out of the second story window and made his
escape. Looney and the rest were bound over,
and the fight waa ‘‘continentally busted.’’ Looney
claimed at the time that he lost $3,000 by the misad-
venture, and he suspected that it wasa ‘‘put up
ye on the pan of Ben Hogan to avoid meeting

en. iS

In his answer, however, to the petition of Capt.
McCloy, Looney pleaded that the boatjhad been
chartered for an immoral purpose, and to carry @
crowd of carrion-crows to witness a brutal act,
violative of the law of tlie land.

Capt. McCloy testified that the Looney-tica on
the Continental broke into the pantry, and smashed
the crockery and queensware ; took the er aay ate
office by storm and carried off a valuable field
giase, and kicked in sdveral of the state-room
doors, doing damage amounting to $2,500. Loony
gave his version, and the jury will decide to-day
who ia to blame. In the legal mill setiy 6 is sec-
onded by Mr. toblmgeed. | with Johnny Smith as
bottle-holacr; Capt. McUloy is handled by Mr.
Given Campbell and Judge McGeary.

summary: The St. Louis Globe-Democrat reported on a lawsuit by steamboat owner John McCloy against John Looney for damage to the Continental during an 1873 excursion to a planned fight between Tom Allen and Ben Hogan that never took place.

title: Gambler mentions Eph Holland Tom Allen Goss fight
text:
@ .
St. Ronis Duly 6
A ROBBER’S REMORSE.
A Reformed Cracksman Tells the Story of
His Singular Career of Crime.

His Adventures by Sea and Land as
Soldier, Gambler, Bank-Robber,
Convict and Tramp.

Ten Years in the Ohio Penitentiary—Pardoned
by Gov. Hayes—He Wants to Ge
to Sing Sing.

[From the New York Times, March 19.]

As Justice Kilbreth was about to adjourn
the session of the Tombs Police Court at 11
o’clock yesterday morning, Officer Kennedy,
of the Twenty-seventh Precinct, entered the
court-room, having in custody a most forlorn-
looking man. At the first glance he appeared
to be an ordinary member of the great army
of tramps, but when he had removed the
misshapen piece of felt that did him service
as ahat, he exposed a face bearing none of
the marks ‘that are impressed upon
the countenance of a whining, shuf-
fling beggar. It was a face present-
ing strange contrasts of fat and lear.
The cheek-bones were covered with swollen,
pulpy flesh, but the lower jaws were lean as

the Joins of a greyhound, and were girt about

with a stubby, dirty-looking beard, that was

-onee perhaps clean and flaxen. Notwith-
standing these strange contrasts and the fact

that the upper lip was weak and protruding,

| the face of the prisoner had a resolute look,

to which the steel-blue eyes, well set beneath
ahigh and rounding forehead, contributed
not a little. Patrolman Kennedy made an
affidavit that his prisoner, Christian Hansen,
bad made about twenty attempts to enter
forcibly as many different stores on Broad-
way. When the

HUNGRY-LOOKING MAN

was arraigned before Justice Kilbreth, his
captor testified that shortly before 10 o’ clock
in the morning he noticed Hansen standing on
Broadway, near Warren street. He appeared
to be watching the witness, and when he
seemed satisfied that the latter saw him, he
walked to the door ofa small fancy goods
store, and made a deliberate altempt to force
it open. a to do this, he walked down
Broadway, ap made at Iecast a score
of attempts at burglary. The oflicer fol-
lowed him, but thinking he was simply in-
dulging in a drunken freak, and was too weak
to do any harm, did not attempttoarrest him,
At last, Hansen, apparently becoming des-
perate, worked with determination at the door
of No. 155 Broadway, and had partly moved
it from its fastenings when the officer laid his
hand upon his shoulder and arrested him.
He made no citemet to escape. but, turning
around, told the officer he was starving, and
had deliberately set about committing a felo-
af in order that he might be sent to Sing Slug

prison.

id Justice Kilbreth was greatly suprised when
he learned that the prisoner

WANTED TO GO TO SING SING,

and questioned him as to his reasous for de-

-siring to go to such a place. Ilansen replied,

in broken English, and with a German ac-

cent, ‘*I am poor, and in the gutter; I bave
been only a few weeks out of the Columbus
(O.) State Prison, and though 1 haye tried to
get honest labor I have been unable. People
will do nothing for me; but Tdon’t want to go
back to my old way. I thought I would do
something that would make the Judges seud
me to Sing Sing.’’ ‘*So,’’ said the Justice,
**you do not want to go back to the old crim-
{nal course you say you once followed?’’ **No,
sir. I might do som@ting that would make
me more miserable.’’ Ald. Morris and Dr.
Elisha G. Harris, who were on the bench
with the justice, became intensely interested
in the case of the frank fellow at the bar,
and urged the Justice to examine into his
ease thoroughiy, so that something might be
done for him if his statements proved true.
Justice Kilbreth then asked Hansen ywhat he
was sent to the Columbus prison for” He re-
pee: **In 1866, Land three others robbed a
ank in Cincinnati, and got $400,000 in cash,
bonds, stocks, ete. We started for St. Louis,
and on our way robbed a mail-car safe of

35,000. Twas caught and sent to prison for
twenty years. About five weeks ago

GOV. HAYES PARDONED ME
because lL had behaved myself well for ten
years. WhenlTleft the prisonI was given
3S. «have used that all up, and since Fri-
day night haven’t had anythingtoeat. No-
body would help me, and I made up my mind
to go to prison again.’’ Thinking to pose
the prisoner, Justice Kilbreth asked him if
he sould opena aafe. ‘*Yes, sir, I can,
and without tools, I think.’’ ~**Well,’’ said
the Justice, ‘‘there is a safe in the back room
that no one connected with.this Court can
open.’’ ‘*Showit to me,’’ said Hansen, ea-
gerly. ‘*T will show you how I would
try to break it.’’ He was led into the exam-
ination-room, at the rear of the Court-room,
and shown a small office safe, which looked
sturdy enough to resist almost any pressure.
Justice Kilbreth, Dr. Harris, Aldersien Mor-
ris, Sergt. Woodruff, and several policemen
gathered in a knot around the prisoner, aud
earnestly watched his actions.. First he gave
the knob of the safe door a twitch with a pe-
euliar movement of his right hand, as
if to test the character of the lock.

Then he knelt down and examined the
safe critically. After a moment’s pauso
he said rapidly: ‘‘I would take putty and put
it all round the rim of the door; but I would
leave a hole here [the base of the door, near
the left-hand corner], and another one here
{the right-hand side of the door, near its up-
per corner]. Then I would put some powder
at this bottom hole, and would put the pump
atthe upper hole. As soon as I began to
work the pump the air would be drawn out
of the safe atthe top, and at the same tiine
fhe powder would be pushed into it by thé air
rushing in below.’’ ‘The explanation of the
burglarious process was perfectly clear. The
spectators) marveling at the simplicity of
the method, began a conversation among
themselves, which prevented Hansen from
telling how he would fire the powder when he
had got it into the safe. He said he was very
weak, and asked permission to sit down while
the party talked, After they had satisiled
themselves that the foree of the exploding
powder, exerted along a diagonal line from
the top to the bottom of the safe door, would
blow the door open, Hansen was again asked
questions about his career. Little by little
the story of his life was drawn from him. It
proved to be exceedingly iutcrestiug, and in
some respects instructive.

A MELANCHOLY DANE.

He was born, he eaid, in Copenhagen,
Denmark, in 1834, and in now forty-three
years old. He received a fair education in
an academy in his native place, and learned
to speak German, Norwegian and Swedish.
H{e came to this country in 1863, landing in
New York. ‘The day after his arrival he
enlisted in Company K of the 7th New York
Volunteers (the Steuben Regiment), com-
manded by Col. Schack. With that regiment
he served at Petersburg, and in one of the
battles was wounded in the left shoulder.
When the war was over his regiment was
mustered out of service on Ward’s Island,
and he came to New York. He did not stay
here long; but went to Cincinnati, where he
procured work as a railroad laborer. He was
paid #2 a day, which satisfied his wants and
enabled him to et by a sum fora ‘rainy
day.’’ It was his habit to frequent at yee
asaloon known as ‘*The Buckeye.’’ In this
place he made a number of acquaintances,
some of whom were fellows who lived with-
out working. He did not suspect, however,
that ir ge criminals. One night he was
invited some of these fellows to walk with
them. He accepted the invitation, and, after
walking a short time, he was asked to go into
a house on Fifth street. He went with the
party, and they ascended a flight of steps and
came to a green door, on which one of his
friends knocked several times. The door was
opened, and Hansen and his conductors en-
tered a gambling saloon. ‘*Oh, that was the
time I began to go down, ’’ said he, excitedly.
**The place was hept by those fellows that
made that fight between Tom Allen and
Goss. Hochheimer & Co. were the proprie-
tors named, but Eph. Holland was with
them. He is a scoundrel, that Eph. Hol-
land.’?

FROM GAMBLING TO ROBBERY.

To be brief, Hansen was induced to gamble
away his savings in Holland’s piace. He be-
eame infatuated with gaming, and, besides
losing his money, lost his work. When he
became destitute it was proposed that he
should take part in the robbery of the First
National Bank of Cincinnati, situated at the
corner of Walnut and Fourth streets, which
three of the men he had become ac-
guntacee with in Holland’s had planned.

e accepted the offer. The pe hired a
basement next door to the bank building, and
started what appeared to the pubie to be a
mean kind of a drinking place. At np, Hd
they spent their time breaking through the
foundations of the bank edifice. After about
ten days | were fully prepared for the
robbery, and early on the morning of Febru-
ary 3, 1866, made their way into the cellar
beneath the bank. Thence they broke
through the flooring of the banking-
room. The watchman apparently did
not hearthem at work,and when they a ber ge
in the bank they frightened him into silence.
They then blew open the vault in the manner
described. Hansen said he would break the
sinall safe inthe judicial examination room.
As stated before, they procured in plunder
$400,000, including bonds aud stocks, and
$5,000 in currency. Upon leaving the bank
the money was divided among the burglars,
and Hansen was given $1,000. The entire
party spent the day afier in drinking and in

| gaming in Hochheimer & Co.’s, or Eph
Hfolland’s saloon. ‘They thus spent $1,000.

| Hansen lost the greater part of this sum, be-
cause he was pitted agaiust what gamblers
teria
A ‘*SKIN DEAL.’”

Having recovered from their carousal, the
thieves determined to leave Cincinnati. They
tirst.weut to Richmond, [ud., where they re-
mained for several weeks. Thinking St.
Louis a more congenial place, they deter-
mined togo thither, and, to pay traveling ex-
penses and keep them in spending money for
atime, they prepared to rob the safe of the
mail car of a train on the Vandalia Railway.

| Their plan for the robbery turned out

| Successfully. When the train stopped
at a watering station on the morning of
March 7, 18titi, and all the employes on it had
sgathered about the water tank, leaving the
mail and bageage cars deserted, the four
thieves broke into the mal car, tumbled the
safe out, and, when the train had gone. car-
ried ita mile away, Where they broke it opeu
and secured $5,000. Afterthis exploit they
continued on their way to St. Louis. Hansen
got drunk aud faiicd to tuke the same
measures for sufety taken by his com-
rades. Those three sharp criminals,
whose names Hansen will not reveal,
left the train about three miles east of
the Mississippi River. Lansen siaied in the
car, and was arrested by St. Louis detectives,
He was at tirst suspected of being one of the
gang led by the James brothers, for it was as-
sumed that those despermioes robbed the
mail-car which Hansen ana his comrades had
ee It was so assumed because the
umes boys had a short time before boldly
robbed a train running between Kansas
City and St. Louis. The St. Louis authori-
ties were unable to fasten upon Ilansen the
crime of robbing the mail-car, but from a de-
seription from Cincinnati they recognized
him as one of the burglars of the First Na-
‘tional Bank of that city. He was accordingly
sent back to Cincinnati, where he was tried
before Judge ‘Taft, lately Secretary of War,
who, upon his conviction, sentenced him to
imprisoument for twenty years. His com-
rades in the Ourglary did not desert him, but,
through confederates in Cincinnati, retained
Judge Cox and Emil Roedei to defend him.
This is one reason for his unwillingness to
disclose their names at the preseut time.
PARDONED BY HAYES.

Hansen passed ten years in the Columbus,
~O., State Penitentiary without once being
punished for disregard of discipline. It was
this good record that induced Governor, now

President Hayes, to pardon himin the first
week of February last. When Hansen
deft the prison he was handed $5, $20
of which was his share of gate money
set apart for well-disciplined prisoners,
and $45 of which were due him from the
contractors for machine work, under whom
he worked in the Pe itee ary « With this sum
he determined to begin the world anew, vow-
ing positively he would uever again commit a
criminal act for the sake of money. He was
given arailway pass to Cincinnat!l, where he
inade a short stay, going thence to Pittsburg.
It was his intention to preevure work as a farin
or railway laborer iu Pennsyivania. He
left the cars’ at Pittsburg and = walked
to Philadelphia. His treatment on his
pedestrian tour, «as he describes it,
would embitter the mind of a less unfortunate
man, and make him rejoice to tura bis band
ageiust humanity. He was either scorned as
a miserable tramp, or when he frankly told
the story of his life was driven oif as if he
were the embodiment of a playue. In Phila-
deiphia Hansen could procure no aid, so he
walked on, ina miserable plight, to this city.
In New Jersey he met with no Good Samari-
tan, and was not more fortunate” in
his search for one in this city.
People scouted him, and even the
Danish Consul, to whom he told
his story, he says, dismissed him witha pres-

-entof four cents. Since he has been in this
city Liansen has slept at niyhtina five+cent
lodgiog-house at No. 107 Greenwich street.
On Friday last he spent his last cent, and
from that time until noon yesterday he ate
nothing. ‘The fact that he was famishing was
proven by his rapid consumption of a tin dish
of soup and an immense loaf of bread given
him in the Lombs prison. :

| PROMISES.

-_ Hansen promised Dr. Harris, Justice Kil-
breth and Alderman Morris that if they st
cure him labor he will henceforward lead an
honest life. Alderman Morris gave him a
small sum of money, and promised to send
him a suit of clothes this morning. He was
“deeply moyed by his syinpathetic treatment,
and returned thanks with his eyes full of
tears. lis case is to be brought to the no-
tice of the Prisoners’ Aid Society by Df. Har-
ris to-day. He was committed to the Tombs
ona charge of disorderly conduct, but will be
released if his tale proves to be true, and aid
will theasbe given hjim to avoid crime in the
future,

len’s face with his left, and be followed this up
with another, ever phd in retura heavily on the
eye. This nettled Gilbert, and he rushed in at
Allen, and received a fair ‘‘crusher’’ full on the
nose, Causing the blood to flow profusely. Allen
did not follow his advantage up, but waited until
Gilbert recovered himseif, and then let him have
another hot-’un on the jaw, which made the
Lincoln man wince. Some merry exchanges fol-
Jowed, Allen repeatedly visiting the face and Gil-
bert the body, and arally inthe latter's corner
Was ail in favor of Alien, who at the termination
slung out his left heavily on Giiberi’s head, the
force of which sent him down. Time, 4 min. 10
sec.

Round 2—Gilbert was upto time, again bent
on forcing the fighting, for which he got pretty
well peppered. He let go his left and missed,
aud then they came to close quarters, Gilbert de-
livering most of his blows on Tom’s body, and,
after a sharp rally, the round closed with Gilbert
again going down. Time, 1 min. °

Round 3—This was all in favor of Allen, who at
orce planted his left on Gilbert's frontispiece,
which now wore & very sorry appearance. Gil-
bert, anxious to close, tried to rush in at his for-
midable opponent, and Lp the penalty, receiv-
ing beet & and, in mading a lunging hit with
his right, he slipped down on his knees. Time,
4036 sec.

Round 4—This was. another brief affair, Gil-
bert, who led off on Allen’s head, receiving in re-
turn heavy punishment on the face. They closed,
Tom operating on Gilbert’s face, and the latter
on Allen’s nous (once or twice hitting below the
belt, not seeming to know what he was abont),
and finally Allen, with an upper-cut (a clincher)
full on the jaw, knocked Gilbert off bis legs and
he went down, as inthe three previous rounds.
Time, 38X sec.

Round 5—This time Gilbert was slow in respond-
ing to the call of time,and was evidently a beaten
man; nevertheless, be ied off, and Allen did not
retaliate, evidently not being desirous of finish-
ing matters. ‘Throughout the round Gilbert
scarcely made a point, and again went down at
the Onish. Time, 1 min. 6% sec.

Round 6—Allen at once let fly on the left side of
Gilbert’s head, and the latter planted his left on
Tom's body, and they gog to cleee quarters, Gil-
best purens his ola tactics, hitting Tom again
below the belt. This nettled Tom, who at once
setabouthis man in rare style, oaining every
point. Severaltimes Ailen planted his left fuil
ou bis ais oy i face, once or twice under the
jaw, making him fairly wince; and the Lincoln
Man seemed unable to strike a blow, rushing in
madly with bis head forward,and finally he reeled
and went down on his knees. Time, 1 min. 57%
sec.

Round 7, and last—Gilbert in this, asin pre-
vious rounds, showed himself a wrong reader of
an excellent rule ofthe Ring, namely, ‘‘to hit,
stop and get away.’’ He ‘‘hit,’’ but did not
land, he ‘*stopped’’ Allen’s blows, but he used
his head for *‘stopping’’ purposes, and as soon
as be could get to bis corner, he ‘‘got away,’’
and did notcome back. Allen, who was evident-
ly conscious of his own superiority, had been us-
ing his man very mercifully, but getting repeat-
ealy hit below the belt, wentin to make a (nish of
it. Direcily they came together, the men closed,
Allen having allthe vest of the in-flehiing, and
hens on’’ his opponent with two or three
heavy blows, while Gilbert was unable to retall-
ate with anything like power. A short rally ended
by Gilbert being forced off by ANleu,whou he was
Allempting to Lis and coming to grief on the
platform. Time, 31% seconds.

Allen claimed a foul, which tho referee at once
diallowed, ordering them to fighton, Giibert,
80 s0cn as he recovered his legs, made his way
ont of the ring, and not coming back, ‘‘time’’
was called, and Allen only responding to the
summons, was declared the winner, after boxing 16
—_ 45 sec. So terminated a very ove-sided con-
test.
