title: Professional Prizefighters Donovan and McClellan
text:
THE FIGHT
was finally fixed for to-night, and tickets were
sold at $10 each. About 200 brokers, aldermen
and sporting men gathered in Monstrey’s sport-
ing establishment. There were three rows of
benches. Neura stage about fifteen by twenty
feet, at sides and rear of the stage, were foils,
masks, armor, boxing-gloves, etc. On the left
of the room was a row of closets, and on top of
them was a single row of benches. There were
but two professional fighters in the audience,
and they were adenitted with regular $10 tickets.
| THR PRINCIPALS APPEAR.
-— At 8:25 the applause was begun, and MeClel-
Ian and Donovan stepped on the stage. Johnny
| Dwyer, who-is soon to fight Ryan, of Troy,
for the championship of the “world, and
Ned Mallahan, one of Joe Colburn's old-
time friends, were seconds for McClellan. Joe
Goss, who fought Tom Allen in Kentucky, and
who won the fight through a foul invented by
himself, and Jerry Donovan were seconds for
Donovan. Jim Coburn, Joe's brother, was
umpire for McClellan, and Andy Sheehan, for
whom .
JOHN MORRISSEY
had a hearty dislike, was umpire for Don-
ovan. Billy Borst, the horseman, was chosen
referee. All things being in readiness, time
was called, and the principals and seconds ad-
vanced to the center of the stage and shook
hands. Donovan was unquestionably in better
condition than McClellan, but the odds
in the betting were in favor of the latter; the
sudience were hushed for a moment, and then
bang! bang! bang! and McClellan, driven by
Donovan's terrific raps, dashed against tne
wall. Both were in full ring costume, bare to
their waists and wearing knee breeches, long
stockings and henvy shoes. They- wore
hard gloves and meant to do harm.
| THE FIRST ROUND.
It wasat once apparent that there was no
\humbug about the set to, that somebody wes to
be whipped. When Donovan battered Me-
Clellan’s head ugainst the wall, the latter suc-
ceeded in clinching with his desperate antag-
onist, and fora moment seemed to have the
advantage of him. Donovan freed himself,
end gave McClellan a terrific neck blow, and
followed this up by forcing the tavorite to his
corner, pounding him terribly all the way.
There was a gash in McClellan's head, and his
fuce was covered with blood when he ieil into
his chair, as his friends crieql ‘‘Time’s up.
First blood for Donovan.’’
THE SECOND ROUND
lasted about one minute. McClellan seemed to
cast aside the science which he boasted of, and
began to claw and make frantic dashes at Don-
ovan, who saw his opportunity, and knocked
him sprawling on the floor. The first knock-
down was ‘of course claimed sand allowed for
Donovan. By this time those who had bet their
money on McClellan began to see their favorite
wasno match for Donovan. He was almost
winded. The wound on his head and the bard
knocks on his ribs were quickly telliag, and
miuny were satisfied he was doomed. Dwyer
and Mallahan sponged and fanned him. Dono-
van smiled and sat upright in his chair.
THE THIKD ROUND,
When time was-called for the third round
both men were cautious. It was ‘thought that.
McCiellan’s Ione reach would scientifically fin- |
ish Donovan. fe began to torce the fighting,
and Donovan stopped bim with an iron-like
grip. McClellan's seconds looked at the roof of
the closets, where sat the referee and umpire,
and sereamed, ‘*What are you doing, Jim (Co-
burn)? They are fixing things over there. Why
don’t you attend to your man?’’ Donovan
broke away at this, and with a rush like a but-
tering rain, floored MeClellan, who was picked
up limp and bleeding and carried to his corner, |
THE FOURTH
round opened with Donovan glistening with
sweat and as lively asx could be. McClellan was
seemingly usedup. He clinched with Donovan
aud succeeded in feebly pounding him on the
ribs; he tripped Donovan and both fell. Mec-
Clellan wis ingeniously fanned and rubbed,and
although apparently more dend than alive,
arose when time was called and plunged at
Donovan, hitting him square in the fades: This
excited Donovan, who ground his teeth and
bounded towards McClellan, almost crushing
him against the wall, and throwing him, limp,
bleeding and nearly breathless, to the floor.
Again McClellan's seconds put bim on_ his
feet to meet Donovan, who was as fresh
wpparently as when he began the tight.
MeClellan made two or three desperate
efforts to show that there was yet some fight
in him, but Donovan haminered his face and
drove him to his corner. McClellan dropped
into his chair, and Donovan centinued to pound
him in the face and on the body, until Meclel-
lun’s frieuds sent up a great shout of
‘*FOUL!’” ‘*FOUL.’’ |
The room was in an_=uproar. Donovan |
backed uway, glaring at McClellan and his sec- |
onds. The latter shook their fists at the ref- |
eree, and Dwyer, the Brooklyn bruiser, louder —
than the rest, Claimed the fight for Mc-
Clellan. The referee decided that
the fight should go on, but in
the mid-t of confusion McClellan put on dis
jucket, und stepping over the ropes staggercd
away. The reicree at this decided the fight in
favor of Donovan, and while everybody shook
lis fists and yelled ‘‘police,’’ Capt. Williams
dashed into the hall,

MOUNTING THE STAGE, TE SHOUTED,
‘‘Gentlemen, this must stop instantly; clear
the hall.’’ It was cleared with celerity. Mc-
Clellan and Donevan were paid for their ser-
vices out of the gate money. There were many
private bets on MecOlellan, and his friends
were disconsolate. It had been rumored that
Billy Edwards was backed to fight the winner
of last night's battle, bnt he said that snch was
not the fact, that he had been two years out of
training, and that he does not cure to engage
ina prize fight. The man who most

FEROCTOUSLY RESISTED M*CLELLAN'S CLAIM
that he had won the fight was Joe Goss. The
tight, wiich was one of thesharpest and fierc-
est of hard ylove contests on record, lasted
oily twenty minutes. Donovan walked briskly |
to his home without a scratch, while McClellan,
wilh blackened eyes and chopped scalp and
bruised ribs, wen" inournfully away in a coach.

SOHNNY SULLIVAN’S CAREER. :

Youthful, pure-blooded, and never having
been debiltated by intoxicants or tobaceo,
John L. Sullivan, ot Boston, sprang into no-
toriety at a bound. Although a ‘'novice’’—
never having set foot in the magie circle—Sul-
Hvan, since attaining his majority four years
ago, has been regurded asa light of dazzling
brilliancy in the fistic firmament; Bouts with
the gloves, in which be bested every man that
faced him, made Sullivan’s reputation. Well
knit, stout as an ox, standing 5 feet 10% iu his
stocking feet, and weighing 17 pounds when
in condition, gifted with piuck and, above all,
the knack of fighting with both hands,it was not
at all surprising that early in his career John-
ny becume an aspirunt for laurelg where the
naked fists and not gloves were tramps. After
**knocking out’’ each of the ambitious few
who met him in mimic encounters on the stage
Sullivan gublished a standing offer of $200 to
any che who would face Him for four rognds
under the Murquis of Queensbury’s rules, but
his skill and burd-hitting powers were beldin
such Gread thatthe challenge went begging.
Shortly after Tom Allen’ bad been
swindled out of oa vietory over
Goss (on a fraudulent. claim of foul
near Cincinnati, in 1876, Sullivan's fame be-
gan to make itself manifest, and he was re-
garded Ly knowimg ones us the coming cham-
pion. Goss, who wasin the ‘sere and yellow
leaf,'? having been before the public as a pugi-
list since 1869, when he made his d¢butin ‘tithe
squared cirele’* with Jack"RKRooke, was not per-
mitted to retain his tile as champion for any
length ef time. The following year Johnny
Dwyer, of Brooklyn, becaine possessed of the
championship by default, his deposit to fight
any inan in the world for the title never having
Leen covered. On May 9,879, Dwyer won the_
champicoship legitimately by a yictory over
Jimmy Ebiotty at Long Point, Canada.

. RYAN AND His RECORD,

Dwyer’s triumph brought Paddy Ryan prom-
inently before the public. The later had
iong beeh wellthought of by his townsmen

of Troy. He was a Tipperary chap, born at
 Tharlis, March 15, 1853. A giant in stature—
6 feet 1 inch—and weighing 220 pounds,” he
had frequently shown whut He @ould do in
rough-and:tumble encounters. Game as a-
pebble and unusually clever with his hands
for one of hisinches, the championship was
considered within his reach, On April 10,
1878, the upshot of a chance meeting be-
tween Dwyer and Ryan and their friends was
the arranging of preliminuries tor afight for
$1,000 a side within fifty miles of Buffalo, on
Cxnadian soil. This came to naught, but a
second meeting was held and a Matth made
for $2,000 and the championship, to occur be-
tween July 15 and.25. On the nightof June 22-
Ryan was to have sparred ut a! benefit for a
Brooklyn bill-poster, but us there was some
hitch about pay, did nét do so. s While pro-
eeeding to the terry after the show Ryan was
attacked by a gang of roughs, stabbed in the
left side and kicked in the head. Dwyer
proved that he wasin no way to blame for
tue outrage, and Rynn's wounds were dresse!
at the bouse of Johnny’s principal backer.
His injuries of course ended Kyan’s truininz,
and th match with Dwyer was declared off.
Ryan had never been inside or a ring until he

off, owing to numerous postponements, and
he was compelled to surrender after a desper-
ate struggle that lasted lhour and 24 minutes.

During the lullin pugilistic affwirs after the

hid been performing such wonders with the
**mittens,”’ became ambitious to win laurels
in a flercer field, and when Mr. Richard K.
Fox, of New York, offered to match Ryan ~
aguinst all who desired to meet bin, Sullivan |
started for Chicago, where he had a satisfac- |
tory interview with Mr. M. ©. McDonald,
(more familiarly known as ‘‘Mike’’), a gen- |
tleman who hus always manifested a willing-—
ness to help aiong any little seance in the sport- |
ing line that was likely to furnish fun for the
fraternity. Little time was lost after the
interview alluded to before closing with Fox's
offer, and as a result the present match for
$2,500 a side and the championship became a
fixture. Aside from the above conditions the

December 1 Ryan commenced his prelim-

CONJECTURE AS-TO THE OUTCOME.

The moment that the ‘‘mill’’ became a cer-

esthat SeHivan would win, and the general

tions’ of their confidence that the

GONE TO THE DOGS.
Noted Prize-Fighters Who Took to

eity. In afew months more he had to give

**Well there’s Tom Allen. He wasn’t ex-
actiy knocked out by. Coburn, but he was dis-
ote barnes gg oe t and had to run away to

ing@o the Penitentiary ,and he has lost nearly

title: Joe Goss Dies; Boxer Recalls his Fight with Tom Allen
text:
Death of Joe Goss.

Joe Goss, the well-known pucilst, died at Boston

In a late article “Macon,” anticipating his decease,

title: Tom Allen listed among English fighters visiting America
text:
JACK AND JOE.
eS ee a a
THE CHANCES OF A FIGHT BETWEEN DEMP-
SEY AND ILLINGSWORTH.

New York Clubmen Anxious to See Dlings-
worth “‘Do” Dempsey—The Ring Record of
the Famous Irish Pugilist Dan Donnelly—
*‘Deaf’’ Burke at New Orileans—Sullivan vs.
Smith—Macon’s Melange.

Special Correspondence ofthe POst-DISPATCH.
PHILADELPHIA, April 1.—Sporting men here-

abouts do not view with favor the report that

comes from England of the willingness of the
friends of Jem Smith to back him against Sul-
livan for $5,000, especially as they see by read-
ing between the lines that an effort is being
made to ‘‘gammon” the “big fellow” into fight-
ingin England. The English are famed for
their skill in making matches. They have a
proverb which says ‘‘a match well made is
half won,’’ and itis evident that in yielding
to Sullivan the amount of the stakes,
they intend to exact from him a con-
cession as to the battle place, which will
give himlittle or no chance to win them.

This is plain from the fact that they say that

Smith would haye no chanoe to win in Amer-

ica, astatement which has no foundation in

fact. English fighters, asarule, have been

exceedingly well treated inthis country. I

know of but one exception, that of ‘‘Deaf’’

Burke, at New Orleans, where he was chased

out of the ring when he was besting one

O’Connell. That was over forty years ago.

Since then Ben Caunt, Bob Caunt, Tom Allen,

Joe Goss, George Ryall, Ned O’Baldwin, Jem

Mace, Charley Mitchell, Jack Burke, - Alf

Greenfield and dozens of other English pugs

have visited the country, fought in it, and re-

ceived the squarest of treatment. No Ameri-
can has ever received justice in England,
who attempted to wrest the cham-
pionship from one of its sons. I have
but to pointto the caseof Heenan to justify
what Ihave said. However, the machinations
of the tricksters will come to naught, for Sul-
livan told me that under no circumstances
would he consent to fight anywhere but in Ire-
land or America. He is the butcher, and if
they don’t like his price they need not buy his
meat. He has the butt of the whip in his hand,
and if he lets it go he has no one to blame buat
himseif if he is well lashed.
*
+ =

Hardly a week passes that I do not receive
letters from parties in different parts of the

Union asking me to make comparisons be-

tween fighters who are dead and gone and

those of the present day. Of course I cannot
jo so conclusively. I only know of the old-
timers by tradition or by what is told of them
in Boxiana or Pugilistica. The other day an
old ‘Hibernian of 70’’ wrote me a long epistie
in which he sought to show that John L. Sul-
livan wouidn’t have had, as he calied it, ‘‘the
taste of a chance’’ with Dan Donnelly. He
wound up by asking me to publish my opinion
on the subject. When one who has reached
the Psalimist’s three score years and ten takes
such trouble to convince a youugster like me
of the faith thatis in him, I think itis but due
his years that I should comply with |
his request. I shall do 50 by
showing what Donnelly did. In the first place |
he beat all the ‘‘gossoons’’ about Dublin.
Then a third-rate English fighter named Hall,
who was giving sparring exhibitions in Ire-
land, wasinatched against him in a regular
ring fight. Dan’s strength enabled him to |
win this fight readily. Then George Cooper, |
who Was reputed to be the best twelve-stone |
man in Ergiand, visited the ‘‘Ould Dart,’’ and
he too was matched against the ‘‘Irish Cham-
pion.’’ They fought on the historic ‘‘Cur-
ragh of Kildare,’’ about twenty miles from

Dublin, and Donnelly not only had the back-

ing of Mistress Capt. Kelly and the sporting

pentry, but of what would now be called ‘‘the
gang’’as well. The old song tells us that

‘*In eleven rounds there was nine

knock-downs, besides he bruk his

jawbone.’’ The rounds and the
knock-downs were all right, but historians dif-
fer as to the amount of injury Cooper's jaw-
bone received. The weight of evidence does
not bear out the report that it was fractured.
Cooper was a good man, however, and in
whipping him Donnelly convinced the En-
glish that he was a tip-topper and fit to fight
most anyone they had. While on alittle jam-
boree he was inveigiled to England, where he
was matched against Tom Oliver, the trial
man of his day. Ten days before the fight
Donnelly was so unfortunate as to be thrown
from the stage coach, 50 bruising his right
arm that it was of little use to him during the
earlier part of the tight. Though he was
much heavier taller and ionger in the
reach than Oliver, it took him nearly
two hours to win. These threefights comprise
Donnelly’s entire ring record. Tom Cribb
was ase ae of England then, ready and
willing to fight ail contestants, but Donnelly
made no effort to dispute his title in a twenty-
four-foot ring. It was notCribb’s place to
challenge him. Hall, his first opponent, was
beaten by several other men;so was Cooper.

Cas Hickman whipped him with a punch inthe

jaw. His friends ssid it was an accident, so

they fought a second time, and again Hickman
put him to sleep inajiffy. The united time of
both fights was but five minutes. If

Donnelly was a wonder, what must Hickman

have been? and yet he never dared to pit

himself against Tom Cribb. Oliver was a very

—< man, but half a dozen others shared with
onnelly the honor of making him cry

“‘peccavi.’’ The fighters of to-day in Hd es-

timation in skill and agility as far exceed those

of a generation ago as sang ge those of a gen-
eration ahead of them. y private opinion
publicly expressed is that if Donnelly were
alive to-day and in rull possession of his pugil-
istic powers he would have a hard timein

staying three rounds with John L. Sullivan. I

think by that time John would have him lymg

in a corner as dead, almost, for the time bein

as he is now in reality. But in saying this I

wish to be clearly understood as being guilty

of no treason to Ireland.
“* - +

The Marine’s card setting forth his view
of the fight between himself and Dempsey
came somewhat in the shape of a surprise, in-
asmuch as he had publicly announced since
the battle that he lost purely because Demp-
sey was the better man. Now he claims that

remaining three rounds, backing his state-
ment — with a monetary forfeit for anew

do not suit emeory challenging him to fight
him six rounds Marguis of Queensberry rules,
in any city im the country, in which
such a contest is permisiable and offer-
ing to donate the entire receipts to
charity. The fact that this statement and
challenge has been drawn out by Dempsey’s
neglect to keep a bargain as toa benefit with
him does not detract from the other fact that
he backs his challenge with his money. I think
that they will meet again, but Ido not for the
life of me see how LeBlanche figures out that
he can whip Dempsey. Ithink the next time
they meet he wiil be defeated worse than he
was before. reine ane seems disposed to fight
somewhat shy of Joe Ilingsworth. Not that
he is afraid of him, but because he knows he is
a first-class man and has a backing thatis ex-
tremely formidable. The Ulingsworth boys
havea _— in the politics of their ward and
are besides the especial pets of the clubmen
of New York. ino, would delight
these latter better than to have the ‘“‘amateur
pe wesses poe ME of New York defeat the ‘‘profes-
sional midale-weight’’ champion of America,
and if they come together they will do alli in
their td to effect this consummation. It will
be dollars to cents that Illingsworth will be
handled by Billy Edwards and Dempsey’s
especial bete noir, Arthur Chambers, whom
the Marine says he was prevented by Dempsey
from ne second him. Public sentiment fs
as — most with the yeec champion
as it is with the railway president, and Demp-
sey, like -—. Gould, sometimes finds it con.
venient to abate his pretensions. After ex.
amining Fox’s rules for contests
for the diamond belt, he says he
will so far conform to them as to waive

title: Tom Allen Cheated Out of Title by Goss Gang Says Correspondent
text:
] 664 99
PADDY RYAN’S “GUFE.
. a
HE BLOWS ABOUT CROSSING THE ATLANTIC
TO FIGHT JEM SMITH.

Plenty of Chances for Him at Home—Arthur
Chambers’ Fistic and Other Attractions—
The Dumb-Bell Exercise—Jack Fogarty
and Joe Illingsworth—Sporting Gossip.

Special Correspondence of the PosT-DIsPATCH.

PHILADELPHIA, May 27.—It is reported that
Paddy Ryan thinks of crossing the briny to
make a match with Jem Smith, to come off in
Ireland. I don’t think Paddy has any such
idea but if he has he should dismiss it from his
mind. Apart from the fact that it is extremely
doubtful if he could fight Smith in Ireland,
there remains another back of it which should
restrain him, and that is that he is physically
incapable of fighting any fairly good man with
any hopes of success. When he became rupt-
ured he should have retired from the ring.
He then could have done so with something of
areputation. He had outlasted Joe Goss, who
had been dubbed Champion of America be-
cause the gang back of him had robbed Tom
Allen out of the fight he had with him at
Walton, Ky., and so had obtained the title for
him. He never had a ghostof a show with
Sullivan at Mississippi City, and the flurry he
made with him at Madison Square Garden was
all bounce. He was informed that the instant
there was ashow of slugging the fight would
be stopped and the affair lasted just thirty-
four seconds.

PADDY’S CHANCES HERE.

He need not go across the water to obtain a
fight. Dominick McCaffrey is very peacefully
inclined toward the generality of mankind, but
he thinks Paddy treated him like a hog at the
picnic ofthe Hibernians at Troy, @ couple
summers ago, and he is just aching to get a
chance athim. Hecan have a four, six or
eight round contest. Dominick don’t think it
worth while to make itjany longer as he be-
lieves that he can do Ryan up in the shorter
number of rounds. My advice to Paddy
is, do not fight at all, but if he will
not take it, it well for him to know
that he can ‘get one nearer home
than Ireland. If he wants to demonstrate that
he can scrapa bit, perhaps he had better
tackle Jack Ashton. Ashton, like himself, is
not very scientific, and if he can get away with
Madden’s — in mepeite like good style
poeete will believe that peng there is
stuif in him yet, and then there will be some
sensein his talkingof fighting “Suen tee
Parson Davies told me that Bill Shereff, the
Prussian, went around Paddy like a cooper
| round a barrel, and most any of the second-
raters can do the Prussian. ~ private opin-
| ion publicly expressed is that Ryan is merely
| blowing for advertising purposes.
| THE DUMB-BELL EXERCISE.

‘*There are no real good heavy weights in
England now,’’ said Arthur Chambers to me
the other day. ‘‘Jem Smith is about the best
they have and he is no match for Sullivan.
Without doubt, I think the best of the English
fighters who came to this country was George
ites mig the Nottingham slasher. Why didn’t
he do better with Alf Greenfield? ‘I’ll tell
you. Simply because he wasn’t in condition
for one thing, but principally because |]
couldn’t get him to exercise with dumb bells.
Do I consider them good thingsto use? The
best things in the world to teach a man how ta
hit fast and paecnen. They must not weigh
more than a pound and a quarter, ora pound
and a nalf, and they should be used three times
aday. The best times are when you get up tn
the morning before you wash, in the middle
of the day ana just before you go to bed. Take
them firmly in your hands, spread your legs
welland square yourself just as eu y you
were going to fight. Then hit out left and
Tight as fast and as hard as you can fora minute
or two by the watch—three if zoe can. Then
goatitagain. Then take another rest—you'll
wantit—and then try the bells a third time.
After that be rubbed down and you’ll find that
if you do this three times a day fora month it
will give your blows more speed and force
than anything else that you cando. A man
who fights needs all the strength he can get in
hisarms. If — are tirea he can neither hit
nor stop, and if he can’t do these he can’t
keep on. He must quit.’’

ARTHUR CHAMBERS’ PROPOSITION.

Arthur tells me that he has not a made the
match between Jimmy Mitchell and Harry
Gilmore, but he is willing to and he will back
Mitchell, not oniy against Gilmore but against
Jack McAuliffe or Billy Frazer of Boston, at
from 126 to 130 pounds, for $1,000, the fight to
be ten rounds and to take place in private in
New York. Chambers declares that he will
not go to Canada for any matches. He thinks
Gotham a good enough place for anybody to
scrap in, and I quite agree with him. He is
also willing to back Joe Acton to wrestle any
man in the world—Muldoon or Evan Lewis,
the Strangler, preferred—either catch-as-
catch-can or Greco-Roman fashion, for $1,006
aside. Here is a chance for handsome William
or for ie me Davies’ man. A match
of this ind in Cincinnati, where
Muldoon is so popular and  deserv-
edly so, or in Chicago, where Lewis is wel!
known, ought to draw like a blister plaster.
He has still another proposition to make. He
saw Tommy Warren fight in Cincinnati and at
Chicago, and he thinks him a etc my good
little man, but in view of the difficulty he has
in getting anyone of his size to ye him, he
thinks Tommy might give away afew pounds
and have a go with Jimmy Mitchell for a purse
or share of the weed money. He says that for
such a match Jimmy would get down to 124
pounds, and he thinks that ten rounds would
about tell which was the top sawyer. I think
so too.

M’CAFFREY AND SULLIVAN.

As yet McCaffrey has received no response
to his offer to fight the champion to a finish at
the Polo Gioonta, in New York,on the Fourth
of July. Now that the authorities have put a
stop to boxing in Chicago, I doubt if anything
will come of it. I presume the Sullivan-
Mitchell affair will be deciared off. What a
pity that sporting men cannot actin harmony.
Their dissensions kill the geese that eo theixz
golden eggs. I don’t know who is right o1
wrongin the matter, but I do know that the
places in which glove fights can eeoase in
public are yearly becoming fewer and fewer.
Of course ‘‘slugging’’ is the chief cause o:
this, but staaning is what the populace
wants. A pre ers of Queensberry fight in En-
gland is an entirely different thing, I am told,
from a contest of the same name in this cqun.
try. There men really spar for scientific
points, while here the ‘‘points’’ are merely
‘*blinds’’ to enable the police to wink at the
affair. The men do the best and hardest they
ean to knock each other senseless, and the
man who accomplishes this feat, or comes the
nearest to it, isthe victor, even if he has not
scored another point in the match. I don’t
think a genuine Marguis of Queensberry con-
test between, even say Burke and Mitchell,
would attract a paying audiencein any city in
the country. Sullivan has taught the people
that science, unaccompanied by hard blows, is
not worth cen ag and they seem to have
gotten the lesson by heart.

FOGARTY AND ILLINGSWORTH.

There is a bare at agen sey 4 that Jack Fogarty
and Joe Ilingsworth may be permitted to bo3
in public in New York, but if the priv Soge is
accorded them I opine it will be with the ee
itive promise that there will be no knocking
out. ny of this character nnn them
would be like the oft talked of but never real.
ized performance of the play of ‘‘Hamlet,’'
with the part of the melancholy Dane omitted
—the nearest approach to which
I ever saw was when an ex-cleric
of Mlinois was the prince and te 4
proposed star of the evening. Jack would
all right in such a contest, but where would
Illingsworth be? Itistrue he might stamp on
the stage and make a noise, to say nothing o:
raising a dust—but Chinese warfare is not ef.
fective in conquering men like Fogarty. I
takes hard knocks and plenty of them to
make him see the error of his way, and so fa!
no one but Dempse; has been able to adminis.
ter the dose that he ‘equires. He is daily get.
ting bigger and tougaer, and I hardly believe
that in a friendly th match Joe can give him
enough knuckle oll to make any impression on
him. MACON.

The recent freedom with which challenges
for championships have been issued has pro-
yoxed considerable discussion affecting the
standing ef championships in general. In a
conversation touching the championships of
pugilism and how they have been won, the
veteran Tom Kelly said: ‘‘Thereis the alleged
qpampionship for middle-weights. You hear
agreat deal  f talk about itand you see how
this and that fighter is matched tofight some-
pody else for it. Well, the ‘middle-
weight championship’ means nothing.
It is an empty title; has no belt attached to it
and it has never been foughtfor. Jack Demp-
acy is called the middle-weight champion but
he is no more 80 than Burke who can fight at
middle-weight or Mitchell who can do the
same thing. Sullivan can be properly be
called the heavy-weight champion of Amer-
tea, for the reason that he whipped Ryan at

the fight was for the title. The belts that fly
ground the country for the middle-weight
jight-weight and heavy-weight cham-
pionships are mo more worthy than

any pelt that anybody can go out and buy and

offer. All fights for the championship must be
according to London geogptes. 3 rules, with
pare fists, and any fight for a championship

professionals. A man may fight for three
minutes in order to get his opponent in a cer-
tgin position, and just when he gets him there
he is called away and all his tactics os for
nothing. That isnot what I call fair fighting.
A round should never end until one man
js knocked down. That is the legitimate end
ofaround, andit was in this manner that

City. The title to any championship must be

London prize-ring rules, with bare fists, of
course. A — between Smith and |
fullivan wouid be for the championship
gui no championship could be won under

telis me that he will not fight Sullivan east of

and if he fights he’s got to fight fair. You can

title: Prize Ring History Lists Tom Allen Among American Champions
text:
SS ee
INTERNATIONAL PUGILISM,
Big Men of the Past Who Crossed the Water
and Fought Well.
T. P. Evans in Boston Globe.

Never in the nistory of the prize-ring has
Great Britain been invaded with such an array
of foreign pugilists as at present. From the
time when pugilism first obtained a foothold
in the United States, champions not content
with victories on their own soil, went abroad
to do battle with the sons of Britain. The
greatest of these upheld the dignity of the con-
tinent with unparalleled success.

Mollineux, the colored champion, did battle
with the redoubtable Tom Cribb, and the
history of the prize ring tells us that had the
warrior been shown fair play the undefeated
Cribb would have been worsted. Charley
Freeman, on British ground, upheld his own
until he met with an at 2 death.

Yankee Sullivan braved the perils of the At-
lantic to meet the gailant Hammer Lane, and
he succeeded in placing the stars and stripes
above the union jack. All judges of pugilism
who witnessed the contest pronounced him
the greatest phenomenon that ever put
up a hand. Charley Lynch met the
best men of his weight, and encountered
such shining lights of the prize-ring as Simon
Finighty and Young Shaw. Bob Smith, the
colored wonder, rurely ever talked about, was,
in the writer’s opinion, one of the greatest
fighters thet ever lived. His decisive victories
over Tom and Harry Allen remain as two of
the hardest figets ever recorded in the history
of the prize-ring.

Ot the number who have crossed the
ebannel George Roake was perhaps the
most unlucky, being very easily defeated
by Denny Harrington. John C. Heenan’s
memorable battle with Tom Sayers still
lives fresh within the memory of ring-goers.
The whole history of fistiana does not furnish
us with a pugilist so unfortunate as the brave,
kind-hearted and gentlemanly Heenan. His
two contests in England were wrested from
him unfairly. After the Heenan and Sayers
and the Heenan and King fights American
pugilists remained at home until Joe Coburn
crossed to do battle with Jem Mace. The pro-
——_ contest, however, endedina complete

zle.

After this America was invaded by British
pugilists, who found that the rigorous arm of
the law prevented them from getting a living
athome. They, too, found the new continent
cer more lucrative for their business than the
old. .

According to the records, we have had nine-
teen champions of the American prize ring up
to the present, viz.: Tom Hyer, Yankee Sulli-
van, Dominick Bradley, John Morrissey,
John C. Heenan, Joe Coburn, Mike McCoole,
Jim Dunn, Bill Davis, Aaron Jones, Tom
Allen, Ned O’Baldwin, Joe Wormald, Jem
Mace, Joe Goss, Jim Elliott, Johnny Dwyer,
Paddy Ryan and Jobn L. Sullivan.

The last named opened a new era in the
posewee world by offering any man a stipu-

ated sum who would stand before him three
or four rounds. The men who have gone down
before him prove that he is the greatest fighter
that has lived since Jas. Figg boasted of being
the first champion. For several years John
L. has been contemplating a teur to Europe,
but not until the fall of ’87 were his plans car-
ried out.
summary: The St. Louis Post-Dispatch published a history of international pugilism, listing Tom Allen among nineteen American champions and noting Bob Smith's victories over Tom and Harry Allen.

range the series, but failed to secure the

the greater portion of the time prior to the

sons. Itnow remainstfor him to change bis
route and play the spring series for the
world’s championship with the Browns. The
series, itissafetosay, will no doubt be ar-
rauged.

title: Tom Allen Gives Opinion of Prize Fight
text:
M’MANUS-FLINT MILL.
SE
TOM ALLEN GIVES HIS OPINION OF ‘THE
PRIZE FIGHT YESTERDAY.

Flint Failed to Take His Second’s Advice and
Lost the Battle Thereby—Incidents of the
Trip—Kilrain and Mitchell Versus the
American Exchange—Base Ball News and
Gossip—Sporting Matters. ° ;

The result of the prize fight between Mo-
Manus and Flint near St. Clair, Mo., yester-
day, was disoussed pro and con to-day among
the sports about town. The general opinion
seemed to be that the St. Louis man had the
best of the battle and would undoubtedly have
won it had he not given up at the merest show
of rally on the part of McManus.

TOM ALLEN, )
who seconded Flintin the fight, sald to-day
that his man inflicted more punishment on |
McManus than the latter served to Flint and
that, although not beaten much about tbe
head and face beyond aswollen cheek and a
cut lip, he sustained severe punishment about
the body. ‘‘If you noticed it,’’ said Allen,
*‘all the fighting was done over in the other
man’s corner. Four biows were not struck
outside that corner, and if Flint had taken)
my advice and waited for his man
to face him as he should have done the result
would be different. I kepttelling him to stay
in his corner, not to go out over to the other
man’s and that he’d win but, no, he knew
more about it thanI did and he got licked.
Flint is a more acientific fighter than McManus
and he should have walked on that line, If
science is your hold you ought to make science
your play. Itold himto go at his man, hit
him a <1p and then come away and
go at im again as before, but he
wouldn’, and he paid the penalty.
Instead of taking my advice he would rush
over to the opposite corner and hug the man
bythe neck. This gave the man as much ofa
chance to hit him as he had to hit the man,
andthe consequence was that the man gave
him enough. When it comes to tn-fighting,
adummy hagas much show to whip a scien-
tiflo man as a scientific man has to whip him.
No, sir, Flint showed himself to bea quitter,
and I had to throw up the sponge.’’

KELLY'S SaGE COUNSEL.

In addition to the advantage which came
from wa gpa refusal to take the ad-
vice of hisolder andable second, McManus
had the benefit of Tom Kelly’s sage instruc-
tions. Kelly handled his man in iine style,
and McManus absorbed his advice without a
word of protest. Kelly told Mack not to worry
Flint at all, but let him indulge his tendency
to visit him every round in his own corner
and not to <o out of it except when necessary.
McManus followed his instructions, and much
of the credit attaching to the victory rightly
belongs to the veteran trainer and coach,

**Well, we won the fight,’’ said Tom when
the battle. was over, ‘‘butI teil you that we,
pulled it right out of the fire.’’ The Kelly—
Sweeney—McManus crowd won considerabie
money on the battle, probably somewhere in.
the neighborhood of $800, and counting the
stake and the purse in with this roll they had
about $1,500 to divide. Flint was presented |
with a purse of $100 subscribed and gathered |
by McManus on the train returning to the city#

INCIDENTS OF THE FIGBT.

Whether decency of conduct Is the exact
thing to be observed by people who go to
prize fights is probably a question open to dis-
cussion, but it is most certain that the crowd
who attended the McManus—Flint affair yes-
terday never knew what decency in any of its
departments meant, or else they completely
forgot what little they ever did know about
the matter. It had been stated ‘‘that several
very nice gentlemen’’ would be at the fight, but
a close examination failed to develop them.
The majority of these present were in a
state of beastly intoxication before the train
left, on the way, during the progress ofthe
mill and even afterit. Onthe way down one
of the ‘‘spectators,’’ a well-known, fat at-
torney, was eminently unfitted to take care of
himself, and as all his friends were as drunk
as he was and the sopver people inthe party
didn’t care, the said attorney managed to
make things very lively.

At w point about thirty miles west of the
city the fat attorney marched to the rear end
of the rear carand announced in tones thick
from whisky, that ‘‘he would now proceed to
demolish the windowinan abrupt and dia-
bolical manner,’’ and followed up his an-
nouncement by putting his foot through it.

But little attention, however, was paid
either to him or tothe window, and for the
rest of the trip the attorney was conspicuous
for his general ubiquity. The rest of the
passengers demonstrated the elegance of
their manners to everybody’s satisfaction
by falling over one another pell mell and
throwing chicken and ham sandwiches and
hard boiledeggs at one another. One man
cameon board loaded down with a basket
fuil of whisky (in bottles) and this goodly
supply was supplemented withtwo jugs fuil
of the same liquor, carried by a friend.
About the time the fight had finished the
liquor was nearly gone, but the men were so
thoroughly soaked with alcohol that the ef-
fects had not been wornoff even after the
train had reached Grand avenue.

On the return trip a number of the party In-
dulged in the refinedand elevating game of
**‘craps,’’ over which there were several
fignts, without loss of blood, however. Short-
ly after the train had pulied ont of St. Clair
some festive drunkard inthe crowd thought
be would amuse himself by emptying the
chambers of his revolver without scrupulous
attention astothe direction he aimed at, and
the veces oy played hide andseek with their
heads until the firing ceased.

Flint, all battered up, lay on the floor of the
baggage car and was viewed as though he
were a curiosity by the ‘‘gentiemen’’ who
found a delight in

FEASTING THEIR GAZE

with the sight of his fearfully swollen, black-

ened and bruised face and distorted features.

McManus did not appear to be suffering in-

tense pain from the punishment he hud re-

ceived, and discussed the fight intelligently
as he walked through the train collecting the
purse for his defeated adversary.

Altogether the atfair was about as disgust-
Ing an exhibition as anyone would care to
see and the brutality, naturalto all prize
fights, wasemphasized by the remarks and
the comments made upon the various plays
bythe men around thering. It was one con-
tinuous howl without rhyme or reason.
Several ‘‘inhabitants’’ about the locality ar-
rived on coGarem pee! poe as the men were about
to enter the ring and the crowd became terribly
alarmed when someone get the rumor
afioat that they were none other than the
Sheriff ofthe county and his posse. These
fears were dissipated when it became known
that the new arrivals were a country doctor,
who wanted to see blood, and a few railroad
hands. The country ‘‘blokies,’’ as they
were called, seemed to gloat over the bisod.
letting and bellowed themselves hoarse at the
fight, which, as they said, was the greatest
thing on earth.

text:
TOM ALLEN,
Retired Champion Pugilist of the World, 619
Market street. Free concert; also, boxing by
the most scientific boxers of the city every
evening.
OO
THE ORIGIN OF INN SIGNS,

QUEER OLD HOSTELRIES THAT NESTLE IN

THE ROMANTIC MOUNTAINS ACCOUNT FOR

IT,

What is the origin of signs? The earliest
signs are ceftainly heraldic. We have still in
many Willages the ‘‘So-and-so Arms,’’ with
the shi¢id of the lord of the manor em-
biazoned upon it, with all its quarterings. |
or we have the Red Lion, or
the White Hart, or the Swan, all either crests
or cognizances of a family, or of a sovereign |
or queen. The Swan sign is said to date from
Anne of Cleves; the White Hart was the badge |
of Richard Il., and inns with this sign proba-
bly were erected in that reign, and have kept.
this sign unchanged since. We know of inns
under the name of the Rose, whichthere can
be little question came into life as hostelries |
in the time of the Yorkists and Lancastrians. |
The Wheat Sheaf was the Burleigh badge, the
Elephant that of Beaumont, the Bull’s
Head was a Boleyn cognizance, the
Blue Boar the badge of the De
Veres, earls of Oxford, the Green Dragon
of the earls of Pembroke, the Falcon of the |
Marquis of Winchester. It does not, however, |
follow that the inns that have these signs date
from the periods when, let us say, Anne
Boleyn was queen, because they bear the
token of the bull’s head, or from the reign of
Queen Elizabeth, when Burleigh was in
power, because of the wheat sheaf, for it

| will not infrequently be found that they take
their titles and signs from a much more local
origin, the coatior cognizance of the squire
| who holds the manor,
There was a reason for this—the inn was
originally the place where the true
landiord—that is, the lord of the
-manor—received his guests, and
every traveller was his guest. In Iceland at
| the present day there is but one inn at Reyk-
| javik, the capital, and that is kept by a Dane.
The traveller on the island goes to any
farmhouse or parsonage and is taken
‘in. Indeed, by law a traveller can-
not be refused hospitality. When
he leaves he either makes a present of money
or something else that will be valued, but
this isapresentand nota payment. Inmany
parts of Tyrol, it is much thesame. ‘he
excursionist is put up at the priest’s house.
The writer has been thus received, among
! — places, at Heiligkreutz, in the Oetz
hal.
In the evening the room—the cure’s parlor—
was filled with peasants who asked for wine,
and were supplicd. When they left they put
| money in the hand of the pastor’s sister,
while he, smoking his pipe, looked out of the
window. When the writer left next morn-
ing the same farce was enacted. Farther up
the same valley is Vent, where again
the cure receives travellers and his sister re-
ceives the payment, but there a definite
charge is made, but at Helligkreutz what was
given was rt age as a present.
|. The priests who entertain do not, of course,
hang up signs over their doors. The pastor is
supposed to be given to hospitality and would
give of his all freely and cheerfully if he could
afford it, but of late years, as travellers have
become more numerous, his pittance has be-
come smaller, sothat his hospitality can no
longer be gratuitous. In the old romances of
Chivalry we read of travellers always seeking
the castle of some knight, and asking, almost
demanding, lodging and entertaiument.—
(Cornhill Magazine,

title: Tom Allen knocked out Dan Daly street fight altercation
text:
evil IN ONE ROUND-
Tom Allen, Ex-Champion, Knocked
| Out by Dan Daly.
- Tom A lien, the ex-champion of the world
was knocked out in one round (rules barred)
by Dan Daly, champion middle weight of
Missouri, at an early hour yesterday morn-
ing. From statements made by a number of
spectators it appears that about 1:30 o’clock
yesterday morning Dan Daly was sitting
in front of his saloon on Seventh
street between Market and Chestnut streets
trying keep cool with the aid of a fan when
three men ran by, followed by Tom Allen,
Dutch Neil, Steve Hearn and Jack Ryan.
The fugitive disappeared around the corner
of Seventh and Chestnut streets and the
pursuers approached Mr. Daly. Allen, who
appeared to be very mad, claimed that one of
the three men who had been calling him vile
names, was in Daly’s saloon. Dan arose
from his chair and told Allen that he must be
| mistaken, as he neyer saw the men _ before,
and most certainly was not hid-
ing them. Allen became infuriated,
and, it is said, accused Dan
of doing things to hurt his (Allen’s) business.
| Charley Daly, Dan’s brother, who was in the
house, heard the loud talking, joined those on
the outside and tried to pacify the irate ex-
champion. AJlon was not to be quieted, how-
ever, and it is alleged that as soon as Charley
interfered he tried to strike him. Dan, who
is much heayier than -his brother, became
riled and threw off his coat and made for Allen.
while Charley paid close attention to Neal
| Hearn and Ryan, who were crowding rather
close upon the principals of the meeting.
Allen retreated into the street and declared
that he did not want to fight, to which Dan
Daly replied: ‘You came here looking for
trouble, Tom, and youshan’t depart in peace,”’
and with this he struck Tom a terrible blow
in the stomach. Allen put up his armsand tried
to ward off the blows aimed at him by the
younger pugilist, but he might just as well
have tried to escape a pile-driver. Daly fur-
ther added insult to injury by telling him that
perhaps he could fight at one time, but that
now he was
A CHESTNUT.
Allen retreated to the middle of the street
and Dan, not desiring to have a repetition of
the Sullivan and Mitchell runaway battle,
closed in on his adversary and struck him a
terrific blow under the chin, felling him to
the ground. The victor calmily surveyed his
work and waited for his victim to rise, but
Allen was done up and he cried out “‘enougk..”’
About this time Officers Pat Scully and Eck-
hard appeared in the distance and Dan retired
inside of his saloon, leavi#§g the ex-champion
to be gobbled.
__ While Dan was fighting with Allen, his
‘brother Charley was not idle. He made’ for
Dutch Neil and Steve Hearn whom he de-
clared he could whip in two minutes, but
they managed to get out of his way before
being séricusly injured. Jack Ryan hada
base ball bat which he swung around his head
in a dangerous manner and came near strik-
ing several spectators. Johnny Gaiten’s bar-
tender threw himself upon Ryan and inflicted
several bruises on the latter’s physiognomy.
Charley Daly gave himself up to the police
and was taken to the Chestnut Street station
incompany with Allen, where they were
both released on bond.
summary: The St. Louis Republic reported that Tom Allen, the ex-champion pugilist, was knocked out in one round by Dan Daly during a street brawl near Daly's saloon on Seventh Street.

title: Tom Allen Appeals to Law to Recover Stake Money Dispute
text:
THE WORLD OF SPORT.
TOM ALLEN GOES TO LAW TO RECOVER
STAKE MONEY,

Annual Meeting of the Scorers’ League
—Sullivan Challenges Kilrain—The
Association Delegates Home-
ward Bound—Miscellany.

For more than 80 years Tom Allen has not
been on speaking terms with law. During
the greater part of that period the law has
had Tom on the run, and he was compelled to
step around pretty lively to keep out of its
clutches. Therefore, the very edifying spec-
tacle of Tom Allen appealing to the law for
protection shows that prize-fighting as well
as politics makes strange bed-fellows.

Allen yesterday entered suit against Bill
Clark, the final stakeholder in the Daly-Mce-
Manus match, and gave his grounds for ac-
tion in the following petition:

The plaintiff states that on the 16th day of Octo-
ber, 188k, he and one Dan Daly enteredintoa
wager depending upon the result of a boxin
match with gloves between Dan Daly and Hugh
McManus, which was to take place on the lith
day of December, 1888. That while the event
upon whichthe said wager was made was still
contingent and unknown the plaintiff deposited in
the hands of the defendant, as stakeholder, the
sum of $1,000, to abide the result of such wager,
That afterwards, to-wit on December 5, 1888. plain-
tiff demanded from said defendant the said sum
of $1,009 and payment was refused, wherefore he
prays judgment for said sum of $1,000, interest
and costs. :

For another and criees cause of action the
plaintiff says that on the 5th of December, 1888, at
the City of St. Louis, the defendant received from
the Globe Printing Co. the sum of $75) to the use
of plaintiff. That thereafter and before this action
the plaintiff Gemanded payment thereof from de-
fendant, and that no part has been paid, where-
fore plaintiff prays judgment for $75), interest and
costs. Rowe & MORRIS,

Attorneys for Plaintiff.

Last night Allen called at Tue REPUBLIC
office and submitted the following card for
publication:

To the Editor of The Republic.

I wish in a few words to explain to
the public the character of articles of
agreement in a match for money. Dan
Daly and Hugh McManus made a match ‘and drew
up articles of agreement by which both’ were
bound, These articles say that if either man fails
te live up te them the one so failing is to forfeit
allthe money. The last deposit of $250 a side was
due December 4. I put up ef money in
the Globe- Democrat office according tb the articles,
and received a receipt. I heard the next morning
that Daly’s #250 was not up so I went to the oflice
and at 12 o'clock claimed a forfeit. On December
5 Chas. Daly called at the office and posted the
final deposit of #250. I met Mr. Murphy and asked
him why he had not acknowledged my deposit in
the paper and he said Daly's moncy was not up.
Itold him that I had been there at noon and
claimed forfeit. He then said he had been at
Daly’s the night before and they haa offered
him the money. All deposits were, according
to the articles, to be made at the office of the pa-
per, and as Murphy’s name does not appear in the
articles, he had no power to receive money out-
side the office. Iam willing to leave the matter
to the Clipper, the Spirit of the Times or the Police
Gazetie, and will abide by their decision on my
claim for $750 forfeit for Hugh McManus.

TOM ALLEN,

The temporary stakeholder who ought to
know takes issue with Allen and says Daly’s
money was up on time and thatthe money
was turned over to Clark, the final stake-
holder.
summary: The St. Louis Republic reported that Tom Allen sued Bill Clark, the final stakeholder in a Daly-McManus boxing match, to recover $1,000 in disputed stakes, marking an unusual instance of the former prize-fighter seeking legal remedy.

title: Jem Mace Defeats Tom Allen
text:
VERY FEW OF THEM WEALTHY,
iow the Champion Pugilists Made
Money and Lost it.

From the New York Herald, .

More reckless with his suddenly a
wealth than the gambler is the successful pu-
gilist, The profession, especially at present,
is a lucrative one, but the fighters who have
retained fortunes after making them can
readily be counted on the fingers, while the
spendthrift gladiators are numberless. Sud-.
den relaxation from severe training periods
may account for much of this profligacy, Cer-
tain it is that no class of men are more thor-
oughly satisfied’ to let the morrow look out for
itself than champion pugiliSts.

No better example of an extravagant

pugilist exists than John L. Sullivan, It
was he who developed the knock-out blow,
and by making 4, 6 and 10 round contests as

full of uncertainty and danger as tho old

‘fitish fights mado pugilism the remunera-

| tive profession that it now is. ‘hough

grossly overestimated the “Big Fellow’s”’

"earnings have been treble those of any fighter
who came before him, yet Sullivan now has
little or no money. Jake Kilrain is said to be

as extravagant as was John L,

- Joe Coburn, whoin his old age has had to
hustle for dollars in match making
with other old _ timers, is another
warning example. Jem Mace, whose
benefit in Londen the other day was noted,
is another. Mace and Coburn were the won-
ders of their day, and though they didn’t
make as much money in fights or exhibitions
as the latter}day champions they made more

in other ways. Both these great fighters of

the past are now working hard for dollars.

Old Sam Collyer,,.whose three tremendous

battles with Billy Edwards for the light-
weight championship will long be remem-
bered, has not been a Sunday-school-boy, and
his effort to make money by engaging in a
six-round contest with the young champion
of the 133-pound class (Jack McAuliffe) ex-

cited much sympathy. Dooney Harris, |
another clever old timer and once champion

of the middle-weights, is about town locking

out for odd jobs. ais SBA -

Jem Ward,one of England’s greatest heavy-
weights, died not long ago at the age of 86,
in the semi-charitable Licensed Victuallers’ |
Institution. ‘om Sayers, another famed
champion of England, would have died in >
want but for a life pension presented him |
after his memorable drawn battle with John
C. Heenan, Old Tom Allen, who met defeat |
at the hands of Jem Mace not far from the
svot where John L. Sullivan beat Paddy
Ryan, is living after a fashion in St. Louis.
Yankee Sullivan, one of the most famous of
the old-timers, made and spent big ,»money, |
but died, it is said, at the hands of: vigilantes |
in San Francisco. Australian Kelly, who.
fought the longest battle on record with Jon-
athan Smith in Australia, and was then
beaten in this country in 30 minutes by
Ned Price, lives in New Jersey. .He has
very little property. And soitis with many
of the pugilists who do not set up in saloons,
Mike Donovan, Jim O’ Neil, who fought the
longest battle on record in’‘this country, and
Billy McClean are teaching the young of
this city how to put up their hands. »

Tom King, the heavy-weight who beat and
was beaten by Jem Mace, acquired a splendid
fortune og a book-maker in England and heads
the list of pugilists who did not let swollen
heads run away with business sense. Two
hundred and fifty thousand dollars is what
the late waterman, wrestler, pugilist, painter
and book-maker left as the fruit of his indus-
try and wisdom. Charley Mitchell is almost
penurious and is said to be worth
$50,000. Jack Dempsey didn’t have any
money when he began work this year, but |
the contests with McCaffrey and Mike Dono--
van paid well and he has made a good salary |
most of the time in sparring in variety thea-
tres, besides doing well with his saloon. |
McCaffrey was very careful with his money
when he made it, but as he has been idle so
long he is getting desperate now. |

John C. Heenan made money also, though |
not’ by fighting, for he never had the good
fortune to hear a referee pronounce his name—
as winner of:a prize fight. He becamea
gambler and died in Wyoming Territory,
while on a Western trip, fairly well off.
John Morrissey, though the winner of every
prize tight he ever engaged in, made his |
money, not from pugilism, but as a gambler
and politician. A pugilistic champion whocan
make money and keep it is Arthur Chambers.
Arthur was light-weight champion of Eng-
land and America, and, starting a saloon with
a little money, he is now rated worth $60,000.
Billy Edwards, the efficient sergeant-at-arms
of the Hoffman House cafe, who swept all
before him years ago, is said to hold consid-
erable property. |

Dublin Trieks, who got his start in busi-
ness life by beating Orville (“Awful’’) Gard-_
ner, became worth $500,000. Tricks had a
hard time to beat Gardner and his gang, but
he did it. Once in this battle Gardner, when
hit very hard on the nose, declared that his
shoulder blade was broken. Gardner after-
ward turned revivalist. Tom Kelly is sup-
posed to*have $10,000 worth of real estate in
St. Louis, where he does a prosperous saloon
business. His coming set-to with Joe
Coburn, who recently met Prof. Bill Clarke
ina blackened glove contest, was arranged
only because he feels the need of excitement.
Ed Price, who fought a draw at Spy Pond in
Massachusetts with Coburn years ago and
was one of the best men.in America, is a
lawyer in this city now.

Perhaps the richest of the old time cham-
pions is Barney Aaron, son of the famous
Star of the East, who fought and beat the
best light weights of his day. Barney made
most of his money after leaving the ring, and
is now in the employ of the book-makers on
the big Eastern tracks.

Rare exceptions were the old time battles
that could compare in the amount of stakes
with those of the present day. The only
ones 1 call to mind are the $10,000 Hyer-
Yankee Sullivan battle and the one for $10,000
betaveen Heenan and King at Wadhurst,
England. Heenan and Sayers fought fora
paltry $1,000 a side, which was equalled by
the amount at staké in the jug handled fight
between Reagan and Dempsey. How the
old timers would have opened their eyes at
the “big fellow’s’”? forfeit and challenge the

other day !—85,000 slapped down for a fight-

-er’s first deposit, as was done by Sullivan

and his backers.

title: Boxing Critic Compares Historical Pugilists Including Tom Allen to Modern Fighters
text:
CONCERNING “SLUGGERS.’’
Charlie Sails for ‘‘Lunnon’’—John ELE, Not
Drunk—Fighting Tips.

By Telegraph to the PosT-DISPATCH.

NEw York, January 19.—‘‘Charlie is over
the water and Charlie is over the sea,’’ that
is, he ison the ‘‘briny’’ and will soon again
be in dear old ‘’Lunnon.’’ The »vdoxing
champion of England got a glorious send-off,
too, Jack Dempsey’s farewell address being &
lively one. I saw ‘‘Mister’’ Mitchell two
nights previous to his departure, he being
with Al Smith and ‘‘Parson’’ Davies in Bang’s
Broadway palace. I do not remember having
seen Mitchell look so well on any By y
occasion as he did then, and my wo: for it,
he looked big enough and able to
whip almost any man who wears
shoe leather. Of course I know he won’t
make the attempt. He has declared himself
averse to fighting and pleads bad hands as ap
excuse. Doubtiess he has bad fists, but Ido
not think thatis allthatails him, and I think
that if the truth was known Charlie is fearful
of meeting Dempsey. Not that he would be
afraid to fight Jack, but he knows the —
idolize Dempsey and detest him. He willnot,
I believe,ever meet Dempsey in the ring and all
that Jack can say or do will not induce him to
go in fora finish fight. Itis useless for Jack
to make any more proposalsto him, and the
best thing he can do is to ignore the English -
man.

JOHN L.’S JAMBOREE.

According to reports from Boston Jobn L.
was quietly indulging in intoxicants the past
week, notwithstanding his vows to remain an
abstainer. The news caused much sur-
prise here. and John’s — were
greatly chagrinned. I investigated the
case fully, and the result was I
learned the report was greatly exaggerated.
John doubtless took a few drinks and was
thereby made rather jovisl. But it was not
true, as reported, that he was agg drunk.
It seems very strange that only in Boston is
John found to behave so. He invariably be-
haves well here and also in other cities.
There, however, bis every action {is noted and
every drink taken nz him commented upon.
Just why this is I donotknow. Idothink,
however, that it is an evidence that the big
eg is not without enemies in the city of his

irth.

It takes a’man who knows nothing at all
about pugilism to write intelligently about it,
or, at least that would seem to be the idea of
the man who wrote an article on the subject
published in the January number ofthe Man-
hattan Athletic Club Chronicle. The individual
in question did not mean to touch on the fistic
art in a general way, but startedin with the
evident intention of criticising the recent con-
test between Dempsey and Donovan. But like
all who know little or nothing of a subject. he
was soon beyond his depth, and floundered
about in a helpless way until he finally found
something to wind upon. Of course, as the
article in question would fill a column of the
Post-DisPpatcu, I will not reproduce it. I
will, however, quote from it, andI believe
that all who know what fighting is will sce
how puerile is the work in question.

AN OPINION ON DEMPSEY.

In criticising Dempsey’s form he says:

**He bears so much resemblance to the won-
derwe have been led tosuppose him asthe
building In which he boxed does to a palace.
In the first place he is shaped anythieg but
artistically, holding his left hand too low, his
right too high; his left shoulder and —_ el-
bow too far forward, suggesting that his dis-
position was more to parry blows than to
strike them. His boxing was not first-class,
particularly in the use ofhis left, which he
swung with a stiff elbow, from his thigh to, or
rather somewherein the direction of, his ad-
versary’s face or body.’’

Shades of Tom Cribb. Wasthereever such
an idiotic criticism as the above? In the name
of all that is good on earth, have professors of
the artof boxing, critics with years of ex-
perience been crazy in believing that Demp-
sey’s left hand is his best andthat by reason
of his attitude his length of reach was in-
creased to his advantage and disadvantage of
his opponent? But let that goand follow the
article in question.

**Donovan, who hasavery fairly straight
delivery, strikes with precision and fate:
ment and is, altogether, a fair rep-
resentative of a good, old-fashioned
fighter. * * * Although many blows were
struck during the contest, neither man landed
one well-timed, clean, positive hit. * * *

**Donovan’s straight hitting and good judg-
ment gave him a decided advantage all
through, and proved, or rather re-proyeda,
what was conclusively proved generations
ago, that the straighterthe hitter the better
the boxer.’’

Now, of course we all know whatthe writer
ofthe above means. It must be apparent to
allthat if Donovan ‘‘strikes with precision
and judgment,’’ but did not ‘‘iand one well-
timed, clean, positive hit,’’ his ‘‘straight hit-
ting and good judgment gave him a decided
advantage.’’ The above also proves what

. A COMICAL CUSS

the writer must be. limagine that he did not
meanto prove anything as to the respective
merits of the style of attack and defense of
Dempsey and Donovan, but that he merely
desired to gain renown as ahumorist. Surely
he has succeeded and it is agreat pity that his
name is not known.

Another paragraph of the article which will
be read with interest is the foliowing:

‘*We had noticed an improvement in Demp-
sey’s hitting when he boxed with
Joe Coburn a few months ago,
but it seems that his form ieft him
when engaged in an actual contest with a
better boxer than himseif.’’

And still another: ‘‘We would also suggest
that it would be more to the benefit of the
public if those who write up boxing forthe
press were men who had seen such first-class
pugilists as we mentioned in our April num-
ber. Then their readers would not be misied
into erroneous impressions, through favorit-
ism or wantof knowledge.’’

It will, of course, be a surprise to some
people to learn that Dempsey out-

pointed Coburn, but was BO
match for Donovan, although it is
known that with Joe and Mike at their best the
latter was not in the same class as the former.
It will also please the able critics of pugilism
to learn that this know-nothing of the game,
because they did not, presumably, witness
the work of the men, mentioned in a previous
issues of the Comical. I suppose, like myself,
they are ignorant or tne identity of the men
previously mentioned by the writer quoted.
SOME OF THE OLD ’UNS.

But I am confident, like myself, they believe
he alluded to Nat Langham, Tom Sayers, John
C. Heenan, Jem Mace and Tom Allen.
Admitting that he did, I fail to see how he can
hope to teibs that those men were superior
to the fighters of to-day. Heenan never won
afight, although he should have gained a de-
cision over Tom Sayers, who had previously
been whipped by Nat Langham, whom Harry
Orme defeated. Then, too, Heenan was
whipped by Morrissey and King, the lattex
being beaten by Mace, with whom Coburn
fought two drawn battles. Mace also
beat Allen, who was whipped by
Goss, whom Ryan defeated. Paddy in
turn being knocked silly in short order by
John L. Sullivan. So of all those whom]
suppose this able (?) writer mentioned not
one was an ‘‘undefeated.’” Whereas Demp-
sey never sustained a defeat in the ring.
Donovan won and held the middle- weight
championship, and Sullivan never had an op-
ponent who tried him until good fortune on
Mitchell's part enabled the latter to obtain a
verdict of ‘‘draw’’ with the ‘‘big feliow.’’

P. J.

title: Tom Allen Comments on Fighter's Condition Before Championship
text:
Il’S ALL THE TALK,
Pugilism and the Pending Fight the
Absorbing Sunday Topic in
the Crescent City.

New Orteans, La., July 7.—There is noth-
ing of a Sunday character about the aspect of
this city today. St. Charles, Washington
und Canal, Rampart and Prytania streets are
slive with people, mostly nonresident, how-
syer, wha have come to witness the great
“mill” and who are anxious at all cost not to
miss any details of the great encounter. The
jemand for seats in the inner ring was
30 great this morning that by 10
Sclock the entire capacity of the ring, 800
seats, had been disposed of. Then the festive
speculator began to get in his work and soon
it began to be whispered about that inner
ring tickets could be purchased from specu-
ators at prices ranging from $25 to $0. Sey-
>ral tickets were disposed of at prices mid-
way between these figures, but in one or two
~ases outside price was paid.

Col R. B. Garrett, general southern ar
senger agent of the Queen and Crescent °
road Company, estimates that there will be
2,500 people on the eroence, and that gate
receipts will approximate $30,000, Of this
;mount the railroad company only receives
2 a ticket—say $5,000 in all. The remainder
will be divided between the combatants, after
first deducting expenses. The understand-
ing is that if, from any cause, the — is
prevented, the purchasers of tickets
will get all their money _ back
but $2 for actual railroad fares. The
net proceeds of the gate money will be di-
vided in the following proportions: Sixty per
— to the winner and 40 per cent. to the

oser.

The St. Charles Hotel, which is directly o
posite the Queen and Crescent ticket office, 1s
the accepted headquarters of the visiting
sae | and its famous rotunda and piazza has
been trowded all day with visiting pugilistic
celebrities. Tom Allen, Joe pangs ME
St. Joe Kid, Joe Murphy, ike
Cleary and a multitude of other fistic
heroes were prominent figures in the vicin-
ity of the hotel during the progress of the
day. To-morrow’s fight was of course the
prevailing topic of discussion. Sullivan con-
tinues the favorite of the talent, but —
sentiment, that is to say, a public sentiment
which is backed by pa and not money,
is all in favor of Kilrain. The genteel element
of the community are almost unanimously
in favor of Kilrain. They consider the
Boston man nothing better than 4
brute, and want to see him whipped.
but they are notinclined to back their pref.
erence. At the clubs to-day the genera.
sentiment was: “We hoped Kilrain will
win,” but when abet was offered the clut
men wanted 2to1. Even the ladies are simi
larly inclined and their sympathies are with
the Baltimore man.

AT SULLIVAN'S HEADQUARTERS,

At Sullivan’s headquarters to-day there
was no departure from the usual air of quiet
confidence. Among the visitors were
Sheriff Malloy, Chief of Police
Hughes of Louisville; Jake Bar
nett of New York and Charles yi
Johnson, one of Suilivan’s backers. They
were entertained in the parlors by Muldoon
while Sullivan remained in seclusion on the
floor above. Sullivan passed a lazy, luxurious
day. His appetite is enormous. For break.
fast he ate a good-sized bass, five soft-broiled
eggs, a half loaf Graham bread ja half dozen
sliced tomatoes. The only liquid he took was
acupoftea. After breakfast Muldoon oh
him a shave, during the course of which
he fell asleep, and while in that condition
Muldoon left him. At 1 o’clock he dined,
consuming his usual quota of three chickens
with rice und chicken broth, anda balf loaf
of bread.

There is still some conflict of opinion as to
Kilrain’s condition. Some think he is too
fat; others too lean. A reporter surprised
Tom Allen, the famous pugilist, taking a
lemonade inthe rotunda of the St. Charles
Hotel. He was asked for his opinion. He
said, ‘I am for Kilrain.”

The reporter requested an opinion as to Kil
rain’s condition. Allen replied;

“It is good, bat | would iike him better if
he were not so fat. I like to seé the cheek.
bones sticking out.”

So there you are. The talent generally con.
sider Kilrain too light and Tom thinks him
too heavy. Everybody is at sea and the bet-
ting is taking curious shoots. Bets are being
made that Sullivan will win in less than six
rounds, and so it goes. Thus far little money
has been wagered here. The Kilrain men in.
sist on odds of two to one. The other side ure
willing to concede $100 to 875, but there is nc
disposition to close at these figures.
summary: The St. Louis Republic reported that Tom Allen, the famous pugilist, was spotted at the St. Charles Hotel in New Orleans offering his expert opinion on a fighter's physical condition in preparation for a major championship bout.

At midnight it was reported that
Gov. Nicholls had been concil-
iated. He issued a proclamation
calling on the Queen & Crescent Railroad Co.
to furnish transportation by reeular or special
train for the State militia, to curry them to
the scene of the fight, forthe purpose of pre-
venting the mill. The railroad company
bowed graciously to the gubernatorial de-
cree and informed Nicholls that they would
be delighted t» carry the soldiers to

terms of the proclamation, but they were very
sorry to say that they could not letthe Gov-

a.m. As the fighters were already

103 miles from New Orleans, and the excur-
sionists under way this arrangement could
not do any harmina the way of deferring the
fight, and when the sports heard of the rail-
road company’s sharp trick they laughed
heartily.

The principals and seconds left the city on
special trains comprising the Kilrain party,
Mitchell, Masterson, Moore and Stevenson.
With Snilivan were Muldoon,Cleary and Wake-
ly. Harding, the representative of R. K. Fox,
was fired bodily from the speciai train carry-
ing the Suliivan party. The men arrived on
the ground at 6:30 o’clock last night.

SULLIVAN’S BARBER.

The Post-DiIspatcH correspondent yester-
day caught the tonsorial artist who cared for
Suilivan. In response to the question:
‘How did you find Sullivan?’’ he
said: ‘‘Sullivan is aging. His hair is gray and
his eye has Jost its brilliancy; yet when speak-
ing of himself he does not seem to apprehend
any difficulty in besting his man. While he
also says Kilrainis better than Ryan he will
lick him just the same.’’ Sullivan is only
drinking Bass’ ale. Kilrain is using cham-
pagne moderately.

A notable trio of the past age of pugilists
are he e, Tom Allen, Joe Coburn and Tom
Kelly. They all agreed upon Kilrain being
the winner.

Tom Allen said yesterday that Kilrain wouid
win. ‘‘Heisagoodun,’’ said Tom, ‘‘or the
big money would not be staked for him.’’

The Daly brothers, who are here, were
equally confident of John L. winning,

THE MONEY FOUGHT FOR.

The money involved inthe fight was very
much greater than in any battle known in tne
b story ofthe prize ring, The stakes were
$10.000 a side, making $20,000 altogether.
About 800 inner ring tickets were soid at $15
each or $12,000 altogether. It is reported
that 3,00 outer ring tickets went at $10,
which makes $30,000. The total of the money
for which the men contested therefore was
$62,000. Of this the stakes ali go to the winner.
The ‘‘gate momey,’’ after expenses are paid,
was distributed in the proportion of 60 per
cent to the winner and 40 per cent to
the loser. The Queen & Crescent
Railway got $2 a ticket for every ‘‘excursion-

—For writing up the Weir-Murphy fight

California Athletic club has expelled M. J.

was struck down suddenly with paralysis,
but eventually recovered 80 far as to be able
to get about. He, however, had another
stroke on January 16, and, getting gradually
worse, ne expired at his residence, Hungary
street, Sheffield, three days later.

The Kansas Conference to Be Held To-

Day—Insurance Companies Sue the

[ron Mountain for Cotton Losses ;
—Central Traffic Association.

Special to The Republic,

Cuicaco, IL, Feb. 7.—The reduction of
Nebraska grain rates complicates the West.
ern freight problem more than the announced
reduction of the Burlington anc Northern.
The reduction is not enough to even furnish
an object lesson to the farmers in the way 0!
a break in the market for it amounts to only
from 4¢ cents to2cents a bushel. On the
other hand the reduction, being on through
business only, will work greatly tc
the detriment of lines ending &t
the Missouri River. Instead of breaking
bulk at the river as has been the case
heretofore, all grain at the reduced rate will
be carried to Chicago or the seaboard on
through bills of lading. The St. Paul, Chicago,
St. Paul and Kansas City and the Alton are
thus deprived of their shares of what has
heretofore been competitive business. Vice-
President McMullin of the Alton says his road
will meet the rate vd shrinking the local the
amount of the reduction in the throagh rate
if the- reduction cuts much of a figure in
changing the © routin of grain.
President Stickney of the Chicago, St. Paul
and Kansas City is also prepared to make the
same reduction, but in any event the farmers
wil! not get the benefit of the reduction, the
price of corn already having gone down to an
amount equal to the reduction in rates.

Chairman Walker headed last night a dele-
gation of railroad men who went to Topeka to
consider to-morrow the lowering of grain rates
in Kansas. Aconferénce will be held with
the Kansas Railroad Commission, which has
made a demand on the Transmissouri Asso-
ciation for a reduction of grain rates in Kan-
sas. From the strictures 9 Nebraska on the
board of transportation of that State for
accepting such a small reduction in rates, it
is the general opinion that the roads must
concede a greater Yeduction in Kansas,
although a determined attempt will be made
to use the Nebraska reduction asa precedent.

THE KANSAS CONFERENCE.

Special to The Repubile.

Topexa, Kas.,Feb. 7.—The representatives
of all the railroads will meet with Gov. Hum-
phrey to-morrow to discuss the question of
an emergency corn rate. The conference is
in ip to a letter in which he stated that
the situation demanded a reduction of the
rates oncorn. At present it cost nearly as
mutch to — itto market as the corn is
worth. It will be poor gy | to have united
action by the lines east of the Missouri River
as well as in Kansas.

Freight Traffic Complications.

Special to The Republic.

Curcaco, Feb. 7.—Two additional compli-
cations in the Western situation developed
to-day. The Milwaukee and Northern, con-
necting with the Sooand Canadian Pacific
at Pembina, notified their competitors that
they would put in force between Fort
Howard and Green Bay, Wis., and New
York and Boston rates on grain and other
freight much less than the present rates.
Some of the new tariffs have been issued but
none have as yet reached Chicago. The old
roads heretofore participating in this traffic
will have to meet the Northern competition
by rates from Chicago and Milwaukee, which
will cause a general reduction to all points in
Northern Michigan and Northern Wisconsin
and a consequent rearrangement of through
rates. The other complication is notice from
the Manitoba, or Great Northern, thatif the
Burlington and Northern puts in its proposed
reduction it will meet at the Missouri River
at Sioux City the through rate over the
Burlington and Northern to St. Paul. This
would wipe out the tariffs of the Chicago-
Missouri River lines, and it is hardly thought
matters will come to such a crisis.

Edwin Gould’s Progress.

Special to The Republic.

Datuas, Tex., Feb. 7.—Messrs. Edwin
Gould, W. B. Doddridge, H. G. Fleming and
A. H. Swanson and other prominent railway
officials spent the day in Dallas, In a confer-
ence with leading citizens it was decided to
bring the Cotton Pe 3 road into Dallas with-
out delay. Col. at ‘Meek and_ President
Morgan Jones of the Fort Worth and
Denver are also here, and it is understood
that this road has secured entrance into Dal-
las also.

HE SHINES ON SHERMAN,

Special to The Republic,

Superman, Tex., Feb. 7,—Edwin Gould,
Receiver Swanson and General Manager
Doddridge of the Cotton Belt route arrived
here to-night on atour of inspection of their
lines. The citizens will entertain the party
to-morrow and will show them over the city.
They wilt leave here for St. Louis to-morrow
evening.

Gone Up in Smoke.

Special to The Republic.

Livre Rock, Ark., Feb. 7.—Just $6,103,900
worth of railroad bonds went up in smoke to-
day in the big stove of the State Treasurer’s
office while the Governor and his staff gazed
on officially. This burnt offering consisted
of $160,000 Arkansas Central Railroad
bonds with $836,000 coupons at-
tached ; $498,000 Little Rock and
Fort Smith, with $1,045,500 coupons attached.
These bonds were made under an act ap-
proved July 21, 1568. fois 4 were deposited in
the Treasurer's office, but never issued.
Other bonds of this same series are still in
existence, bearing the date of April 1, 1869,
and signed by P. C. and J.R. Berry. These
bonds, it will be remembered, bad their origin
in a private scheme of Gov. Clayton’s admin-
istration to encourage railroad building in
Arkansas by means of State aid.

The Cotton {nsurance Case.

Special to The Republic.

Litrie Rock, Ark., Feb. 7.—The mucb
postponed and celebrated suit of the Marine
Insurance Co. of London vs. the St. Louis,
Tron Mountain and Southern Railway Com-
pany was begun in the United States Court
here to-day. Twelve of the most prominent
business menof Little Rock compose the
jury. This is one of the many cases that
arose from the great cotton fire
in. this city in i877, at which several
thdusand bales of cotton were destroyed.
The insurance companies, 80 in all, paid the
losses, and afe now claiming damages from
the [ron Mountain people, alleging that the
fire originated from @ passing engine on the
river bank, near where the cotton was etored.
Eight hundred thousand dollars is the aggre.
gate amount of damages to the insurance
companies. The present case will continue
for several days.

A Costa Rica Kailroad.

Cuicaco, Feb. 7.—Senor Manual Aragon,
delegate to the Pan-American congress from
Costa Rica, now in this city, yesterday re-
ceived acablegram from home stating that
his government had just issued a grant to an
English company tobuild a railroad from Sau
Jose to Esperda. “That is excellent news,”
he remarked. ‘“‘When that division is com-
pleted Costa Rica will have an interoceanic
railway, and one can go across the peninsula
in 10 hours. The road will be 36 miles long.
Although it will be built across the Andes,
there are no difficult feats of engineering and
the line ought to be finished in a year. With
the Nicaragua canal and a railway from the
Pacific to the Atlantic, Costa Rica will have
a regular American boom.”

They Want Less Work.

One of the sections of a bill prepared bj
the Federation of Railway Men to be pre
sented to the different State Legislatures
calls for the employment of one brakeman
for each 10 freight cars while en route
Another section of the bill reads as follows:
“The regular day for train service and fo
persons employed for such purposes shall be
eight hours out of each 24, and no man shal
be required or compelled to work for any
longer time or any more hours within each
24 hours.” The 100,000 members of the fed.
eration in support of this measure assert
that railroad accidents occur more frequently
because trainmen are overworked than from
any other cause.

Immigrant Cleartng House.

New York, Feb. 7.—The presidents of the
Trunk lines met —— to tackle the
knotty problem of the immigrant clearing
house, and were unable to do anything with
it. Atthe last meeting Mr. Depew was ap
aoe a committee to labor with Mr.

3ioan of the Lackawanna, but his efforts
availed noting. The whole subject was
referred to arb g =
