More Ives-Staynor Trouble.

Batrmore, Md., Feb. 7.—An attachment
under the act of 1888 against non-residents
was issued from the Court of Common Pleas
to-day at the suit of the Mineral Range
Railroad Company of Michigan against
Henry S. Ives, Geo, B. Staynor and Thos.
C. Doremus, who compose the firm of Henry
S. Ives & Co. of New York. The claim of the
Mineral Range Co. against Ives & Co. is for
$450,968. It is represented that Ives & Co.
were the financial agents in New York of the
Mineral Range Co., and are indebted to it for
securities, property and money received. The
object of bringing the attachment
in this judicial foriadiction is
to summon Mr. bert Garrett
as garnishee to the amount of ge This
was paid to him by Ives nearly three years
ago asapartof the consideration tor the
purchase of the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad
stock held and controlled by Mr. Garrett and
as a guarantee of good faith in the transac-
tion, The vatiroet company claims that Mr.
Garrett 1s not entitled to retain the money
paid him by Ives, ona that it is subject to
attachment in his hands by the creditors of
Ives & Co. Mr. Garrett holds that the mon
was forfeited to him vy Ives’ failure to carry
out his ae of the contract and purchase the
stock. Ives was to have paid $225 a share for
it, the par value being $100. He found he
could not raise the money, although the time
was extended a month. Mr. Garrett sailed
for Europe soon after the expiration of the )
time. |

meal. The burglars bad gone about thei:
workinthe most daring manner. A clear
white cloth had been spread over the table
and plates, knives and forks iaid upon it
The edibles were taken from the refrig
erator apd consisted of roast beef
ham, cantaloupe, potatoes, milk, bread
butter, watermelon and various dishe
of dessert. The contents of a bottle contain
ing whiskey and sulphur, which was used b:
the family for medicinal purposes, had als
disappeared.

It is believed that the robbers had secrete:
themselves in the dwelling before the occu
pants retired, and began their work when a)
were asleep.

Coburn was America’s leading pugilist
twenty-five years «go, and bis career from
boyhood was one of many exciting incidents.
He was born on July 4, 1835, in the County
Armagh, Ireland, and came to this country
when 8 years of age.

He grew up in the Sixteenth Ward, this city,
and at the age of 18 yeurs he became
prominentas a fighter by whipping all the
boys of the ward. He joined the Volunteer
Fire Department four years later, after learn-
ing the trade of a bricklayer. He was a
member of Croton EngineUo. No. 16, at
thattime liccated in West Twentieth street.
While in the Fire Department the firemen
matched him against a Brooklyn boy, whom
he bested easily in four rounds.

FIRST BIG FIGHT.

Coburn first became notorious as a fighter

by defeating ‘‘Awful’’ Gardner, one cf the

cleverest men of bis day, in six rounds, with
gloves, in Hibernia Hall, on Prince street.

He was then locked upon as a coming cham-

pion. About this time Ned Price, anoted

English boxer, but pow a well-known crim!-

nal lawyer, challenged’ any man in the werld

to fight him. Coburn went to Boston and
arranged a match.

They fought at Still Pond, Mass., and after
three hours and twenty-five minutes of des-
perate fightingthe referee declared the battle
adraw on account of darkness. Both men
were confined to their rooms fortwo weeks
from the terridie punishment they received.
Ceburn issued a challenge to fight Price
again, but the iatterrefused. This was Co-
burn’s first London rule contest, and the
battle was one of the greatest ever witnessed
in America up to that period.

In the latter part of 1858 Coburn whipped
Harry Gribbin in a half hour at Harper’s
Ferry, Va.

THE BATTLE

was for $1,000 aside. Hen Winkles, the West-
ern crack, was next beaten by Joe in eighteen
minutes, under London rules, for a $i,000
stake. Coburn was then matched to fight
Mike McCool,the ‘*Terror of the Mississippi,’’
for $2,500 a side and the championship of
America. He defeated McCool in one hour
and ten minutes. Coburn escaped without a
scratch. The battle cook piace in the summer
of 18363. He was matched to fight McCool
again ayear later. The battle was to have
taken place on the outskirts of Indianapolis,
buta sheriff appeared upon the scene and ar-
rested both principais. They were sentenced
to forty days’ imprisonment. After thelr re-
lease the match fell through.

Patsey Fivuancame over from England in
the spring of 1567 and issued a challenge. Co-
burn accepted, and they fought in a saioon for
$1,000 a side. Fiynn lasted two minutes and
thirty seconds. A short time after Coburn
whipped Oon Fitzgerald, a New Yerker,

WITH TWO PUNCHES,

one in the st mach and the other on the neck.

His next important match was in England

with Jem Mace for $5,000 a side and the cham-

pionship ofthe world. Before making the
match, however, the Mace party pitted Joe

Goss, Tom Aflen and Bill Rayel against Joe to

see what he coulddo. He bested them all.

Coburn tossed for caoice of battle ground

with Mace, which wasto be within 600 miles

of London. Coburn won the toss, and he
selected the county iu which he was born.

Mace finally forfeited the £200. Coburn re-

turned to America and challenged Mace, but

ithe latter wouldn’t accept. Fimally Mace
~_ to America and opened a saicon on

I'wenty-third street near Sixth avenue.

- This was in thespring of 1870. Mace, upon

being challenged continually by Coburn, re-

plied that he didn’t come here to fight, but
to live in peace. Dan Noble, a prominent
sporting man, who subsequentiy died in
prison in London, wasa warm friend of Co-
burn’s. He bet Joe $50 that he was afraid to
go over to

MACE’S SALOON

and punch him in the face. Coburn ac-

cepted the wagerin an instant. Coburn met

Mace and tried todraw him on to fight, but

Mace declined. Coburn finally called hima

cur, and then blackened his eye bya blow of

his fist. Mace could do nothing after this |
but challenge Coburn. Joe wus only too)
giad to meet hisold rival, and «match wa
ppednily arranged. They met at Port Dover,

Canada. Alter fighting one hour and fifteen

minutes, and neither having strueka biow,

the Sheriff and a posse of deputies appeared
and ordered them off Canadian soil. Dick

Hollywood, the referee, commanded the men

to meet at the Reade House, Erie, Pa., at8

e’clock the following morning. Coburn, on
arriving at the hotel, went to Mace’s room
and offered to fight him then and there.

Mace refused to do anything but what the
referee ordered. Hollywood then named
Kaneas City as the place of fighting. Coburn
declined, as it wasa violation of the rules,
which called for the battle ground to be within
500 miles of New York. The men were matched
again for $5,000 aside and the championship.
The battle took place at Bay City, Miss., in
the latter partof 1572, and during a terrible
rainetorm. After fighting three hours and
thirty minutes, and a greater part of the time
up to their Knees in the mud, the referee
Called the fight a draw.

Coburn after this battle made tours of the
country with combination companies. Dur-
ing tie yeur of i884 he went through the
States with John L. Sullivan. Of late years
he has been in the saloon business.

Coburn had a large number of friends, and
was generally considered a geod-natured
man. He got into many disagreeabie scrapes,
however, the most unfortunate of which was
his shooting of a policeman, for which he was
tried, convicted aud sent to the State Prison
for a sort term.

Joe Coburn is dead. Twenty-five years |

Coburn was born in County Armagh, Ire-

York City, and at the age of 18 he became

Cobura first became known to fame as a

arkness. Both men *were contined to

His next important match was in England

championship of the world. Erato an hiNe

Joe Goss, Tom Allen and Bill = against |
Joe to see what he could do. He bested
them all. Coburn tossed for choice of battle, |
grouud with Mace, which was to be within
500 miles of London. Coburn won the toss,
and he selected the county in which he was
born. Mace finally forfeited the £200,

Coburn returned to America and challenged
Mace, but the latter would notaccept. This
was in the spring of 1870. Mace, upon being
challenged continually by Coburn, replied that
he did pt ervey here to fight, but tolive in
peace. H as finally henge: on toa fight,
‘however. They met at Port Dover, Canada.
After fighting ono hour and’ 15 mioutes, and
neither having struck a blow, the Sheriff or-
dered them off Canadian soil. Dick Holly-
wood, the referee, commanded the mento
meet at the Reade House, Erie, Pa., at 8
o'clock the following morning. Coburn, on
arriving at the hotel, went to Mace’s room

there. Mace refused to do sages

Coburn after this battle made tours of the
country with combinations. During the
year of 1884 he went through the States

three days he had been unconscious most of

THE RING.

Tem McGregor,the St. Joe Kid, who has
spent so much of his time in St. Louis for the
past year or so, is now in Galveston and has
put up $100 with E. T. Dodds, manager. of the
Gaiveston Athletic Club, io fight either
Arthur Upham or P.J.Pitzlin. It is ex-
pected the club will offer a purse for the
fight in case a match ismade. McGregor
has sent to the Police Gazette the following
characteristic letter:

GALVESTON, Tex., Jan. 1, 1891.
Richard K. Fox: ;

I see that Prof. P. J. Pitzlin is itching for a
go with Jack Dempsey. I Know it is all to
swell Pitzlin, but I will bet a thousand to a
hundred that he will itch for many days after
if he ever should be so unfortunate as to run
against Dempsey. I have one hundred up
with E. T. Dodds, manager of the club, to’
fight Pitzlin for any amount from a broken |
Cigarette up to any amount he can rake,
scrape, beg or borrow. He claimed he fought
and defeated me in three rounds, which
everyone in St. Louis knows is _ the biggest
untruth he ever told in his life. The only way
he would fight was for me to split the money
with him, win or lose, so lI think itis no more
than right for meto be heard in the Police
Gazette. Respectfully yours, .

| L. S. MCGREGOR, St. Joe Kid.
- The Philadelphia papers passed over with
-twoorthree lines of commenta four-round
bout that took place atthe Philadelphia A.
C. last Wednesday night between Billy Dacey
of this city and Waiter Campbell, the boxing
instructor of the Athletic Club of the Schuyl-
kill Navy and universally the idol of all
Quaker City lovers of sparring, says the
New York Sun. ANew York drummer who
was atthe bout told a Sun reporter on Satur-
day, however, that the go was oneof the
liveliest and, at the same time,most interest-
ingly scientific he had ever seen. As this
criticism was made by one who has followed
athletics from youth, and who never misses
a good scrap that comes off within twenty
miles of wherever he may be, ftis worth re-
cording. The gentleman who has no per-
sonal interest in eit her man, added that per-
haps the papers didn’t make much of the go
because the Philadelphia Adonis got the
worst of it.

The men boxed with two-ounce gloves, an
unusually small glove fora public show. Im-.

mediately aiter they shook hands Campbell
stepped back. and bang! bang! went one fist
afterthe other con Dacey’s right cheek. The
blows landed like lightning, and cut the New
Yorker’s cheek a little under the eye, besides
raising something of acushion. Dacey was
taken by surprise, not having expected to
take part in more than an ordinary peer
bout, ae the size of the gloves shoul
have warned him that something unusual
was up.

He rallied inan instant, however, and it
could be seen that he realized that he was up
against something. He measured the situa-
tion correctly and promptiy proceeded to
hammer the -handsonie Campbell, who ranks
asa boxer with any instructor in the coun-
try. Dacey couldn’t reach his face, as Camp-
bell was tootall, but he gotin some of the
wickedest kind of punches on the Philadel-
phian’s stomach and continued fast work on
Campbell’s wind throughout the four rounds
without receiving another blow that hurt.
According tothe Sun reporter’s informant if
the bout had lasted another round Campbell
would have had to give up or be knocked out.

title: Carroll Never Had Chance to Win
text:
PENDRAGON ON COBURN.
<= Se :
THE ENGLISH SPORTING WRITER DIS-
CUSSES THE DECEASED PUGILIST.
Jack McAuliffe and Billy Myer Matched—
The Association Again Put Into the
Soup by the National League—Sporting
News in General.

Henry Sampson, whoas Pendragon of the
London Referee has a world-wide reputation
as a writer in pugilism, reviews the late Joe
Coburn as follows:

**In the course of last week two old-time
fighting men passed away, Harry Poulson
and Joe Coburn, the one an Englishman and
the other an American. Isuppose it is cor-
rect to say that Joe Coburn was an American.
He was always an American, and very much
an American, asa fighting man; as a matter
of absolute nationality he was born at
Armagh, in the now more than ever
distressful country, somewhere about fifty-
six or fifty-seven years ago, and was, at the
beginning of the hegira which took place
shortly afterward, transported to the land of
the star-spangled banner. Thereis not much
opportunity of knowing exactly what class of
fighter Coburn was, and whenhe came over
here with the expressed intention of fighting
Mace, who was then champion, the men did
not get into the ring, and, sofar as I know,
Coburn never showed his form even with the
gloves in this country. The conditions
of the match with Mace were
that it should be for £500 a side, the
battie to be fought in Ireland, and Coburn
was to receive £100 for traveling and other
expenses. Coburn received his £100, but on
his arrival in Dublin, where the high con-
tracting parties all met, he would not consent
to enter the ring or take off his clothes unless
his mother or his aunt, or some other near
and dear relation, was appointed referee.
The affair ended in one ofthe hollowest and
most lamentable failures that even the prize
ring has been able tobringabout. To say
this is to say a great deal, as some of the
worst and most ludicrous flascos this world
has ever known must, one way or another,
have come in connection with prize fight-
ing. But it was so, and there is no
use attempting to disguise or deny it. Ire-
member the circumstances (just over twenty-
six years ago) perfectly well, and don’t know
where their equal could be found for blatant
false pretense and arrant humbug. Till this
day what class of man Coburn really was re-
mains a mystery. If he could fight Mace for
three hours 2nd a half, even in a swamp, and
our old man really meant fighting, he must
have been abit of a goodone. But ourold
man didn’t always mean fighting; and it
might have happened besides that any undue
desire on his part to punch Coburn’s head
would have ended in his own being riddled
with a score or so of bullets.

MYER AND M’AULIFFE MATCHED.

Jack McAuliffe of Brooklyn,the light-weight
champion of America, and Billy Myer, the
Streator Cyclone, have been matched to fight
with gloves for a stake of $,000a side and the
largest purse that can be secured. James
Colville of Boston is McAuliffe’s backer and
Alf Kennedy of Streator, Ill., is Myer’s. A
deposit of $250 a side has been made with Bud
Renaud of New Orleans. A purse of $7,000
has been offered for the contest by the
Olympic Club, but McAuliffe hopes to receive
an offer of $10,000 from the Puritan Club of
Long Island City. If the latter organization
secures the contest there will not be any
stake or side bet, the purse only being fought
for. This is because the officers of the club
are friends of McAuliffe, and while Myer is
willing to fight the New Yorker even before
that organization, he and his backer do not
feel disposed to risk any stake money to the
decision of men who are Known to sympathize
with and favor his antagonist. The match
between Jimmy Carrell and Jack McAullife,
for which the Olympic Club offered $10,000 and
the Puritans $11,000, willnot be made, Fitz-
simmons’ trainer declaring that there is
more money in managing the New Zealander.
It would appear from this that despite all his
howling and talk Carroll was not very anxious
for a return battle with the New Yorker, but
was satified to stand pat on his defeat al-
ready sustained. McAuliffe’s friends
always declared that the news-
paper reports of the fight before the
California Club were all highly coiored in
Carroll’s favor, and that there was notruth
in the assertion that the crafty little English-
man hadthe best of the contest up tothe
time that McAuliffe delivered the knock-out
blow. The McAuliffe men say that Carroll
never had achanceto win, the New Yorker
outclassing him from the star Billy Myer
has been anxious fora go with either of the
men,and McAuliffe in particular. He has
agreed to fight the New Yorker even before
the latter’s favorite ciub, the Puritan, and
has also agreed to the champion’s conditions
as to weight, 135 pounds, give or take two
pounds. This permits the men to weigh in
ati37 pounds, four pounds above the gen-
erally accepted light-weight limit, which is
133 pounds. The Queensbury rules limit,
however, ts 140 pounds and McAuliffe has
been standing on this fact. He is getting too
heavy to train down to i133 pounds without
weakening himself. Dick Roche, the head of
the Puritan Club, was McaAuliffe’s backer
when the latter fought Myer a draw, and
only the Streator boy’s great desire to have
another go at the champion would induce
him to fight before that club.

JACK FOGHRTY TO RETIRE.

Pringle in the Pittsbug Dispetch has always
been a friend and admirer of Jack Fogarty,
the Pennsylvania middle-weight. He has
held that Fogarty was a mere boy when he
fought and was defeated by Jack Dempsey
and that he had not fully developed, and
therefore not the fighter he should be now
that he has reached maturity. Hereis what
Pringle has to say of his favorite:

Jack Fogarty, after vainly trying to se-
cure a battle with any middle-weight in
America, or any other country, for that mat-
ter, has decided to retire from all pugilistic
business. His judgment in this instance may
be wisest, certainly he will in the long run
be the gainer. I have always held the
opinion that Fogarty. wouid be a
dangerous opponent for any man his weight.
Apparently champions and aspiring cham-
plons have held a similar opinion, because
they have steadily declined to meet him, I
Know personally that all Kinds of efforts have
been made in behalf of Fogarty to secure him
a contest with eitherLa Blanche, Dempsey,
Young Mitchell, in short, any middle-weight
inthe world. Theclubs or ‘‘pub-clubs,’’ as
somebody calis them, have strictly adhered
to their custom of keeping their favorites busy
and asa result some ofthe veriest pugilistic
frauds have been put into these pub-club
rings to fight for big purses, real or alleged.
It is a pity that Fogarty has not hada chance
since he became a man to tackle one ofthe
very best ofthe champions. He may, how-
ever, change hismind. He says he won’t.

THE RING.

Many champions have falien hard and suad-
den, but few with the severity and speed of
Jack Dempsey, writes Macon. His skill and
quickness were so great that, though he was
never more thana good ten-stone man, his.
Many victims were men bigger, stronger and
heavier than himself, and finally deceived
him and his admirers into the belief that,bar-
ring the champion of allchampions, he was_
virtually invincible. |

His defeat by La Blanche did not naturally
change this opinion, forit was looked upon
asanunilucky fluke due to a chance blow,
put the pitiable exhibition he made with Bob
Fitzsimmons emphasizes in the most marked
manner the old sporting proverb: ‘‘A good
little man cannot whip a good big one.’’

Now let me say right here that, though
there was less than five pounds difference in
the weight of the Australian and Dempsey,
in reality Jack was at least two sizes smaller
than his opponent. This difference was so
apparent when they faced each other for the
first round that a gentleman who sat inthe
box immediately behind my seat exclaimed:
“*Why,this man Fitzsimmons is big enough
to fight Sullivan!’’ and so he was. Dempsey
looked like a pigmy in front of him.

The Australianisthe biggest man for his
weight leversaw, with one exception, and
that was the late Tom Ryan, the sporting |
printer. Tom was five feet ten inches tall, if
Iremember rightly, and could fight well and |
strong at 108 pounds. Ihave seen him spar
with Joe Coburn, Tom Allienand Jem Mace,
and make a rattling good showing with them,
too. In fact, they could do nothing with him
as longas they Wayed lightly. They had to
put steam to their blows to keep him from
being all over them.

Well, Fitzsimmons is better than Jake Kil-
rain, Jack Ashton, Joe Lannon or George
Godfrey, and his frame is as large as either’s.
Up tothe time that he defeated Billy Mc-
Carthy in California he was as poor as a
church mouse. He didn’t have the money
to pay for even a steerage passage from Mel-
bourne to this country, and he came here asa
stowaway, and worked his passage after his
discovery on the ship by washing down the
decks and such like employment. A pint of
porter or a dram of grog was the extent of his
liquid refreshment a year ago. Now he is
drinking champagne, and by the time he has
devoured the tenderloins of a score of Amer-
ican beeves he will have the meat on his
frame that nature designed it tocarry. Then
he willbe in his proper class, and he will
have to <o up against the Choyinskis and the
Peter Noians of the ring, and not the 154-
pounders.

MRS. WOODWORTH’S TEMPLE.
The Lady Evangelist Again Agitates the
Raising of Money.

- Last night Mrs. Woodworth announced
from the pulpit her intention of building her
proposed temple in this city, and urged those

having made donations to pay in the
amounts, as she desired to purchase the lot
as soon as possible.

‘*We must havea house of worship in St.
Louis at all hazards,’’ said Mrs. Woodworth,
‘‘and when we get a lot the securing of funds
to erect a permanent structure will be more
easy, as the people will see that we are thor-
oughly in earnest, and be more willing to
make donations.

| Rev. Wm. Jones, pastor of the Floating
Bethel of Cincinnati, a reformed sport and
sailor, preached for Mrs. Woodworth last
night and will do soagain. Mr. Jones tellsa
story of his Mfe that rivals that of Francis
Murphy. At the age of 16 he was
a prize fighter, being backed as
a boy wonder inthe ring by Tom Allen of St.
Louis. Heafterwards became a sailor and
developed the usual tendency of people so
employed for strong drink. He was arrested
and locked up thirty-nine times by the police
on various offenses. Several years ago he
reformed and has since been working among
the poorer classes in Cincinnati. Rev. Jones
is a forceful, though not learned talker, and
thinks that Mrs. Woodworth is a wonderful
worker. He will probably go back to Cincin-
nati Tuesday.

Rev. H. H. Spiherof Springfield, Ill., who
hadso much success in preaching for Mrs.
Woodworth last week, is expected to return
the latter partof this week and again get
down to work. Rev. Spiher regards St. Louis
one of the best flelds in which he has yet been
engaged with Mrs. Woodworth, and says
that he expects to see a magnificent temple
erected here for the glorification of the
**power.’*’ Mrs. Woodworth promises to soon
give out a list of late cures, which, she says,
are growing more numerous at each meeting.

The Doe’s Origin.
{From Harper’s Young People.)

Dogs belong to the species that naturalist
call Canide. Thisis a family of carnivorou:
mammals, to be found in nearly every part of
the globe. The dog existed ina domesticated
state during prehistoric times, and therefore
we are unable to solve the question of its ori-
gin. Baron Georges Cuvier, the gréat French
naturalist, who could, it is said, ary ae single
bone of an animal, even though it longed
to an extinct race, consfruct the complete
skeleton of the animal and determine to what
species it belonged, said that the dog is ‘‘the
completest, the most singular, and the most
useful conquest ever made by man.’’ The
naturalists ‘do not agree in their theories in
regard to the origin of the dog.

Some suppose that allthe breeds of modern
dogs have sprung from.a single source, while
others maintain thatthey are the product of
the ee of several distinct species. Of
those who favor the first idea, the majority
think that the parent of the Gog is the wolf;
some others favor the jackal, while a few are
inclined to believe that dogs are descended

.from an extinct species. These latter point to
the fossil remains of alarge dog found in the

d aan tertiary deposits as the probable wild
stock.

Those who think the wolf to have been the
parent base their theory on the general re-
semblance of the wild wolf to some modern
dogs, and to the further fact that) the tao aod
Maux frequently capture and tame wolves
and cross them with their dogs, so as toim-
prove the breed. The jackal theorists use the
same arguments as those who favor the wolf
idea, and they hayeas many facts to warrant
the supposition. fe ,

But the prevalent idea to-day is that the doz
is a mixture of several species, living and ex-
tinct. This opinion is founded upon the con-
sideration that irom the earliest historic times
there have existed many different ph of
aogs, totally distinct from each other and yet
closely resembling modern forms. |

And then wild hate ee of dogs have existed
in all quarters of the globe, and savages of all
races have been fond of heme | these. It is
unlikely, as Darwin has poin out, that any

one of these breeds should: have

selected for domestication. The fear of

man in wild animals is a gradually acquired

instinct, and before this was developed a race

ofanimals could have becn much more easily
tamed than later. iid

When the Fatkland Islands were first vis-
ited by man. the wild dogs found there ap-
proached him withouteither fear or aversion.

An Important Convention in Session
at Albuquerque, N. M.
Special Dispatch to the Globe-Democrat.

ALBUQUERQUE, N. M., September 16.—Some
three months ago, at the request of numerous
parties interested in the matter, the Governor
of this Territory issued a proclamation call-
ing a general Convention of all those inter-
ested in the sheep and wool industry in all the
States and Territories west of the Mississippi,
to meet at Albuquergue on the 16th and 17th
of rt Sly ABA two days of the annual ex-
hibition of the Territorial Fair. Responses to
that invitation were received by the Commit-
tee of Arrangements from the authorities of
Arizona, Texas, Kansas, Nebraska, Iowa,both
the Dakotas, Montana, wyoming. Colorado
and Idaho, which, including New Mexito,
make twelve States and Territories repre-
sented in the present Convention, The
men who came as delegates are all prac-
tically engaged in the wool business, either as
growers or dealers, and therefore bring to the

iscussion of the subjects coming before the
meeting a snow iodge gainea by Ch eg A
large number of subjects of much interest to
wool men are being brought before tee Con-
vention, and the most cap Saget of these are
probably a resolution in favor of an effort to
secure uniform legislation in all the sheep-
growlng States upon several important points,
such as a genera scab law and laws to Fa
phe the spread of ate rh gy diseases, laws
for the general protection of sheep, an at-
tempt to secure better railway accommoda-
tions, silly net more favorable freight itn 8
and better facilities for the handling ang ng
ping of shéep and wool; the best means to h
adopted to improve the grade of wools: ques-
tions in relation to sorting and handling, and
various other hooks of interest to those en-
gaged in the business. :

ov. Prince called the Convention to order
and delivered the opening address. He re-
fev¥ed to the fact that the delegates were here
in response to his invitation, and he felt grat-
ified to see in attendance such a large number
of intelligent and brogressiye business men,
represcs Sing Roatiy all sections of that great
divéeion of the country west of the Mississippi
River, and feltconfident from the character
of the men he saw before him that their delib-
érations could not fail to result in much good
to the important cause in which they were as-
sembled. . ‘

At the conclusion of his remarks Dr. G, 8.
Easterday, Mayor of the city, welcomed the
delegates to Albuquerque ina tew timely and
pe fold pen remarks, in which he proved
himself as much at home in woo! as in politics
er medicine. The Convention then proceeded
to organize by the election of officers.

<5 Mike Donovan.

HE SENDS THE PROFESSOR A CHECK
THAT WAS PROMPTLY RETURNED.
The Man Who Risked Everything for Him

Gets $250 for His Pains—Starter
Jimmy Rowe’s Career—An Eastern
Writer Scores Von Der Ahe—Gossip

From Turf, Ring and Diamond.

New York, Sept. 20.—Taking up Jim Cor-
bett asa protege turns out a very unsatis-
factory experiment for veteran Mike bono-
van, the boxing instructor of the New York
Athletic Club. Whenthe Californian made
his first visitto the metropolis three years
ago Donovan took a fancy to him and
through his influence Corbett was made a
guest of the New York Athletic Club, an
honor that has fallen to no other pugilist.
The professor was also largely instrumental
in getting on the Corbett-McCaffrey match
and in other ways rendered invaluable ser-
vices to the young stranger,

When Corbett returned to the city after his
battle with Peter Jackson in San Francisco,
the courtesies of the New York Athletic Club
were again extended to htm. Prof. Donovan
proposed the challenge to Sullivan and got
Ed Kearny and other New York Athletic Club
members to put up a large share of Corbett’s
§1,000 . stake. Mike took a prominent
share in making the big match, and
since then has looked after Corbett’s
interests faithfully. It was against the
wishes of prominent officials of the New
York Athletic Club that Donovan went to
New Orleans to act as adviser in Corbett’s
corner, and the matter may yet result unfor-
tunately for him.

After Corbett’s victory Donovan was the
most jubilant man inthe country, for he felt
that he was an especially important factor to
the new champion’s greatness. Corbett won
something like $35,000, and as Donovan had
been in a measure instrumental in obtaining
that money he naturally expected a hand-
some remembrance. Saturday Mike received
a letter from Corbett. There was a familiar
looking narrow slipinthe envelope andthe
professor’s faceexpanded. But ashe read
the figures on the check, the smile
faded. The piece of paper called for $250,
and was so far from Donovan’s expectations
that he immediately returned the check to
Corbett with a few remarks. In reply the
pugilist- asked him what he thought his
services was worth. There was some sur-
prise at Corbett’s action in the matter. Even
those who bear no good will toward the New
York boxing instructor opined that the least
Corbett might have sent would be double the
amount of the check, and that $1,000 would
be nearer the proper caper.

GODDARD ON HIS MUSCLE.
’ PHILADELPHIA, Pa., Sept. 20.—Joe Goddard,
the Australian, bested Dick Wiley of Fair-
mount in three rounds, at the Ariel Athletic
Club, lastnight. The challenger of Corbett
had his man ‘‘out’’ inthe first round when
time was called. The other rounds were
lighter, but Wiley was very groggy at the
end of the third. On Wednesday night at the
Arie] Club Goddard wiil meet Jim McVey,
who helped to train Corbett,
A WELL KNOWN 8ST. LOUIS PUGILIST.

An important omission in Sunday’s article
descriptive of prize fighters who have made
St. Louis their home was the dismissal with a
passing reference of ‘‘Dubiin Tricks,’’ one of
the best Known prize ring characters in this
city in the "60s.

Wm. Blake, or as he was then better
known, Dublin Tricks, was a pugilist of
more than ordinary reputation, who after
his battle with Mike McCoole trained and
handled that worthyin all his subsequent
battles. He also trained Charlie
Gallagher, who met Tom Allen twice,
fefeating him the first time. After
McCoole’s retirement Mr. Blake forsook his
prize-r.ng associations and has followed out
his trade ofshipcarpentering. Throughatyp- |
ographical error Mr. Blake was mentioned
AS a notorious pugiiist instead of a noted one.
Contrary to general opinion he is a native
American. and not of foreign birth. He
boards at the St. Louls House, on Main and
Locust streets, and works for the Anchor
Line and other steamboat companies,

THE ‘‘TERRIBLE BLACKSMITH’’ AFTER FIGHT.

Jim Burge, the Australian Iightweight,
who was known as the ‘‘terrible blacksmith’’
in the Antipodes, and who is now in San
Francisco, is anxious to fight either Billy
Gallagher or George Dawson at 140 pounds,
pr Eilly Dacey, the New York lightweight, or.
any man in America at from 128 to_ 138
pounds. Burge says he fought Dawson three
draws at home and is ready to settle the
— of superiority with him any time he

esires. The ‘‘terridDle blacksmith’’ also
states that his proper fighting weight is from
128 to 130pounds, but he professes to be will-
ing toconcede either Gallagher or Dawson
ten pounds. Ifeitherof the latter accepts
Burge says the conditions must cali
for a weigh-in at the ring side.

Billy Dacey, the New York Hght-
weight, is in San Francisco just at
present, having arrived there with George
Siddons, who is matched to fight Solly Smith
of Los Angeles the latter aps of the present
month, last week. Dacey is always ready or,
atleast, has doneensugh of challenging in
eg years, to lead the public to believe that

eis reomgys be fight anyone at his weight in
America. e now has an opportunity to
demonstrate whether he really is as anxious
to fight as a good many Of his friends believe.

PUGILISTIC POINTERS.

Alarge audience welcomed Jchn L. Sulll-
Van and his new play, entitled ‘‘The Man
from Boston,’’ at Providence, R. 1., last
night.

Since Jim Corbett has become champion he
has recived a number of letters from ladies
and friends in Brooklyn asking him to appear
in that city. Corbett has concluded to oblige
them and will appear Thursday afternoon
and evening in a glovecontest at the Star
Theater.

Tom O’Rourke, George Dixon’s manager,
is making arrangements for a reception the
colored teatherweight champion’s New York
friends will tender him towards the latter
part of the present month in Madison Square
Garden. O’RKourke says that Dixon will meet
JohnnyGrifin for $10,000 a side after next June
when his theatrical contracts expire.

.\ MATCH BETWEEN THE TWO LOCAL
PUGILISTS I3 LIKELY.

Charley Da'ty Offersto Back His Brother
for $500 and Tom Allen Will Furnish
Neil’s Stake—St. Louis Dogs at tha
Pointer Derby—Track Talk—General
Sporting News.

Two local pugilists who are more prone to
ight with their hands than their mouths,a
yuite uncommon proclivity among the local |
fraternity, are going to settle a much-mooted |
jyuestion of superiority. The men referred to
are Johnnie Daly and Frank, alias ‘‘Dutch,’’
Nell. The fightis the outcome of a spirit of
rivairy between the two Market street pugi-
istic resorts. Neil, by iis recent vic-
tories, has become the pride of
tom Kelly’s, and Johonte Daly is
the hero of the habitues of his brother’s re-
sort. There is no personal animosity be-
[weenthe men, but Neil’s recent victories
have led him to belleve that he is the best
manofhis welghtinthecity. Johnnie Daiy
happens to tip the scales in Neil’s neighbor-
hood and, as aconsequence, thinks Dutch is
a littie offon hisjudgment. Both are willing
to put the matter toa test and will glve each
other a bot argument.

Charley Daly announces that he will put up
$500 on behalf of his brother fora finish fight
at catch weights with skin or two-ounce
gloves. Hels willing that the fight should
come off in a room with only five people to a
side witnessing ithe encouter, or he is willing
to have the affair pulled off at Neil’s selec-
tion. Nellis not only willing but anxious
for a go with Johnnie and said yesterday that
jom Allen would see that his $590 was forth-
coming.

Time and place will be decided upon when
the stake money is posted.

Both Dalv and Nell are well known mem-
bers of the local pugilistic fraternity and are
notable more fora willingness to fight than
toissue chaNenges and carry on war in the
newspapers. Both men weigh about 140
pounds. Neilis short and stockily built and
isasureand hardhitter. Daly is taller and
has the advantage of his opponent in reach.
Acontest between the two means a test of
gameness. .

CHICAGO, ILL., November | 18.—‘*Parson’’
Davies arrived in the city from the East to-
jay. Peter Jackson will visit Chicago about
December 5-and remain pee aweek. Josepa
Choynski will arrive about the same time

any reasonable time ‘to | prepare for a

he does think that he| merits some
recornition at Corbett’s hahds. He knows

articles for a battle eight or nine

Wants this affair@off his mind. He fought

leans [announced that, win or lose, Jackson

text:
CRIMSON AND BLUE.

CHARLEY MITCHELL WRITES TOM ALLEN
A CHARACTERISTIC LETTER.
He Says Corbett Will Strike a Surprise
Party Before the Tenth Round—Char-
ley’s Version of His Troubles—Gossip
ofthe Pugilists—Turf Topics—General
Sporting News.
NEw York, Nov. 19.—The sixty days’ reign
of foot-ballas king of sports is nearing Its
end. Foot-ball enthusiasts have no eye
just now for anything but the great game to-
day in Hampden Park, when Yale and Har.
vard will lock horns. The game will be o!
extraordinary interest to the Princeton
eleven, who will tackle the blues on Man-
hattan Field Thanksgiving Day. The tigers
are practicing with a vengeance for the fray,
and they meanto wipe out Pennsylvania’s
defeat If it is withinthe bounds of possibility.
The Princeton boys will attend the Yale-
Harvard match, and then return to Nassau’s
cam pus and see if they can master the tricks
which they may have seen the Yales work.
Yale will probably not use the same signals
in her game with Harvard that she has pre-
pared for the Princeton game, as there might
be a chance to block some of their combina-
tions.
The Greggains-Costello battle, which will
occur on Monday,Nov. 28,at the Co_ey Island
Athietic Cinb, promises to bs one of the
most famous that hasever been decided in
the stakeless ring of the club by the sea.
Both men are masters of the art of boxing
and each aspires to the middle-weight cham-
pionship of the world. The winner will with-
out doubt be matched to fight the victor of
the Hall-Fitzsimmons contest. The future of
Costello and Greggains depenjis upon the out-
come of their meeting on the 28th, and they
are carefully preparing for it—Costello at the
Navesink Highlands with Peter Maher and
Joe McGrath, and Greggains at Saus, Mass.,
uncer the direction of his manager, Martin
Murphy, and Howte Hodgkins. It would
|be difficult to imagine a _ place better
j;suited for a training ground for ath-
| letes than the spot at the Highlands of Nave-

sink where Maher, Costelloand McGrath are

getting in form for their mills. The men are

domiciled ata comfortable hotel just below
| the turreted tuwers inclosing the twin Hghts

of the Highlands. Costelio is training ear-
| nestly, honest!y and ungerudgingly. He fairly
|}loves his work and revels In it all day.
| He means to get in the finest possible condi-
| tlon for his ight with Gregzains on the 28th,
| and if conscientious, preliminary work will
put him there he will be all righton that
; night. His right hand bothers him some
stulll, and heis favoring it considerably. It
| will be remembered that he injured it se-
| verely by falling over a chain fence at Coney
| Island the night of the Choynski-Godfrey

mill. Buffalo now weighs 157!2 pounds, and

} will go Into the ring at 15s or 159 pounds.
| Maher is going it slow in his work and the
casual visitor would say he was indolent
and averse to genuine training. He looks
| very Wellandsays he feels Al, but the me-
| dium of work he did yesterday was a poor
criterion to judge him by. Histrainer, Tom
| Clark, says he is doing all that is necessary
| and that he will be in winning form on Dec.
| 8, when Goddard faces him.
| MeGrath is extremely lazy for a little fellow
| who is going up against such a crack as Billy
Pliimmer, but he may buckle to his work
after awbile and put some ginger into his
gait by the time he meets Plimmer, Dec. 23.

Maher did a little unlooked for sprinting the

| other day to get out of the way of a Long

Branch express on the Shrewsbury River

bridge, and he showed a fine burst of speed

| which possibly saved his life. Sports who

| have a fine eye for ‘‘lines’’ on pugiilsts, say

| Greggains will win his fight with Costello.

| And now for another batch of caloric fight-

}ingtalk. Jimmy Carroll has put up $1,000 to

| bind a match between his clever feather-
weight, Johnny Griffin of Braintree, and the
little Senegambian champion, George Dixon.

Carroll insists, however,that he will not per-

| mit Griffin to fight at less than 120 pounds and
this he adds is two pounds lighter than the
| legitimate avoirdupois of featherwelghts. As
‘Tom O’ Rourke insists just as empratically
| that George shall not scrapat over lis and
| demands the same weight from Griffin, it is
; easy to see thata muss is assured in the near
| future. After Dixon, Carroll says the match
| 1s open to young Griffo of Australia, Billy
| Murphy, Ike Weir or any man in the feather-
weight class. Meanwhile O’Rourke says
there 1s $1,000 for Billy Murphy to cover and
takeon a mill with Dixon at 118 pounds, but
not an ounce heavier. Something tangible
in the fighting line surely ought to come out
of allthis conversation.

Phil Dwyer has denied that he is Corbett’s
backer and says that he never backed a
fighter in his life. What is more, he does
not intend to. Headds, however, that he is
willing to advance him any reasonable
amount. He hasannounced that he will not
in the future hold any more stakes.

The several committees of the New York
Press Club’s proposed athletic carnival at
Madison Square Garden on the afternoon and
evening of Dec. 17 are wouping hard to make
the affair a success. TNe Entertainment
Committee is arranging an athletic pro-
gramme that will eclipse anything of Its kind
ever givenin thecity. Foot-racing, hurdle-
jumping, bicycling, lacrosse, tug-of-war,
foot-bali, wrestling on horseback, fencing on
horseback and other equestrian perform-
ances are some of the sports already decided
upon. Thecommittee will aim to make the
afternoon performance particularly attract-
ive to women and children.

Sporting men are excited over a report
that Al Smith, the well-known sporting man,
had bucked the tiger and won $22,400 in cold
cash. Of this amount he is said to have
won $20,000 at one sitting. If all accounts be
true, this is the way Smith has won his
small fortune. Overa year agoa friend bet
him $600 that he would not abstain from
Mquor a year. smith took the bet and jis
year expired last Sunday. On the day _ fol-
lowing, he went toa gambling resort in West
Twenty-eighth street and began to play faro.
He stayed there two days and two nights,
eating and drinking atthe table and taking
short naps at intervals. When he arose
from the table he was $20,000 richer and
pretty well filled with champagne. He went
home, according tothe story, but returned
next day and played an hour ‘‘for car fare.’’
He won $2,4004n that time. Al Smith has been
a backer of walking matches and of John L,
Sullivan, owns a half interest in the White
Elephant pool room, and has made money in
all these ventures. . fhe only game he never
could beat was theups and downs of stocks
in Wall street.

title: Mitchell says: am sure to fight, as you know, Tom, unless he pulls out

THE RING.

Tom Allen of this city, the noted retired
champion pugilist of the world, has received
a characteristic letter from Charley Mitchell
dated at London, Nov. 7. Mitchell says: ‘‘i
am sure to fight, asyou know, Tom, unless
he pulls out. I shall be better,
stronger and bigger when I face
him than I ever have been in my life, and be-
tween you and melam very sanguine asto
my success. Now youask me on the frank
whatl poms of Corbett. I will say J fancy
him very m@ch. ‘They think I am fat and
done with, but there will bea surprise party
for them in ten rounds, I am
certain.’’ Speaking his assault case,
now pending in court, he says:

**Il appear on my appeal case Jan. 18. Since
my conviction the womanandthe two men
that were witnesses against me have been
jJugged. The woman and one man putto
trial for shoving bad coin were the principal
Witnesses against me; the other got two
years for highway robbery and violence. So
I have a good chance of getting out of it. You
can bet if we had been the mugs they took us
for we should have been robbed, but because
it was me the Magistrate thought he would
like tohave the pleasure and nameof sen-
tencing me.’’

CORBETT AND PETER SHAKE HANDS.

PHILADELPHIA, Pa., Nov. 19.—For the first
time since the celebrated meeting before the
California Athletic Club Champion Corbett
and Peter Jackson, the colored heavyweight,
stood face to face yesterday in a hotel office
in Philadelphia. The meeting was friendly.
Peter extended his hand, saying to the
champion: ‘‘Mr. Corbett, I congratulate you
on your splenaid victory.’’

Corbett replied in a quiet way, thanking
Peter.: No fighting taik was induiged in.

JACKSON’S MOVEMENTS.

cCurcaco, Ili., Nov. 19.—‘*Parson’’ Davies
arrived from the East yesterday. He will be
joined by Peter Jackson and Joe Choynski in
about two weeks and the combination will
make a tour of the Pacific Coast. The ‘‘Par-
son’’ says Jackson is anxious to meet Cor-
bett and thinksthe Californian should sign
articles fora fight with him if he has any in-
tention of meeting him. Jackson Is perfectly
willing to make the date far enoughinto next
year to allow Corbett tomake a good stake
out of his recent victory.

PUGILISTIC POINTERS.

Reddy Gallagher is, from all accounts,
anxious to enter the squared circle.

Louis Jester of Wilkesbarre wants to fig ht
Johnny Keagan at 142 pounds, and he only
wants a purse of $3,000 to fight for.

The Olympic Athletic Club of New Orleans
will give Joe Choynski an opportunity to
meet the winner of the Maher-Goddard con-
test.

Three years ago Bob Fitzsimmons and Jim
Hall were giad tofight in thetrown country
for $45 and fora championship, too. To-day
they are hesitating over an offer of $40,000, or
over 800 times as much money. .

Mike Queenan, the Chicago Stock Yards
«‘Giant,’’ has consented to spar Bill Smith,
the local heavyweight, a six-round coniest
for points. ‘the affair will be pulled off short-
ly, and the ‘‘Stock Yards Giant’’ Is confident
that Smith will come out second best.

Johnny Daly has received word from a
friend named McQuade of Chicago that a good
sized purse wWillin all probability be hung up
for a contest between him and Dick Moore of

**Prize fights aren’t what they used to be,’’
said Andrew Carlson, of New Orleans, at the
Southern. **The replacing of the London
rules with the Queensberry and the introduc-
tion of boxing gloves into championship bat-
tlles have relieved such contests. of much o!
their whilom brutality. It is very seldom
now that you see a blood-curdling encounter
in the equates circle. Science has given it
pometTefinement, and it is possible to say,
with much show of truth of some ring en-
counters, that they are ‘nice, quiet, genteel,
gentlemanly, affairs,’ as I heard the referee
say when Dan Daly was sprinkling everybody
at the ring-side with young Ed Kelly’s blood
just outside of this city some yearsago. I
saw Tom Allen and Mike McCoole fight down
the river in the good old days when steam-
boating was still afive, and I saw long-legged
Charley Gallaghefdoup Tom Allen in three
terrific rounds somewhere near Chester, Il.
There was fighting at that time. Men were
chopped to pieces in the ringand fairly rained
gore. The prise fight of the present day isn’!
Any more like those ‘gos’ than Mrs. Highflyer’s
§ Oo*clock teais like a railroad collision ora
keg of tenpenny nails doing an all-sasshay in

sv. LOUIS SPORTS WILL NOT BE
NUMEROUS AT THE FIGHT.

Fred Warkins Left Last Night With

Five Thousand Dollars to Bet on

Mitchell—Alderman Cronin and Hina

Holl Will Go South To-Night—Vet-

eren Tom Kelly Picks Corbett as

the Winner.

Only a few St. Louisans will be at the
ring-side on Thursday afternoon when Cor-
bett and Mitchell face each other. There
are several reasons why the loeal sporting
fraternity will not turn out on this oe-
casion in the usual number. THe delay in
the announcement of a reduced rate is one
and the fact that each spectator will be
charged $25 and probably $59 is another.
Fred Watkins, the well-known sporting
man, left last night for Jacksonville, car-
| rying in his pocket a certified cneck for
$5,000 and severa) letters from Tom Allen,
who is assisting in Mitchell's training,
telling him that the Englishman could not
lose and that he was in the pink of condi-
tion. Watkins is an enthusiastic admirer
of Mitchell and believe that he will win the
fight, but thinks that owing to the strong
talk put up by the Corbett crowd that he
should get at least 2 to 1 for his money.
He has tried to get that here, but failed.
Allen wrote him that he thought that it
might be possible to get those odds at the
ring-side and Watkins has accordingly has-
tened Southward with his roll. Marshall
McDonald, the well-known criminal law-
yer, feeling in need of a little recreation
and being an admirer of the manly art,
left last night also for Crocodile land.

**e* © ©

To-night Alderman Jim Cronin and Con-
stable Ben Brady will leave for the scene
of the fight. The statesman from the First
Ward yesterday drew from the bank $1,000
which he will take with him to put on
Mitchell. He thinks the Englishman is
a sure winner, and is willing to back his
opinions with his cash. Up to date he has
only mace two bets on the fight, both of
$100 each at odds of $100 to $170. He, too,
has seen Allen's letters and believes that
he can get 2 to 1 for his money tn Florida,
and consequently is not looking for bets at
home.

eeea

Tom Kelly, the veteran pugilist, who has
attended nearly ail of the big fights in the
last 30 years, will skip this one.

“I think Corbett should win this fight,”
said he yesterday afternoon. “I base my
opinions with his cash, Up to date he has
done in public. I consider Corbett the
quickest bie man I ever saw. It is foolish
to try to predict how long the fight will
last. It is may come to an end in five
rounds and it may last fifty. It is also
nonsense to talk about what tactics a man
will pursue in the ring. You see a fight is
a sort of a two-handed affair and you have
to be governed by what the other man
dees, It is all right to set down before a
fight and say: ‘Well, I'll just give ‘im a
stiff punch in the stomach, and follow it
up with a lick on the jaw that'll settle
‘im.’ but you must remember that the other
man has always got something to say about
getting those licks. Everything done in
fighting is done on the moment, a man
sees a chance and takes it. While I think
Corbett will win and am betting my money
that way, it wouid not surprise me to see
Mitchell come out the victor. I have been
to too many prize fights not to have often
seen the best man beaten. I think it was
back in ’69 that Tom Allen met Gallagher
in this city. Although Allen was mani-
festly the best of the two Gallagher got in
one of those punches that puts a man to
sleep and beat Allen in three rounds. The
two men met again later and I seconded
Gallagher, but this time Allen was not s0
careless as to give the other man a chance
and won the fight easily. Now, about the
present fight, I think,both men are so clever
that there will be very few openings left,
but I believe that if there is any chance
Corbett will be the quicker to take advan-
tage of it. Mitchell may be the hardest
hitter, but Corbett is so clever in landing
repeatedly that I think he can do the most
damage.”

The Board of Directors of the Pastime
Athletic Club last night issued to the mem-
bers a circular reviewing the past work of
the organization and explaining its pur-
poses in the future, and calling upon them
to work for the organization’s interest by
securing new members) The proposed work
of the club is in the line adopted at the
last meeting of the board and printed at
that time. The review of the history of
the club is very interesting, and is as fol-
lows:

“In January, 1888, seven men formed the
Pastime Athletic Club for the purpose: of
playing baseball in Forest Park. In six
years the club has grown to its present
dimensions. It is now one of the most
prominent athletic clubs in the world, and
has in its ranks some athietic stars of the
first magnitude, whose athletic feats are
now matters of history. Among its mem-
bers are the greatest jumpers in the world,
both as to height and distance, In the run-
ning broad jump, a member of this club
has raised the world’s record to 23 feet 6%
inches, a record which will probably stand
for some time. Its high jumper has jumped
within an inch of the world's record and
will undoubtedly break it. Its champion
boxer finds no one to compete with him for
first place. The P. A, C, holds the swim-
ming championship of the United States.
Its runners are in the front rank. Among
its bicycle riders is the champion of the
State, and this divison alone numbers 125
membérs. In wrestling, the P. A. C. stands
at the very top. It is as thoroughly
equipped in clubhouse and grounds as any
club in the United States. Its clubhouse
cont $91,000, and its elegantly equipped
grounds of about 12 acres more than $40,-
om. It is a public enterprise of which St.
Louis should be proud, and which lately
has attracted the attention of the news-
paper-reading public which its importance
warrants.”

“ert 8

The members of the Forest Park Road
Race Association wiil hold a meeting at the
St. Louis Cycling Club on Wednesday even-
ing for the purpose of electing officers and
making arrangements for holding the an-
nual race. The date is to be selected, and
will be either May 26 or June 2. This event
has grown in prominence until it is no
longer merely a local affair, but attracts
riders from all over the country. Efforts
will be meade to have the coming race sur-
pass all previous events, both in the num-
ber of starters and in the value of the
prize list. DOMINO.”

Alderman Cronin, clad in raiment be-
itting a city father, and carrying two bag-
gage checks which called for Saratogas
containing more gorgeous apparel, left last
night for the scene of the Corbett-Mitcheil
ight. His only companion was Ben Brady
of the Second Ward, the other sports who
had determined to make the trip having
backed out during the week. Im his in-
side pocket the statesman from the First
Ward carried a roll which spoke well of
the emoluments of office holding, which he
is willing and ready to wager upon the
fact that Mitchell will succeed in defeat-
Ing his opponent when they meet in the
ring on Thursday afternoon. It consisted
of crisp $100 bills, 10 of which he said he
was willing to put up on the Englishman,
while the others he would keep for spend-
ing money.

Cronin is a personal friend of Mitchell,
and ever since the Englishman has. been
in training has been in correspondence
with him. Just what Mitchell has told
him regarding his prospects for winning
the fight Cronin last night refused to make
known, saying that he regarded the let-
ters as confidential. However, he said the’
Englishman's arguments were strong
enough for him to stand a tap on his bank
roll.

“Only let the fight take place,’ said the
Alderman last night as he fixed himself
comfortably in the seat of the Pullman in
which he will make the long trip, “and
Charlie will make a sucker of that blg guy
that beet Sullivan when he was out of con-
dition. Why, he'll make a monkey out of
him before the fight has gone on five
rounds. I have always thought that a
clever man like Mitchell could go. up
against that lanky Californian and make
him look sick, bet now that I know that
Charlie is fit'to fight for a kingdom, and
that is what Tom Allen said in his last
letter, I think it’s a cinch. Say, I think it
is as easy for Mitchell to lick that fellow
as it was to get a railway bill through the
House of Delegates last year after the
special committee, of which I was chair-
man, had recommended its passage. How
is he going to do it? Don’t ask me that.
Mitchell has already devided upon the tac-
tics he will pursue, and I know what they
will be, but it wouldn't be right for me to
talk about them, It might put the other
fellow next, see? Just you go and put
your money up on Mitchell, and you will
thank your uncle for his advice.”

Then Cronin took another whiff at one of
the ‘“‘Alderman’s Best'’ and under its ex-
hilarating influence began to further dilate
upon Mitchell's superiority. Brady also is
2 Mitchell enthusiast, but has the fever in
. milder form than his stalwart companion,
nithough he is willing to put up a couple
of hundred on the man of his choice.

* e¢* *

But little betting has been done locally
upon the result of the fight. Only a few
bets have so far been made, and those
mostly of the ten-dollar size, with Corbett
as the favorite. The big bettors favoring
both men have been unable to agree upon
satisfactory terms. Joe Uliman was willing
to bet $15,000 upon Corbett at odds of 65 to
100 on, but when he left for San Francisco
last night he said he had not been able to
make a bet. Fred Watkins offered to take
35,000 of the money if he would lengthen the
pdds to 2 to 1, but this the St. Louis book-
maker refused to do.

It is doubtful if the St. Louis delegation
at the ring side numbers 10 altogether. The
only lovers of fistic events who have left
up to date are Marshall MeDonald,, Fred
Watkins, Tom Ailen, Alderman Cronin,
Louis Lemp and Ben Brady.

*“* © *

“In the days of heat racing more money
was wagered on the horses than now,”
sail Judge Carter at the Southern last
night. “It was almost wonderful the
amount of coin that would be put up on
an event of that kind. Speaking of heat
racing reminds me of a romantic incident
which occurred a number of years ago at
Union City, Tenn., near my home, Mata-
gorda, who belonged to Hayden & Barry,
was one of the best heat racing mares in
the country at that time. At the Union
City Fair Grounds she was entered in a
heat race, best three out of five, and was a
strong favorite. She won the first two
heats easily, and in the third came into
the stretch considerable distance in front
of the others. Just at this critical moment
a women took it into her head to cross
the track, believing that she could do so
with safety. She had miscalculated the
speed of the mare, and Matagorda run into
her and knocked her down, stumbling her-
self and being distanced for the heat. The
woman was 80 badly injured that she died
several weeks later, but believing that she
herself was to blame for the accident she
had a clause made in her will, leaving
Hayden & Barry $500, the amount of the
purse which Matagorda would have won
had the accident not happened.”

title: Fistic Legends Joe Goss and Tom Allen in Historical Review
text:
Even the excitement of the Civil War
was not sufficient to obliterate interest in
fistic contests, and when ‘the late unpleas-
antness’’ was over it found Joe Coburn,
champion of America, and a pretty able
list of lesser fistic lights revolving around
him. Dominick Bradley and Sam Rankin,
who had fought a prize battle for ‘the
honor and glofy of God,"’ had both retired,
but big Mike McCool was very much in evi-
dence, and he and Ton? Allen made things
pugilistic very lively in the West. ‘‘The
Irish Gtant,’’ Ned O' Baldwin, had been fol-
lowed to this country by Jem Mace, and
they, with Jose Donnald, were keeping up
their end in this part of the country.
O'’Baldwin was jailed, and Mace, after
fights with Coburn and Allen, left the land.
Then there was quite a fistic lull, broken by
spasmodic intervals of activity, such as
when Johnny Dwyer beat Jimmy Elliott.
At one time two bald-headed old men, Joe

ae think we will,” was the response, “If

The Last Goss Fight.

The famous Joe Goss fight in Kentucky
in September, 1876, is well remembered.
It was a matter of unusual moment even
in the career of a man with such a wide
experience as Tom Allen’s. It resulted in
his going out of the country and remain-
ing away for a long time, while his ad-
versary spent a good many months in a
Kentucky jail. At this fight, against the
wishes of the Allen crowd, ‘Eph’? Holland
of New York was made referee.

Just before the opening of the mill Hol-
land stepped to the edge of the great crowd,
and, flourishing a roll of money, anh-
nounced that he was ready to lay a bet of
$1.00 on Goss. Fred Watkins, who was
backing Allen, got out a clean $1,000 bill
and handed it to Holland, who had ap-
pointed himself stakeholder. At a moment
when it looked as if Goss would be out at
any second his friends pressed forward and
eried that it was his battle. All that the
Allen men could do did not stem the tide,
and Holland gave the fight to Goss on an
alleged foul. Watkins and his friends
claimed their money, but Holland gave
them the laugh. He said that his thousand
was only a corncob wrapped in a $10 bill.
Goss was arrested and sent to prison for
a year and a half for this fight, but Allen
got away and by going through Canada
succeeded in reaching a steamer for Eng-
land. He was about $25,000 to the good at
that time, as a result of his many suc-
cesses, and, with the money, he made a
book through England and lost most of it.

It 's an interesting fact that the last
fight that Allen had in England before com-
ing to this country in 1869 was with Joe
Goss. and the last fight he had in America
before fleeing to his native land in 1877
was with the same man. The first fight
was for the middle weight championship
and was a draw after 34 rounds.

Allen had three fights in England after
his return. The first was with Tompkin
Gilbert, who had 100 pounds and the cham-
pionship of England. He had heard that
Allen was the American champion, and
he sought to rob him of the title. It

Jack Wilkes, the St. Louis welterweight,

anxious to get a match for his man with

a tvwenty-five-round draw in the arena of

McCoy was superior to O’Brien in scientific
sparring, but his blows lacked force.

Tom Allen, the retired champion, and his
old backer, Fred Watkins, are regular pa-
trons of the races at the Fair Grounds. Al-
len always has his field glasses strung
across his shoulders and like a true English-
man, a ale race gives him as much pleas-
ure as the cashing-in of a winning ticket.

THE STORY OF AUNT BETSY.
Its Moral Indicates that the New
Woman Is All Right.
From the New York Evening Sun.

“When,” said a woman of mature years
and experience, ‘‘I hear persons complain, as
I sometimes do, of the craving of young
women nowadays to rush out into the
world and seek their fortunes, instead of
staying at home and letting fortunes seek
them, I am tempted to tell the story of
Aunt Betsy. She wasn’t out father’s, but.
our grandfather's sister, and therefore our
great-aunt. She was one of a large family,
ail of whom married and scattered but her-
self. Whether she had ever had wooers or
not I don't know; no halo of ASA of
the sort hung around her when I knew her,
which was about peat f years ago, when I
Was @ very little girlk When my grand-
father died one clause of his will was found
‘to read: ‘To my daughter Betsy, a home.’
It was no uncommon clause in wills of that
day. It was the accepted way to dispose of
an unmarried daughter, and it meant that
the son who Inherited the homestead should
also inherit Aunt Betsy. He was to provide
her with shelter, food and raiment fur the
balance of her life. It so happened that my
grandfather was the happy heir in this in-
stance.

“Aunt Betsy was at once removed from
the spacious second-story front chamber
that she had occupied as eldest daughter
and hg ensconced in a little downstairs
room. Such a thing as her going out and
seeking independence by earning her own
living never occurred to any one. Ag cir-
cumstances stood, she was looked on as
comfortably provided for, and my srand-
father would have been much incensed at
uny one suggesting that she wus not. Had
she not everything that a woman could pos-
sibly want? An unmarried woman, that is
tu say. When my grandfather died my
father in his turn inherited the homestead
and Aunt Betsy. It was then that she came
into my life. I remember her as a queer,
unattractive little personality, that we su-
perciliously referred to as an old inaid be-
hind her back, although ready to tear the
eyes out of other children who dared to
offer such sn insult to even this least es-
teemed relative.

“We didn't love her in the least; we felt
that she was somehow only tolerated among
us, and we saw that she received but Ittle
consideration from our elders. She had noth-
| ing in common with children, end we enil-
dren had nothing in common with her. Why,
she never had any money to give us, or
with which to buy things for us: conse-
quently, there was never anything tu be
Ras ‘out of her,’ and childish standards are
apt to be commercial.

“She used tu help about the house a little,
but with increasing years she wasn't equal
to even that little, and su spent most of
her time in the tiny nook that belonged to
her sola She had a cat she was very fond
of, and remember that the walls of her
room Were gay with a flowered paper that
1 greatly admired and privately thought
much tvo good for Aunt Betsy. The sun
used to wet round to the one window of her
room about 3 o'clock in the afternoon, when
she never failed to be there. If she happened
to be in another part of the house at that
hour she would scurry away to her room tuo
greet the coming of the bright patch of sun-
light that never failed her except on a rainy
day. She called it ‘my company.’ She
Ualited a great deal, stockings and mittens
and mufflers ard other uninteresting and
useful things, It never onee occurred to any
of us grown-ups or childreu that there was
anything pathetic about her. Even when she |
died our chief feeling was a sense of re-
lief. Only of late years have I come to
realize huw lonely she must have been in
her utter devendence upon us and in her
lack of love. Thank heaven, though, there
can be no Aunt Betsy nowadays. You
may object as you choose to the present in-
flux of women tnto professional and busi- |
ness life; it is infinitely preferable to the
one-time ‘To my daughter Betsy, a home.’ |
I don't belfeve in bloomers, nor in many
other things that the ‘emancipated’ woman
demands, but neither do I believe In Aunt
I3etsys and the conditions that create |
them.” ?

Death of Fred Watkins.

After a brief illness, Fred Watkins, one of
St. Louis’ widest-known citizens, died Fri-
day night from an apoplectic stroke, super-
induced by a clot on the brain. Watkins
was in his 59th year. He was a member of
the wholesale hide and leather firm of Wat-
kins & Lieber. |The decedent was a native
of Birmingham, England, but he came to St.
Louis in ides. His brother was then in the
leather business here; and after a time they
entered into partnership. Leonard A. Wat-
kins, Fred's brother, afterward went to
Denver, Colo. He died recently and his
family are expected to arrive here to-mor-
row. Another brother, Father Jeffrey
Xavier, of the Christian Brothers’ College,
at Memphis, is expected to reach here to-
wef when the funeral arrangements will be
made.

Fred Watkins was a graduate of Trinity
College (England). He was an enthusiastic
<4 Be arnae and “backed” Tom Allen when
the latter was champion pugilist of the
world. His was a familiar figure at the
ringside at most of the bie pugilistic con-
tests in America during the last quarter of
A century.

Drs. Powers and W. F. Kier attended the
deceased before his death. Watkins had
been found seriously ill in his room Friday
morning, but death did not come until
twelve hours later. S

Tom Allen Says That Peter Had a

Tom Allen, the veteran ex-champion pu-
gilist of America, returned from New York }
last night. He went to Gotham to take
in the Maher-Choynski fight at Tom |
O’Rourke’s Broadway Club Monday night. |
In the Broadway Club arena each con-
testant is allowed one attendant. This po- |
sition {s generally assigned to an active
handler, thus doing away with the old ring ;
custom of having a corner full of advisers.
behind each fighter. The Maher party were
anxious to have Allen on hand te advise
Peter and a special seat was reserved for
him at the ring side. He was in close com-
munication with the big Irishman through+
out the battle, and was given great credit
by Maher's friends fer the clever style of

action he mapped out. In conversation with
| a Republe representative last night, Alen
| talked interestingly of the fight and other
pugiistic matters of public concern, |
| “Peter was the most confldent fighter I
| have ever seen enter the ring,” said the
| Veterans. “On the other hand, Choynski
-was just the opposite. Maher had him
| beat from the start. The Californian landed
a great deal oftener in the first three
} rounds, but his blows lacked steam and
were ineffective. Maher was eager to close
| on him, but we all advised him to take his
time. Choynski was as active as a cat,
but he wore himseif out completely, and
| had nothing left to sustain him when Peter
cornered him and forced the affair to a
finish.

“AS soon as the big Irishman closed on
him ft was all over. At short range he had
no chance whatever, and two guod punehes
sent him down and out.

“The battle was scientifically fought, and
one of the most interesting 1 have seen in
many a day. The betting was all in Maher's
favor, I won several hundred, but was
forced to give big odds to get my money on,
The biggest bet I saw made was $2,000 to
$1,000 on Peter, Bookmaker Ike Thompson
taking the Maher and Joe Willman of St.
Louis the Choynski end. The Californian
entered the ring with the largest head of
halr I ever saw on a prize fighter,

“In fact, you would think he had been
training for a football contest. The house
was worth $14,700, so [I was told. The club
kept 40 per cent and the fighters got the
other 60. Choynski was foxy enough to get
a0 per cent of that. Maher is undecided as
to his plans for the future. He has just
signed to fight Steve O'Donnell again, and
is to get $2,500 for the battle. This sbouid
prove the easfest money he ever earned in
the ring. Before I left for home he asked
me if I was coming on to see the battle.

“What for?’ aays Tf.

““Well,.l guess you are right,’ replied.
Peter; ‘it will be over before you llght a
cigar.’

“The last time they met Maher finished
O'Donnell inside of a round. New York is
full of old-tine ehters, During my stay
they kept me busy handing out money to

| them, I never fed less than a dozen at every
| meal. Billy Edwards seems to be doing
well, and Barney Aaron has a good job
| calling off the winners in the betting rings
-on the Eastern Circult. Dan Dwyer, who
was here boxing with Sullivan several
| years ago, has a hard luck story. I saw
| Dick Roche, the old king of St. Louts pool
alley, and they tell me things have not
- heen going his way for some time. Al Smith
| is on Easy street. I raised both him and
| Roche. =
| “Charlie Genslinger of the Eohemian Club
told me he is very confident of his ability
| to bring off the Corbett-Fitzsimmons fight
in New Yori. According to CharHe, there
is no doubt that they can fight there if
they are so disposed. I think so, too,, from

title: Tom Allen Comments on Slavin-Armstrong Fight
text:
NK SLAVIN

OF FRA ,

| SR

THE MAN WHO WANTED TO MEET

| JOHN L. SULLIVAN BEATEN BY
AN USNHKNOWN NEGRO.

Speed of Race Horses, Jack Rabbits
and Greyhounds Discussed—
Sporting Gossip.

Frank Slavin, the burly Australian pu-
eilist, has seen his best days. At one time
he appeared to have a great future before
him in the ring, but ever since his fight with
Peter Jackson tn Londan, which resulted in
a victory for the giant black, Slavin has
experienced nothing but reverses... Slavin
was one of Jackson's pupiis in the Anti-
podes, afid after Peter came to America he
claimed the Australian championship. No-
body disputed his claim until he followed
Jackson to this country. Sullivan was still
the American champion when Slavin ar-
rived, end Frank endeavored to arrange a
battle with the Boston boy.

He came tp St. Louis to see Sullivan about
the matter, and John J. told him that he
would fight nobody until after his trip to
Australia. Slavin and Mitchell then toured
the United States, the former posing as the
Australian champion, notwithstanding the
fact that Jackson was also claiming the
same title. The result of the controversy
was the fight that tock place in London,
which settled Slavin's hash, as far as the
Australian or any other championship was
concerned. Slavin’s history since then is of
little interest to the public, beyond some
facts in connection with his recent defeat
‘at the hands of Bob Armstrong, “Parson”
Davies’ big black.

Tom Allen, the retired champion, met
Slavin in New York while he (Allen) was
there to attend the Maher-Choynski fight.
Up to that time Slavin nad no idea of fight-
ing Armstrong. As a matter of fact he had
wrenched his back while training for his
g0 with Steve O'Donnell, and was really in
no condition to fight anybody. ‘He told
me,” said Allen yesterday, ‘‘that he was in
hard luck. Armstrong came East from Chi-
eago with Davies and Choynski, and I sup-
pose Slavin, on account of his financial dis-
tress, grabbed at the chance to meet the
negro. I see that..bhe demanded his 30 per
cent of the gate receipts before the battle
was begun. I guess the poor fellow knew he
was up against it, and was willing to, take
a good beating for the coin. From what I
know of the condition he was In the fight
could not have resulted other than it did.”

IN THE INTERESTS OF IRRIGATION.
Proposed Large Federal Reservoir to
, Be Constructed Near Denver.
| DENVER, COLO., December 11.—Capt.
Hiram M. Chittenden, of the Corps of En-
gingers of the United States army, arrived
in Denver to-day, and called at the office of
State Engineer Sumner to look over the
topographical maps of Colorado, with a
view to selecting the most desirable site
for a great water storage reservoir. .

Capt. Chittenden’s mission is one of ex-
traordinary importance to the agricultural
interests of Colorado, and marks the com-

| mencement of Federal interest in Western
‘irfigation projects. The idea is to establish
a Government storage reservoir or lake in
the mountain on the eastern side of the di-
_vide, which will save huge volumes of
Water, which now run to waste in the
_spring. The project will, when completed,
open up vast areas of now arid région to
cultivation.

A start was made last spring, when Con-
gress passed the bill authorizing the con-
struction of great Federal reservoirs, one in
Wyoming and one in Colorado. The bill
earried with it an appropriation of $200,000
to defray the expenses of the surveys and
other preliminary work.

“I have about decided that the proper
Place to locate the reservoir would be at
the headwaters of the Plate,” stated Capt.
Chittenden. “‘The Platte is the great dis-
tributer of water in Colorado and North-
western Nebraska. I will start out in a few
days and look over the South Park region,
but active work can not be commencat un.
til heavy snows disappear.”’

gineers, holding its fifth annual meeting in

A. J. Flanner. I thought the fight would

itzsimmons would come out on top. Fitz-
simmons well earned his victory, and is de-
serving of the laurels. me

the fight. Corbett was my favorite, and I
backed him heavily. I looked upon him as
a@ sure winner from Fitzsimmons, and am
