William Francis. I was greatly astounded
by Fitzsimmons’ victory. He deserved it, I
guess, but I can’t for the life of me see how

e earned it.

Fred Berg. Corbett was my favorite. He
lost and so did I. Fitzsimmons won, and
so did some friends of mine.

Fhed Cummins. I liked the champion, but
was a friend of the Cornishman. Fifty dol-
lars was the whole amount of my betting
on the fight, and I lost that.

Tom Hughes; It always did look to me
like anybody’s fight. Corbett was my favor-
ite, and I am sorry the Cornishman beat
him. I thought it an even proposition, and
aie my money at home.

an Carrigg, turfman, of Council Bluffs,
Io. I picked Corbett and lost. I’d pick him

again, because the rounds show that he is
Fitzsimmons’ superior from a_ scientific
| Standpoint, and that means that he can
| pitas aio Cornishman. Three blows knocked
Corbett out. The first one was on Jim’s
neck, and the second was on his wind.
These blows affected Corbett’s heart action,
and the idea < blow over his heart finished
the disaster the other two blows had start-
ed. No man under the sun could have with-
stood this dressing.
AL SPINK’S DIAGNOSIS.

It is the old story over again. Jack will
always meet his mdster. To my mind, the
funniest thing about to-day’s victory for
Fitz is that nearly all the so-called knowing
ones phophesied his defeat. According to the
reports, Corbett had all the best of the bat-
tle in the early stages. He Sepppaced to
have fought very rapidly, an to have
worn himself out before the tenth round.
Fitz, too, put in some good strokes in the
early stages, but it looks as though he had
played possum some, and saved himself for
the run up the stretch. He a Ph pean all of
that army who follow the doings of the
prize ring. They, above all others, had look-
ed for no such battle from Fitz. I can not
liken him to any of the gladiators of the
present generation. He carried himself
bravely from the commencement, and
chouae facing a much bigger man, and one
who had been held up to him as invincible,
he assumed the aggressive from the start.
And though Corbett tapped him hard and
made the claret fly early in the game, Fitz
never flinched from the punishment, but
stooc up to his work nobly and well. Fac-
ing the odds he did and fighting the fight
he did, he deserved to win. As usual, I sup-
pose, the fancy will now take their fling
at Corbett. So much was expected of him
by his close friends and admirers that noth-
ing but victory would likely satisfy them.
They did not take into .consideration the
fearful mental strain their champion must
have undergone. With him there was all
to lose. With Fitz, all that was needed was
for him to put up a game fight, and if it
lasted a dozen rounds or so, his fortune
was made. It would have been no disgrace
for the king of the middle-weights to have
gone down in that fashion. But Corbett.
He must win. To be beaten by a so-called
middle-weight was out of the question.
And so entered the ring with his whole
fortune and very life at stake. The battle
can not be likened to any of the struggles
for the world’s belt that have taken place
in the past twenty-five years. Ryan took
the championship from poor old Joe Goss,
and then Sullivan, who was at his best,
wrested it easily from Ryan. When Kilrain
and Sullivan fought with bare fists at
Richburg I heard old Tom Allen say at the
ring side, ‘‘They fight like a pair of old
wash women.” Kilrain then proved him-
self cf no account, while Sullivan showed
that he had bat | nearly reached the jump-
ing off place. ullivan’s battle with Mit-
chell was a sprinting match, and this brings
us to the meeting between Corbett and Sul-
livan. In the Olympic Club arena that night
Sullivan was pounded around like a foot-
ball, and Corbett came away with the title
without Sullivan getting in a clear blow.
Then came the battle between Corbett and
Mitchell, in which the Englishman was poor
clay in the other’s hand. To-day’s fight for
world’s honors was between two well-
matched men. True, Corbett had the best
of it in weight, but as I said before, the
responsibilities rested heaviest upon him,
nad that perhaps as much as anything else
led to his defeat. He went at the Australian
from the jump, and I think Corbett’s fail-
ure to finish him the first six rounds broke
his heart. took the very life out of him, and
left him an easy mark for Fitz. Tut tne
battle, after al’, was a royal one. and beth
men carried themselves nobly and well.
Ending as it did, it gives Corbett a chance
to say that he is entitled to another crack
at Bob, and that the latter will mnak2 good
the opportunity at the right time ind place,
goes without saying.

Wayman C. McCreery, Collector of Inter-
nal Revenue. I had Fitzsimmons picked
from the start. Tuesday I forecasted the
fight, and in all of its material points it
resulted as I predicted it would. It took
Fitzsimmons longer to finish Corbett than
I judged it would, but then he defeated the
Californian, and that’s enough.

Jim Cronin, the alderman from the First
ward. Don’t talk to me. I'm dead sore.
And it all happened on St. Patrick’s day,
too. I backed Corbett, and I am not sorry
for it. Notwithstanding Ris defeat, he is
the best fighter in the world to-day. I bet
Eddie Foy, the burlesquer, a linen duster
when he was here before, the conditions
being that the loser would have to wear it.
Come and see me to-morrow and you'll see
me attired in one.

liarry Sharp, the fighter. I picked Cor-
bett, and Fitzsimmons’ victory was a total
surprise to me. He must be a wonder, as
the Californian has always looked like the
champion of them all,

William Garen, manager of Havlin’s The-
ater. Corbett looked like a winner to me,
and I bet a good deal on his chances. This
ag htag eyeid business tmnakes me sick, and
n the future I wouldn’t bet stage pecan
on anybody winning, no matter how muc
one fighter: would seem to outclass. the
other.

Aug. Froebel, Jr., the restaurateur
Fitzsimmons won, and I do not think Cor-
bett is any more baud seaece than I am. If

Y thought Fitzsimmons the only _ winner

on him, I thought—and plunged ac-

Sent take the short end of every big

SAM ADLER'’S DEDUCTIONS. 7

Sam Adler, Although my sympathies were
with Corbett, I placed my money on Fitz.
The result is just as I expected.  Fitzsim-
mons is really a marvelous penting machine
in human form—born to fight. Corbett, I
think, was born to be something better
than a prize-fighter, yet he is a wonder at
that. But overwhelming odds were against
him yesterday. Fitzsimmons is a man wno
has from diet and constant'training worked
himself into a compact bundle of bone, mus-
cle and sinew. He is a little old, but, like
a well-seasoned hickory bow, which wiil
shoot an arrow further than one twice as
heavy and younger and full of snap. A
man of his sober habits should be at his
best at 40 years. Man's age should not be
judged by the years he has lived, but by the
way he. has lived them. And thus it was I
reasoned out Fitz as the superior of Corbett
as a fighter.

Dore Silver. I fancied Fitz from the time
he was matched to fight Corbett nearly
two years ago. I handled nearly $4000 in
my book on the result, and, favoring the
Cornishman throughout, Stone $900 to the
good. In calculating on the result, I rea-
soned thus:

Fitzsimmons measures 1144 Inches more
from the center of the breastbone to the
shoulder socket of either arm than Cor-
bett. In delivering a blow the spine be-
comes a pivot; therefore, the extra 1%
inches gave the Cornishman a greater lev-
erage, and the blow he strikes is conse-
quently that much harder than Corbett’s.
Again, with his extra length of arm and
this greater distance between his shoulder
and his neck Fitzsimmons can stand with
his side exposed to his opponent and with
his fist thrust straight in the other’s face
as a guard.

In this position Corbett would be unable
to reach Fitzsimmons by _ striking either
around, under or over his nit strong
guard or to break it down, and Fitzsimmons
could keep jabbing his me Lane ey without ex-
posing himself in the least. And in this
way Corbett would be liable to become a
little tired and leave unguarded a vital
spot, which Fitzsimmons, with the instinct
and quickness of a cat, would find with a
right or left hook or a straight blow, backed
up with a swing from his broad shoulders.

BILLY MARQUETTE DISGUSTED.

“Billy” Marquette. I have always prided
myself that I knew something about the
prize ring, but when Corbett, to my mind
the champion of them all, gets knocked
out, I pass up the game, I bet on the Cali-
fornian, but did not lose as much as I want-

then look out for Jim.

est.

Jim _toid me when he played here that he

by several lengths then. At the half they
Were on even terms, and Fitz’s final spurt,

Roy Shumway. The fight on form said as
follows: Corbett fought 17 fights, of which
he won 10, once defeated and 6 draws, total
rounds for all 158. Fitzsimmons fought 22
battles, of which he won 20, once defeated

had much the best of the argument from
form's standpoint. :

Jockey ‘Doc’ Turbiville. The result was
just as I had expected. Fitzsimmons is the
‘fonly.’’ I did not think so much of him until
I was cited to the form book by Roy Shum-
way, who, I think, has the best form on
pe fighters of any one I've argued with.

fully intended to back Corbett at any odds,
but Shum had such a long list of arguments
why Fitz should win that I changed my
mind and backed the Cornishman.

Kid Rogers. IF bet $5300 against $240 on

he would win, or else IT should not have bet
on him. During the fifth round of the battle
I was offered $450 for my ticket, which I rb-
fused, as I thought Corbett would win surp.
I lost my bet, and in future will play Fitz-
simmons every time he fights: He’s a won-
der, and he will run for me in_the future.

Ben Wasserman. I bet on Corbett, and I
think that hoodooed his chances of win-
ning. I thought him a sure winner up to
the seventh round, and was dumbfounded
at his defeat. Fitzsimmons is a much better
fighter than I gave him credit for being.

Capt. Michael O’Malley. I lost $100 on Cor-
bett, and heaven only knows how many
hats. The result was in the nature of a cy-
clone to me.

John Armstrong, ex-journalist—Corbett is
of Irish descent, and I thought he would
surely vanquish Fitzsimmons. My Chem
thies are always with Irish fighters. have
felt Mr. Fitzsimmons’ arm and also Mr.
Corbett’s, and i am free to confess that I
thought the latter’s was _ much the more
powerful. It was a sad St.«Patrick’s day
for us all. It will take me some time to
recover frem the shock Corbett’s downfall
gave me.

_Jack Sheehan: It’s not often I get on a
dead one, but I did when I backed Corbett.
Jim lost, and so did I. I never thought
Fitzsimmons was the fighter he proved
himself to be.

Larry Harrigan: I told you so. I liked
Fitzsimmons from-the time the men were
matched, and his confidence of winning was
shared by me.

Sergt. McFarland: I regret _ Corbett’s
downfall, but, judging from the description
of the fight, the best man won.

Detective Mike Kelly: Corbett lost, but it
is hard for me to believe it. I lost on his
defeat, and think if they ever meet again
the Caiifornian will win. I do not think
that Fitz is his superior,

Gus Bengel—Trainer Delaney’s sudden
change of heart gave mé the impression
that Fitz had a good chance to defeat Cor-
bett. Delaney wrote to friends here last
December that Corbett was a wreck, and
would never be able to put up another stiff
fight. Later on he changed his views when
he got on Jim’s staff, and said Corbett was
never better nor stronger in his life.

CITY TO GET OUT OF THE BIDDLE
STREET TEMPLE.

A Building That Has Sheltered Revel-
ers, Artists, Criminals, Mission-
aries and the Police.

In another month the Second District
Police Court will move to its new quar-
ters at Jefferson avenue and Dayton street.
The dingy old building at Broadway and
Riddle street will be remodeled, and a land-
mark will be no more.

The property is owned by the J. T. Dono-
van Real Estate Co. After an occupancy
of 2 years the city will vacate rather than
pay the $300 additional rent asked.

Although badly out of repair the place
cannot be said to be in a dangerous condi-
tion. It war over the needed improvements
the hitch occurred. At an annual rental
of $90 per annum, the city was supposed
to do all repairing. This it failed to do,
but Instead appealed to the owners. Mr.
Donovan stated there was no agreement
that the owners should repair, but if the
elty would pay $1,200 per annum he would
keep the building in good shape. This prop-
osition brought on a wave of economy at
the City Hall. It was decided to save
this rental and utilize the hall at the
Fourth District Sub-Station.

The change will be made about June 1.
The property on which the Biddle street
buiiding stands was formerly a portion of
the Mullanphy estate. It fell to the heirs
of Gen. William S. Harney, who married a
Mullanphy. From the Harneys it came in-
to the possession of the present owner.

Just at the close of the war several mem-
bers of the Harney family conceived the
idea of a market-house on Biddle street,
mear the river. The scheme was properly
indorsed and a building erected. The Har-
mney market extended from the west side of
the present police court house east, across
Broadway, well into Third street. Strange
to say, after the market had been com-
pleted enthusiasm for the project fell to
fuch low ebb that not more than half a
dozen hucksters are known to have exposed
their wares on the premises. After a week
or two these deserted, and for a year or
two the building was unoccupied.

Broadway and Third street were then
Pushed through, dividing the property. The
east portion was subsequently sold and the
city built the Round Top Market on the
Third street and Broadway wedge.

Seme slight architectural changes were
made in the Harney building and it was
leased to the Mozart Society, and known
thereafter as the Mozart Hall. .

It_ was in this epoch, stretching from ’68
to ‘74, the building got its mame and fame.
Here it was men from the river front, flush
with pay, caroused with gaudily bedecked
women and girls. Old Green street, now Lu-
cas avenue, was then in its prime, and ‘“‘so-
cietyv’’ from its vicinity almost nightly
crowded the hall. Biddle street for biocks
would be choked with hacks, while the cab-
bies would he inside refreshing themseives
at Jo Henry’s bar, where the Marshal's of-
fice how is, or mixing with the dancers on
the floor

Green stre@t society was not very exclo-
five those days, but the line was drawn on
certain Furopean nations and invasions by
representatives of those races caused much
blood to be spilled about the corner.

When the old Canterbury Theater at Sixth
Street and Lucas avenue would close for
the evening, the fun would begin at the Mo-
zart. There were such sporting characters
as Peie Burns, Patsey Curtin, English Tom
Hyer and Johnny Parker—all men with na-
tional reputations. The female contingent
was Ijttle less notable. Ella and Mary Rob-
erts Were Known in every city west of the
Ohio river as the smoothest pickpockets in
the business; Biz Moll, the Green street
tigress, carried consternation to the hearts
of all she frowned upon; muscular Annie
Rarrett exhibited her prowess time and
again by putting our the male toughs of
her neighborhood; and Mary Flaherty would
Eve two burly policemen all the troubie
they wanted.

It was when these choice spirits got be-
neath one roof that Capt. O'Connor, com-
manding the Third District, would put on
an extra detail, for a fizht folowed the
dance as surely as day ended the night.

(on one of these occasions Patrolmen
Windler and McQuinn endeavored to —
a disturbance. They were sent to the’ hos-
pital. Word was sent to headquarters tnat
Green street was taking North St. Louis.
Patrolmen Peter Joyce and Victor Cole were
sent to the ;cene. Another wagon load
went to the hospital, but this time it was
not the police.

When dancing grew tiresome the pro-
gramme of entertainment would be changed
to boxing bouts. They were called sparring
matches, but in reality the fighters were
not allowed to leave the ring until some
Dne wes out.

The names of well known fistic ‘heroes
who have battled within those walls would
make a long Ist. Probably the most re-
nowned were Ned O. Baldwin, Joe Coburn,
Jem Mace, Tom Allen, Aaron Jones, Mike
MeCoole, Dublin (Hastings) Tricks and
Charley Gallaher.

After the riotous times the old hall set-
lled down to a more peaceful existence
The dances and prizefights gave way to
-hurch missions and mission schools. These
were abandoned in 1875, and for two years
the place was deserted. In 1877 the city
rented !t for a police court. and it has been
in continuous use ever since. During the
twenty years probably every noted criminal
who ever came West or was reared on Mis-
sour! soil has faced that bar of justice.
Certainly in late years few have escaped,
The bench in this time has been graced by
Judges Dennison, White, McCaffrey, An-
derson. Pollard. Paxton and Stevenson.

The Third District Police Station was tem-
porarily located in the basement during 1868.
summary: The St. Louis Post-Dispatch published a history of the Mozart Hall building at Broadway and Biddle Street, noting that Tom Allen was among the renowned fistic heroes who battled within those walls during the 1868-1874 era of riotous entertainment and boxing bouts.

Fatalities in the Prize _

. *
istic Gossip.
ee
Bpecial Correspondence of The Republic,

is New York, May 1.—The year is but a third
spent, and yet more men have died. from
the effect of fist blows than were ever killed
in the ring in a year. More than half of the
fatalities have occurred since the Corbett-
Fitzsimmons fight, and have been due to
imitations of the blow with which Fitz-
simmons won that battle. The ring was
never so prosperous as now, and it behooves
the directors and managers of athletic clubs
in which rings the major portion of the box-
ing is done, to devise ways and means
of lessening the dangers of fistic contests.
So far, the powers that be in authority have

P| been wonderfully lenient in dealing with the

; survivors of the fatal bouts, but that is
no reason for indifference on the part of
officials of the clubs. Unless they do as 1
suggest, some night there will be a fatal-
ity, and those who aided and abetted in
bringing off the contest will tind themselves
compelled to stand trial for manslaughter.
I hope this will never come to pass, and I
again point out the way to avoid such ca-
lamity.

! In the first place, no man should be al-
lowed to contest in a boxing bout who is not
in good heaith and properly trained. Every
club should employ a competent physician,
who should make at levst four efaminations
of contestants while they are training. He
should pay especial! attention to the condi-

_ tion of the heart of each intending contest-
ant. No man should be permitted to box
whose heart is not inggood condition. I am

. told that Frank Iirne has heart trouble, If
this is true, and 1 got my information from
@ man who is pretty weil informed on ring
matters, he should never be permitted to

\ fight again. There are others who have car-

diac affections. I don't mean that they are
“faint-hearted,”’ in the sense of being curs,
but ‘their hearts are not sound in a physical
Sense, Such men are unlit for a ring con-
test.

: Having ascertained that the contestants
: are physically sound, the managers of clubs

should see that the floors of their rings are
properly carpeted with rubber, felt or other
suitable material, which will prevent shocks
sufficient to cause concussion of the brain,
should the head of either contestant collide
with it sharply. The stakes should also be
emg It is seldom, indeed, that a blow

rom a fist, properly incased in a duly pad-
ded glove, is sharp enough to cause concus-
sion of the brain, but a blow can knock a
eee man down with such suddenness that

is head will strike with terrific force on a
Moor. If the floor is properly rubbered, felt-
ed or padded, such a naw may put its re-
ciplent temporarily to sleep, but not one in
ten thousand times will it kill him. The
rings of the best clubs are thus properly
cared for, but there are plenty throughout
the country that are not. For my part,
I wish the police would prevent all contests
in rings that are not proyjerly made safe,
as above described,

( Two-thirds of the ring fatalities of the

fn have been due to heart and stomach

\ lows. They are by far the most dangerous

blows that can be inflicted in a ring, be-
cause they are not “foul’ and they attack
@ man's vitals. At present, there is no way
of guarding against them or their effects,
except by the shiftiness or skill of the man
they are aimed at. The cleverest men in
the ring have thelr “off’’ moments, when
such blows can be landed—Corbett. A pneu-
matic belt or pad can be made which will
greatly lessen the force of such blows, or
at least their shocking power. Such a belt
or pad properly made would minimize all
danger of men being killed by heart blows
or blows in the pit of the stomach. I hope,
to see the day when no contestant will be
allowed to fight without wearing one. What
club will be enterprising enough to lead the
Way in adopting them?
How to Bet on Fights,

A correspondent. asked me the following
question;

New York City, April 27, 1897.—Dear
Macon: In eases where fighters have con-
tested a second time, what is the percentage
of cases in which the defeated man in the
first fight has reversed the verdict in the
second encounter. FISTICUS.

This is a question that IT am unable to
answer accurately, From m@mory, however,
I will say that, as a rule, the winher of a

‘ first fight generally vanquishes his oppo-

nent in a second encounter. This is tanta-

: mount to saying that in all fistic encounters

the best man generally wins. Tom Cribb
beat Molynewx twice, and Tom Spring twice
defeated Jack Langan, Jack Randall twice
@efeated Martin, the baker, and in the
American ring Billy Wdwards repeatedly
beat Sam Collyer; Fitzsimmons has twice
defeated Peter Maher, who, in turn, has
three times vanquished Steve O'Donnell.
George Dixon has again defeated Johnny
Griffen. There are, however, hg be prey to
the rule, Tom Allen was easily defeated in
his first fight with Charley Gallagher, whom
he, in turn, conquered in their second bat-
tie. Jack Dempsey whipped La Blanche, the
Marine, {n their first fight, but was pivoted
“out” when they met the second time. L
presume ‘‘Fisticus’’ is squinting at the
at? probable result of a second meeting between

4 Corbett and Fitzsimmons in asking his

question. Where the men have fought 10 or

a dozen rounds evenly in a first encounter,

| if I were a bookmaker, I would, as a rule,
lay & to 4 on the winner for choice in a
second encounter. I believe by so doing IL
would ‘‘win out’ seven times in ten,

At the present writing there seems to be
a@ precious small chance of Fitzsimmons and

J Corbett ever coming together again, Fitz

knows in his heart that he was a very
Jucky man in that encounter, and he natur-
ally hesitates to tempt fate again. Asa win-
ner, he isn’t as popular as Corbett is as a
loser, As a matter of fact, Jim seems to
| have gained friends by the fact that he was
unfortunate in the battle. In the fight he
demonstrated beyond the cavil of a doubt
that he is ‘‘n dead game man."’ There were
a good many who doubted this before this
battle, Men who did not take kindly to Jim
before now sympathize with him in his mis-
fortune. Fitz is not a popular champion.
What the American people want in a fistic

‘ idol is a fellew who is ready and willing at

: all times to meet all comers, as Sullivan
was before he broke his arm on Patsy
Cardiff, His willingness to fight even men
like Alf Greenfield, with only ‘ta shave and
a shampoo” training, gave him a dare-
devil reputation that endeared him to the
masses, and made them blind to his mani-
fold faults. Fighters who claim to be
“champions” and then tell fellows who
want a crack at them to “go get_a reputa-
tion” will never rival the “Big Fellow” in
popular favor, By the way, it was Charley
Mitchell, 1 helieve, who first employed this

shrase. That was in a billiard-room ing San

4 Francisco, when Jack Dempsey shook a

fieht at him, Sulllvan afterwards asked it,
and so did ‘Corbett, and now Fitz is poll-
parrotting it. It's a phrase that will not win
any respect for the man who employs it.

Y Kile Will Be an Actor.

I see that Fitz is to have a play written
for him by an old reporter of mine. Bob
hasn't a tithe of the intelligence of either
Sullivan or Corbett, and { wonder how he
will deport himself as an actor, By the
way, some of the seribes of to-day seem to
think tnat only the fighters of the present
date resorted to the stage aS a Means al
making money. This is a mistake. Many
of the old English fighters appeared in plays
(mainly as figureantes, however). Pierce
Evan wrote a’ play called “You and Jerry,
or Life in London,” and one of its scenes
represented ‘fom Cribb's Parlour.” When
it was originally produced the gallant Cribb.
J am told, appeared in it in prepria personna
and was an actor, too, for he gavé a toast,
“God bless ali on us."". Bou Caunt, Bendigo
and Freeman, the American Giant, also ape-
peared in plays. Cribb did a statue act in
his day, but Jem Mace was the first who

, ever made a feature of “Grecian Statu-
ary.” He was a model of the ideal Greek

Be. god in his day,

A friend of mine who had a talk with
John Il. Sullivan in Louisville last week,
tells that the big fellow is in dead earnest
jn challenging Fitzsimmons. Not that he
has the slightest idea that he would stand

; the ghost of a chance with ‘“Lanky Bob,”

‘ but that he believes that vitascopic pictures
of such a bout would give him a revenue
that would maintain him comfortably for
the rest of his life. Ne will hardly have a
chance to face Pitz. The latter sneers con-
temptuously at John I... and says that he
would be afraid to hit him as hard as he has
other men, for fear that he would kill him.

As the Hibernian said of the bull who
lost his life trying to butt a locomotive off
a bridge, so do I say to Steve O'Donnell,
“T like your spunk, but damn your judg-
ment.”” Steve had a third try at Peter
Maher this week, and it must be said for
him that he did « geod deat better than
he did before. He lasted six rounds this
time, and once put Maher on the floor. If
he keeps on fighting Peter and improving
with each encounter, there is a chance that
he may wallop him after 40 or § trials. I

3 am inclined to think that the “Irish Cham-

hy pion” let up @ bit on Steve. If he showed
Tis best form with him, I fear he is going
‘to have a hard time of it when he
faces Sharkey. By the way, I don't much
jike the look of the present status of that

roposed match, There is too much of what

Phe Trish call ‘‘colloquing’’ between the

? meo’s managers. I don’t blame them for
trying to get as big a purse as_ possible, |

ae put they are haggling too much, Why don’t

UPTOWN OFFICE——TE

a ee Sete Re at

I i DRS SERGE SS IEE SE ES

they ‘‘take a chance’ with some club, and |

box for a percentage of the gate. If as-
sured that the contest is to be strictly on
its merits and that each man is well and -
fit, the public will fill any arena in this
vicinity at good prices, Come now, Messrs.

Lynch and quinn. Get together and mean

‘*business.’’

George Dixon is a fistic marvel and no
mistake. A few months ago ft looked as
though he was “getting stale’ and going
back on his form,” but it seems “‘there are
others,”’ and the last one is Johnny Griffin
of Braintree. About a year ago Johnny was
of the opinion that if he could get well and
strong’ he could defeat Dixon easily. He
thinks differently now, I hope.

Dan Creedon has gone to England with old
Jem Mace, and he and “Kid McCoy are as
far apart in a match making sense as
though the latter was in South Africa.
They will probably .come : together in the
fall. Meanwhile the “Kid” is to become an
actor and speak in public on the stage.
Oh, the poor public! how it will suffer from
pugilistic stars the coming fall.

That a nrima donna should attempt to)
sing a difficult role while suffering from
all aggravated case of whooping cough.
would appear not only improbable, but quite
impossible. Yet that is the condition under
which Helen Bertram has been sing-
ing for four weeks at Uhrig’s Cave.
It was a wonderful effort on Miss

Bertram’'s part, and one that few)
singers would have made for any)
audience. It has grown to be a prima don- |
na’s prerogative to refuse to sing for any.
ailment from an aching corn to a misplaced |
curl. Certainly Miss Bertram would have |
been perfectly justified refusing to ap-
pear while suffering from such a distressing
if not dangerous malady, but she had been.
billed to appear, and the people expected to
see her, so she sang. In private Hfe, Miss
Bertram is Mrs. Ted Henley, and there is
a little one. After the manner of children, |
the little one contracted the whooping
cough, and while caring for her Miss Bert- |
ram Was unfortunate enough to catch the
disease. |

She applied most vigorous treatment, but.
it would not yield to sirup and gargles, and
Monday night Just previous to the perform-
ance Miss Bertram was whooping at period-
fe intervals. She was determined fo sing”
the role, however, and prepared for the
performance. During the show few people |
noticed her affliction. There were times, |
however, when she was obliged to stop.
short in the middle of a song, and those
in front could hear a suppressed whooping
sound. In an instant she recovered and
went blithely on. Behind the scenes her
Spare moments were spent in spraying her
throat and endeavoring to mitigate the se-
verity of the whoop.

Everyone knows the whooping sound from
which the cough takes its name, but few
which is “the best man.” In the language
of the slums, “they are out for the stuff,”
and there is no boxing club or syndicate of
sporting men in Ireland who will give half
as big 2 purse as can be obtained in this
country. In the seeond place, if there was
such a club or syndicate, the fight would

not be permitted in “the old dart.” The
most famous fight ever held on “the Cur-
ragh of Kildare’ was the one between Dan
Donnelly and George Cooper, and their prize
was a purse of {(), a measly $00. Imagaine
Maher and Sharkey boxing for 10 times that
amount, if you can. They are both “true
born sons of the sod’ and opal ees too;
but not to that extent, and they would be
foolish if they were.
Dan Stuart Is a Hustler.

Dan Stuart is a marvelous man. He came
into pugilism without experience or any
flourish of trumpets, and yet, by dint of per-

severance and a lavish expenditure of
money, he succeeded in doing what no one
before hicn could do; he brought Corbett and
Fitzsimmons together. It took him two
years to do this and cost him nearly $50,000.
It is now said that he contemplates again
bringing them together. This time he pro-
poses holding another fistic tournament in
Carson City, but at a season of the year
when the meteorological conditions will be
pleasanter for visitors than they were last
March. I know that Corbett is fairly ach-
ing for another chance at Fitz, and I know
| that he believes that if he can get it he will
regain the laurels that Fitz took from his
brow. It will take a lot of persuasion to get
Fitz into a ring with Jim again. He can
make no money by exhibiting himself, how-
ever. He claims thatt even his exhibition
with John L. Sullivan, at Ambrose Park, on
the bth of July, netted him a dead loss of
$300. He is having a very pleasant summer
at his cottage at Rye Beach, but when a
man’s outgo is steady and large and his in-
come nothing, one doesn’t have to be much
of a mathematician to figure out just how
og a moderate-sized bank account will
ast.

A fresh match between Corbett and Fitz
would create great interest wherever the
English tongue is spoken. Not long since I
saw it stated as an evidence of the isolation
of the Klondike gold region that the miners
who left it with their “piles’’ for civiliza-
tion only learned of the result of the Fitz-
Corbett fight and that MeKinley had been
elecfed President of the United States when
they reached Sitka. If Fitz and Jim fight
the betting will favor the Cornishman, I
have no doubt. If so, will takers of the
short end win again?

Corbett Making Biz Money.
Corbett is a very active man nowadays.
He is making good, big money (a thousand
dollars a week, on an average), playing
baseball, and this week he won a bicycle
race at Asbury Park. I hear that. Billy
Brady intends utilizing Jim's well-known
skill as a handball player as a means of
money-making this fall. But for the fact
that Jim doesn’t like football, he might be
seen on the gridiron this winter. I had
quite a chat with him last Sunday evening,
and though he isn’t as “‘chipper’’ as he was
when he was champion, he is in splendid
health, and he told me that he never before
was so strong in his life.
Several champions have essayed to be-
come actors after having gained fame in
the ring, among them John L. Sullivan,
Peter Jackson and Jim Corbett, but it is
seldom that an actor doffs the sock and
buskin for the gloves. Billy Elmer, the Cal-
ifornia Thespian, who has done this, seems
to be even better as a fighter than he was
as a mummee. He has won several good
battles with tough men, and he should be
quite a craze here in the East this winter.
Kid McCoy’s ideas of what constitutes
genuine charity to the striking miners di?-
fers very materially from that held by some
other boxers on charitable occasions, He
demands that all the receipts of his bout
with Jim Freany, which takes place in Cin-
cinnati next Monday night, shall go to the
strikers,and Freany is ‘‘willin’.”". I remember
a big .boxing benefit which was given in
this city once upon a time for the aid of
a fund to furnish free bread to the worthy
poor. It was a big affair, but Charley
Mitchell, one of the ‘‘champions’’ who ap-
peared, got $1,200 for his services, I think
MecCoy’s way the best.
Allen and Joe Goss.
| I met a gentleman the other day who
said: “I read what you had to say in your
letter last week about fighters liking each
other after they had contested in a ring.
You might have given many more incidents
than you did. No two men ever hated each
other worse than Tom Hyer and Yankee
Sullivan did for years, and yet when Sulli-
van fought John Morrissey and was ar-
rested for his participation in the battle, it
| was Hyer who found the bondsman for him,
John Heenan and Tom Sayers became the
warmest of friends after their famous bat-
tle at Fausborough. John Morrissey went
all the way to England to coach Sayers, and
tell him how to whip Heenan, and yet he
and Heenan became very warm friends a
few years thereafter. If I mistake not, it
was Morrissey who set Heenan up in busi-
| ness in New York City. Even in the ring old
enmities are ofttimes forgotten. I remem-
ber a special incident of this kind. It took
place in Kentucky, not far from Cincinnati,
the day that Joe Goss and Tom Allen had
their famous fight. Allen, who saw that his
life was in danger at the hands of the men
back of Goss purposely struck Joe a foul
blow as the best means of getting out of
the dirty mess he was in, For appearance
sake, when a claim of ‘foul’ was made
against him, Allen faintly denied it, when
Goss spoke up: ‘Thee did strike me foul,
Tom,’ said he, ‘but thee didn’t mean to.
Coom on, let’s foight it out.’ I thought that |
that was as chivalrous a speech as ever I
heard one enemy make to another. It didn’t.
avail, though, for the referee, much to Al-
len’s delight, I have no doubt, declared that
Goss was the winner.’’ I remember this oc-
currence well.
MACON McCORMICK.
summary: The St. Louis Republic published a column recounting Tom Allen's famous fight with Joe Goss in Kentucky. Allen deliberately struck a foul blow to escape a dangerous situation, and Goss magnanimously suggested they continue fighting.

A VERY QUEER MINISTER.
One Who Believes in Boxing, but Who
Is Opposed to Football.

In a sermon at Indianapolis Sunday a
Methodist minister roasted football and up-
held pugilistic encounters. He had this to
say of McCoy’s performance there:

“Now for Mr. ‘Kid’ McCoy's exhibition.
Two men at a time were pitted — each
other, both wearing gloves of the bulk of
small pillows, boxing according to well un-

| derstood rules, under the eye of a man of
courage and vigilance; no foul play; every-
thing being fair and in full view; nobody
hurt; no doctors; nobody killed or crippled.
It is said that the show was the real thing.
If prize fighting was meant it was not ‘tbe
| real thing.’ The real thing is a fight to a
) finish with the naked fists, such fights as
Mike McCool and Tom Allen and John Mor-
rissey, John €. Heenan and Jen Mace used
| to indulge in, which were clear kin to the
present college football game, but which
| bore little or no resemblance to the ‘set-
| tos’ at Tomlinson Hall. I have no apology
| to make for witnessing that exhibition. It
| Was a manilier and cleaner show than one-
| half of the football games we have had in
| this city during the last ten years, and I
| believe I have seen them all, Football is
|a manly game, and when played by gentie-
men, and no others spoute play it, it is an
interesting exhibition. If the friends of the
game wish to save it from disrepute they
could get some useful hints by studying the
| methods of such professors of the manly
| art of self-defense ag ‘Kid’ McCoy, Samuel
| Murbarger and Dec Payne."
summary: The St. Louis Post-Dispatch quoted an Indianapolis Methodist minister who referenced Tom Allen's bare-knuckle fights favorably when comparing them to modern football games.

title: Death of Boxer Smith Causes Sensation
text:
The announcement of the death of Smith
will cause something of a sensation in
local and foreign pugilistic circies. He was
one of the best known pugilists in America
and had fought the best men of his day.
His greatest fight was with Joe Goddard
before the Olympic Club of New Orieans.
They met there March 32, 1893, for a $10,400
pee and after 18 rounds of fierce fighting
Smith put Goddard to sleep. Smith, in a
fight at Chicago, nearly wound up the
career of Peter Jackson and he did himself
proud in other battles. His brotner Paddy
Smith, made his home in St. Louis for a
long while. When Griffo flunked that night
in. the Coliseum ‘t was Paddy Smith who
took his place and who so pluckily faced
the drives of the better trained man,
Tommy Tracy. Beth the Smith boys were
born pugilists and of happy-go-lucky dispo-
sition. Both were fond of liquor and Ed's
weakness in this direction yzot him in
troub.e ofien. He was a greut friend of
Tom Allen, and it was the latter who
coached him when he beat Goddard at New
Orleans.

Allen said this morning: “Swift was one
of the gamest fighters that ever entered
the ring. But he was hardly big enough
for the heavyweights of this*day. When
he met Goddard he wetghed abour 160 to
Goddard's 180. Had he had the weight he
would have reached the top in no time.
He was an old friend of mine and I used
to hear from him often until recently."

New York, Dee. 15.—Poor old Paddy Ryan
is dead to the world at last. Pugilistically
he has been “a dead one’ for many years.
Ne was in his forty-eighth year and should
have been in the meridian of manhood

Paddy came to this country when but a
slip of a boy, and was raised in West Troy
Within a mile of the spot where John ©.
Hleenan, “The Benicia Koy,” first sow the
light of day, and just across the Hudson
River from where John Morrissey passed
his early boyhood. Paddy grew up to be a
line specimen of physical manhood, standing
six feet in his stockings und weighing in
the neighborhood of 200 pounds. He passed
& good deal of his boyhood in the vicinity
of the “Birst Lock” in West Troy, and had
many an eneounter there with the tough
citizens who navigated the waters of the
erie Canal ‘The Canallers” were, as a
rato, brawny fellows, aud among them the
rile “might makes right” prevailed very
extensively, Before he was 2l Paddy lke
the here of the old seng

“Could handle any man on the Canawl.”

There are many “tips” in and about Troy
and Ryan secon beeame their fistic idol.

Shortly after Johnny Dwyer of Brooklyn
became champion of America by defeating
Jimmy Elfiett (Yourg Grayback) he cnade
# sparring tour through the country, oc-
companted by his friend and trainer Joe
Goss. Among the places visited was Troy.
The duo attracted much attention, and
there was considerable talk of matching
Ryan against the champion. This talk re-
eulted in the making of a match between
Dwyer and Ryan for $2.000, to take place in
the summer of IS7S. Shortly after Ryan was
enige sed to give a boxing exhibitlon in
Brooklyn with Joe Goss as his sparring
| partner. The men were on hand, but owing
to a disagreement with the promoter ef the
affair over flnanees they did net spar. On
their way back to New York they were
assaulted by a gang of Dwyer's adherents
on lower Pulton street in Brooklyn. Dur-
| ing the melee Ryan was severely stabbed
and ruptured. Paddy was carried into the
siloon of Charley Johnson (whe afterwar is
Was one of the backers of Jonn L. Sulli-
Van against Kilrainy). It was found that,
though his injuries were very severc, they
Were vet fatal, and under proper inedical
care he soun was able to be up and about,
but ever alter he was compelled to wear a
truss.

Willing to Postpone Fight.

This melee ended the match between Ryan
and Dwyer, though the latter offered to
postpone the date of the fight for a reason-
able length of time to enable Kyan to re-
cover from his lujuries.

Paddy's next tstic match was with Joe
Goss, who at one time had figured ag the
American champion, he having been de-
elared the victor over Tom Allen in a fight
Which took plaice in Kentucky not far from
Cincinnati.

Allen had the best of this encounter, but
purpusely struck Goss three foul blows In
the last round in order to save his own life,
he belleving, and I think justly, that he
would have been killed had he won, as a
fang, numbering among others “Red” Leary,
the bank robber, Johnny Dwyer and several
others, were determined to do him up be-
cause they claimed that Alien had given
away some of thelr pals to the police in
England some time before. Goss had been
imported especially from England for the
purpose of fighting Allen.

Rsan and Goss met near Collier's Station,
W. Va... on the Zist of June, 188). They
fought efghty-three rounds, lasting one hour
and twenty-four minutes, when Ryan was
declared the victor. Goss was stale at the
time, but while he had strength and fresh-
wess he far outclassed Ryan in skill and
fistie ability,

Kyan made a tour of the Eastern States
after becoming charapion, and at Springfield
he met, for the first time, John Sullivan,
who was then known as “The Strong Boy of
the Highlands.” Sullivan had attained con-
siderable local reputation by virtually knock-
ing out Joe Goss at a benefit for the latter
given in a Boston theater. Sully wanted to
spar with Ryan, but was contemptuously re-
fused the privilege, Ryan sneeringly dub-
bing him “a would-be fighter."

When I first met Sullivan in Boston,
shortiy after this, he told me he was willing
to fight any man in the world, adding, “‘L
would like to get a chanee at Paddy Ryan.
1 went all the way to Springtield to box him
for nothing, but he wouldn't give me a
chance.”

I said to him: “Well, yeu come to Cincin-
nati for me, and if you make a good show-
ing there—enough to justify me in doing se—
I'll see that you get a chance to fight Ryan.’

Sullivan came to Cincinnati fer me and
boxed John Donaldson (who was murdered a
few years age in Cleveland). He so far out-
classed Donaldson that I saw he had cham-
pionship timber in bim. 1 pronounced him
the coming “champion of America’ and
wrote for him a challenge to Rvan, which
brought about a match between them and a
fight which took plece at Mississippi City,
on the line of the railroad between New Or-
leans and Mobile. This fight took place on
the 7th of February, Iss2, thirty-three years
to a day after Tom Hyer had defeated Yan-
kee Sullivan for the American championship.

Sullivan Offends the Sports.

When John Suiivan went to New Orleans

perate young man. He met Pat Duly; and

Though at that time Sullivan was the
perfection of paysical manheod, the press

ing physician examine him, who promeunced
him a veritatle eross between Hercules and
Apollon. [ visited Ryan at his training

plained of being treuble with diarreea
saw that he was roenially werried; in faet,

On the arriyil of tne train conveying the

Sullivan, on the ether hand. was brim full
of confidence and animai spirits.

The fight was a very fierce one, Sullivan
geing at his man with ereat vigor, and
flooring Paddy repeatedly. In one of the
early rounds of the fight the men clinched
and struggied for a fall (this oattl wus
fought with dare knuckles, under Lenden
prize ring rules, and wrestling was per-
mitted). Paddy, in endeavoring to get an
under hold, compressed his waist, and his
truss slipped down, incommoeding him bad-
ly thereafter. There was only one-half
minute intermission between the rounds in
those days. and Ryan had no chance to re-
place his truss properiy.

Only once was Sullivan in danger, and
that was when Ryan hit him with great
severity on the neck. “Come away. John'
Come away, John!” shouted Goss, who was
Sullivan's principal-second. Instead of tak-
ing this advice, Sullivan wisely clinched and
hung onte Ryan. with his head across his
(Ryan's) shoulders, until the effect of ‘he
blow had passed away. Then he straight-
ened up, pushed right away from him, and
sent him to the grass with a blow which
would have felled an ox.
